Haydar Amoli will remind us, in a major work, of what Shiism and Sufism share: the relationship between prophecy and walayat, between religious law (sharia) and its spiritual meaning, and between the outward (zahir) and the inward (batin). We shall return to this in Book Four, Chapter One.

Yet it is precisely here that their differences also appear. Twelver Shiism, and Shiite spiritual knowledge in particular, has sought to maintain the balance and simultaneous presence of outward and inward meaning, of symbol and what it symbolises. Certain forms of Sufism, by contrast, have often disturbed that balance.

One sign of this imbalance lies in the importance Sufi orders give to their shaykh, or spiritual teacher. The shaykh may be treated as the qutb, the spiritual “pole,” and effectively recognised as the Imam's visible embodiment and successor. A Shiite Sufi teacher such as Sa'd al-Din Hamuyi (died 650 AH / 1252 CE) could have a particularly deep devotion to the Twelfth, Hidden Imam. But in other circumstances, devotion to the shaykh may diminish the significance of the Hidden Imam himself.

For a Shiite whose spirituality centres on the Imam, that is intolerable. It amounts to a kind of usurpation, often accompanied by excessive devotion to the shaykh. More importantly, it violates the spiritual situation created by the Imam's occultation (ghayba)—his withdrawal from ordinary human sight—which is to continue until the end of our present age. Paradoxically, Sufism can then appear to turn the deepest spiritual truths of Shiism into something dependent on a visible human figure.

In this way Sufism would tend to remove the teaching about the Imams altogether. In Sunni Sufism, that is ultimately what happens.

But the balance between outer and inner meaning can be preserved only through the corresponding balance between prophecy and walayat: between the understanding of prophets and the understanding of Imams. The balance is destroyed when the particular spiritual gifts of the Imam are simply transferred to the Prophet. Without a place for the Imam, an authentic understanding of God's oneness—tawhid, the recognition of the One beyond all others—also becomes impossible. Such understanding must avoid two opposing dangers: ta'til, which empties the idea of God into a distant, unknowable abstraction, and tashbih, which makes God too much like a human being. We shall return to both in Chapters Six and Seven.

Now we can see why a Shiite spiritual seeker may regard a Sunni Sufi as someone who has forgotten their own origins. We can also see why that same Shiite might worry that even Shiite Sufism threatens something deeply precious. The Shiite seeker does not necessarily need Sufism, its organised orders, or its shaykhs. Through a personal inward bond with the holy Imams, that person is already travelling a spiritual path, without needing the path to take the visible form of a Sufi order. Their words may sound exactly like those of a Sufi, yet they may belong to no Sufi order at all. Mulla Sadra Shirazi could even write a fairly severe treatise against the Sufis of his own day.

Once we understand this, we may stop misreading major Sufis such as Hallaj, or the relationship between Hallaj and Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi. We misunderstand both the meaning and the place of spiritual knowledge in Islam when we insist that Hallaj was simply a faithful Sunni with no connection to it. This is a Western way of seeing things, barely concealing a wish to defend a particular theological position. It decides in advance that the texts must show Hallaj and Ibn Arabi to be opposites—as though Ibn Arabi were a “monist,” believing that reality is ultimately one, while Hallaj were not.

In truth, either both were monists or neither was. If we use the Western philosophical term monism in its precise sense, neither was. Ruzbihan of Shiraz remains our best guide to understanding Hallaj; Ibn Arabi, in turn, was in a better position than we are to understand what was at stake. Neither Hallaj nor Ibn Arabi sought to “go beyond” Islam or leave it behind, any more than Ghazali did when he worked to bring the mystical life into Sunni Islam. They lived through Islam and brought its hidden spiritual power into actual life. What they did go beyond was a purely legal, social, and political understanding of Islam—an understanding that would, in fact, be the death of its spiritual life.

A Shiite spiritual thinker is particularly well placed to understand Hallaj's tragedy, his preoccupation with the figure of Iblis, and the complexity of Ibn Arabi's life and work. Haydar Amoli will remind us of this again. If Christian teachings about Christ become relevant to our discussion, it is not because Hallaj secretly converted to some Christian “religion of the Cross.” It is because the Shiite teaching about the Imams plays a role in Shiite theology comparable to the role played by teachings about Christ in Christian theology.

Shiite thinkers have often drawn parallels between the Imam and Jesus. For example, Jesus is described as the Seal of the walayat that begins with Adam; the First Imam as the Seal of universal walayat; and the Twelfth Imam as the Seal of the walayat associated with Muhammad. This helps explain those extraordinary sermons in which the Imam calls himself “the second Christ.” We shall also encounter the dreams of the Twelfth Imam's mother in Book Seven.

Whenever Shiite thought about the Imams has faced questions like those faced by Christian thought about Christ, it has tended to adopt answers resembling positions rejected by the Christian councils. But the comparison also shows how flimsy a common theological classification really is: the attempt to divide all religious experience into “natural” and “supernatural” theology or mysticism.

It is far too convenient to lump together under “natural mysticism,” or “Yoga-type mysticism,” spiritual teachings that have little in common. In this scheme, “natural” mysticism means a person trying to unite with an impersonal Absolute, or impersonal Self, through their own powers. “Supernatural” theology, concerned with divine grace, supposedly offers another kind of relationship. However worthy the religious aims behind this division may be, Islamic divine wisdom—irfan and hikmat—has a range of thought and practice broad enough to reject so simple a split.

The Islamic idea of prophecy and the prophetic mission, which does not mean “predicting the future,” certainly cannot be reduced to the model of Yoga. It embraces the whole line of prophets found in the Bible and sees that line continued in Muhammad, who was so deeply attentive to the earlier scriptural revelations. If “natural” religion means a human effort to achieve salvation by one's own strength, neither the prophetic gift nor the spiritual gift of the Imams depends on such effort.

That is precisely why Shiite theology insists that, although people can choose a head of state or establish a religious office, they cannot elect a prophet or an Imam. The very idea is absurd. Nor does a meeting with the Hidden Imam—a form that an unexpected encounter with divine help or grace can take in Shiism—come about simply through human effort. It is no more a union with an impersonal Self than prophecy is. The very meanings of “natural” and “temporal” are transformed.

Through meditation on the Qur'an, Shiite spiritual thinkers are able to embrace the whole cycle of prophecy and religion. Even the Greek sages, for example, are said to have received their wisdom from the “niche of lights” of prophecy. These traditions form the “six days” in which the religious cosmos is created, and these thinkers know that a seventh day will come.

By contrast, is it unfair to speak of the difficulties that official Christian thought has faced in creating a theology of religions broad enough to recognise the sacred book in its full reality, even when that revelation takes the form of the Qur'an? Why raise questions like this? Because in our time we can no longer honestly avoid them. They arise inevitably as soon as we ask, as we are doing here, what we have to learn from Iranian philosophers and spiritual teachers, and what we might do with them and for them. How could we discuss the “spirituality of Iranian Islam” while remaining silent about all this?

At the centre of Islam in its fullest spiritual sense lies the tension between sharia—religious law and the outward duties of faith—and haqiqa, the inward spiritual truth: the deeper understanding of scripture and the discovery of hidden meanings belonging to higher levels of existence and awareness. Both sides are essential. I believe this is entirely true to the outlook of the spiritual sages of Twelver Shiism. Remove either side, and the fullness of Islamic religious life disappears.

Haqiqa is the inner truth of the outward religion, which it therefore presupposes. It is not a licence to do whatever one likes in the name of spiritual freedom. If something is forbidden, discovering its deeper meaning does not make it permitted: the inner meaning of what is forbidden remains connected to a real prohibition. Conversely, religious law without inner spiritual truth is not thereby “saved.” It becomes an empty shell.

If the tension between the two is abolished by removing the inward dimension, we also lose the idea of the purely spiritual community held together by an invisible bond. Religious truth is then identified completely with a social system. And when the structure of traditional society begins to break apart, the very idea of religion is thrown into crisis.

To bring these introductory reflections to a close, I shall turn in the next section to a moving example of what happens when spiritual life is absorbed into society in a Sunni Muslim setting. It leads us to ask whether the situation in Shiite Islam might be different.

At first sight, one essential difference stands out. In Shiism, walayat and the Imamate are understood as inseparable from prophecy and as its necessary continuation. The prophetic mission and the Imamate of the Twelve arise together. In the Shiite understanding, the Imamate is the original and enduring support of haqiqa: the spiritual truth that gives sharia its life. It keeps interpretation of the Qur'an open to other worlds of meaning, as we shall see in Chapters Four and Five, and it keeps that interpretation open to the future.

Without the Imamate, by contrast, any search for haqiqa loses its footing. It lacks a guide and a point of reference by which to steer between the twin dangers of ta'til and tashbih: an agnostic rationalism that leaves God unknowable, and a naive tendency to imagine God in human form.

Let me make this clearer. The Imams are no longer physically present in this world. Their authority cannot even be compared with the often ambiguous authority of a visible “spiritual power” that can place demands on human souls. What matters is their spiritual presence: the Imam as an inward guide to consciousness, and, at the highest level, as the figure who shapes the horizon of our understanding of reality. That is what it means to call the Imam the Guide, the Pole, and the Witness. We shall return to this in Chapter Seven.

In the new world now taking shape, with more and more of the marks of an age of iron, the Prophet's religion risks being stifled and destroyed only if it is forcibly cut off from its spiritual truth and the interpretation that keeps that truth alive. The Imams repeatedly warned against the error of reducing scripture to the time of its revelation. If every Qur'anic verse meant only what it meant for the people and events to which it first referred, the whole Qur'an would already be dead, nothing but a record of the past.

But the Book is alive because its events continue to unfold within human souls, right up to Yawm al-Qiyama, the Day of Resurrection. Its living meaning cannot be tied to one moment of history or to the social order of any particular time and place. Only people who live by the spirit can understand, perceive, and say this. To say that sharia can survive only through haqiqa is to say that spiritual truth alone can bring about the changes needed to keep religion alive, rather than allowing politics and social pressures to distort and suffocate it.

The danger is not confined to Islam. Every religion, Christianity included, risks surrendering its spiritual life to social concerns and institutions. The danger begins within us, when people abandon their own spiritual responsibility and allow themselves to become part of that surrender. Confusing religion with society is hardly a new mistake. Those who will withstand it are not people searching for compromises with “their age,” but those strong enough to become shuhada: witnesses who speak against their age, bearing witness to another world—and to a world that is different even here. To announce that other reality is the heart of the prophetic message.

Neither people nor books can manufacture witnesses like these. But we can at least ask the questions that matter. Will there be, tomorrow, people capable of carrying the inner truth of Islam, so that the meaning of a purely spiritual Islam—one that has nothing to do with the schemes and ambitions of politicians—can become visible in our world?

That question speaks especially to Shiism. At the beginning of its religious year, the remembrance of the tragedy of Karbala is a continuing protest against the powers of this world. And Shiism's hope for the return of the Hidden Imam, which shapes its spiritual life, shows that this question has confronted it from its beginning. Will Shiism still be able to make its voice heard tomorrow, as it did when only a handful of believers stood beside the Imams? We shall return to this in Chapter Three.

4. Problems We Must Face Together

I have just spoken about what happens when spiritual life is absorbed into social life, and about the effects this has on a traditional culture. These effects place a heavy responsibility on everyone who refuses to take part in what, more than a generation ago, was rightly called “the betrayal of the intellectuals.” We hear that expression less often today. Yet surely the betrayal cannot be allowed to become final.

In the West, we have come to realise that many of our social and political ideologies are really forms of theology that have lost their religious character. They grew out of earlier systems of theological thought, but removed the message of a world beyond this one. However far human hopes may reach, they no longer pass beyond death.

We can see this change particularly clearly when religious hopes for a saving figure and a final renewal of the world become hopes for nothing more than social transformation. Once our vision of the end of history has been stripped of its religious meaning, what remains is a story about the supposed “direction of history.”

This did not happen overnight. It was a long process. Turning religion into something secular does not simply mean replacing religious authorities with worldly rulers. The very idea of a “spiritual power” made into institutions and exercised as a form of power is already a step towards turning the spiritual into something worldly and social. That process begins when every form of spiritual knowledge is attacked, as happened for centuries. By cutting itself off from gnosis—knowledge of spiritual realities reached through direct understanding—the institutional Church failed to see that it was preparing the way for an age of agnosticism and a belief that only observable facts count as knowledge.

The authority of religious doctrine was simply replaced by the social authority of shared rules. The person once condemned as a “heretic” became someone accused of “deviation,” or simply someone said to be “maladjusted.” Individual religious experience and every kind of mystical life could now be explained away as a failure to fit into one's social environment. The automatic refusal to recognise what lies beyond ordinary knowledge prevents us from welcoming witnesses to “another world.”

It is painful to see how much of Christianity today is haunted by a particular fear: the fear of being seen as not belonging to “this world,” and therefore of not being taken seriously. People exhaust themselves trying to “keep up with the times,” proclaiming the “priority of social concerns,” and bringing themselves into line with supposed “scientific requirements.” In this frantic race, they lose sight of what matters most. Nikolai Berdyaev identified the tragedy: in its official historical forms, Christianity has given in to the very temptation that Christ rejected.

Yet these secular forms of theology are exactly what the West carries with it wherever it goes, along with the machinery of its material civilisation. By “the West,” I mean both what our newspapers call the West and what they call the East. Many people living in the geographical East are now “Western” in the sense I am using, sometimes more so than people in the geographical West who have not yet lost their bearings. But what happens when these imported ways of thinking reach societies that never had the earlier theological structures from which they developed?

The problem is especially serious for Islam, because Islam and Christianity share the foundations of a prophetic religion. Both honour the names and teachings of many of the same prophets. Yet, as I have noted more than once, the goal of Islamic philosophers and spiritual thinkers has been neither what we usually call theology nor exactly what we usually call philosophy. Their hikmat ilahiya is divine wisdom: a phrase whose two parts correspond directly to the Greek roots of theosophia.

In fact, we could say that separating theology from philosophy is itself the first sign that consciousness is becoming secular. In the West, that separation goes back to Latin scholastic thought, perhaps to Thomas Aquinas's Summa contra Gentiles. Theology becomes the territory reserved for an official “spiritual power,” while philosophy claims every freedom except the freedom to be theology. Here we see the first sign of a world in which even our understanding of reality loses its sacred character.

Divine wisdom, theosophia, is the opposite of that process and its antidote. It can be lived only through what these thinkers call knowledge of the heart (ma'rifat qalbiya), which is why that idea matters so much to Shiite philosophers of divine wisdom. In this way of knowing, theoretical understanding and spiritual experience cannot be separated. Only their union can turn everything a person learns and does into deeper understanding and awareness of the self. That may well be what people today need most.

We should not be surprised, then, that whenever Islamic divine wisdom has faced questions resembling those of Christian theology, it has tended towards answers close in spirit to certain forms of Christianity—particularly those forms pushed “to the margins of history,” to use a fashionable expression, by the decisions of official religious authorities. We have already seen an example of this in Shiite thought about the Imams.

We might now ask where the real dividing lines lie. Do they run between the established religions, or do people with similar spiritual outlooks find one another within those religions, sometimes without their institutions even noticing? Recognising these deeper connections would help us avoid serious misunderstandings. Well-meaning specialists working in another culture sometimes fail to see the inner collapse brought about when people are overwhelmed by ideas that did not grow out of their own experience. Nor do they understand the private ways in which others protect themselves, including their refusal to answer an investigator's intrusive questions. Recognising these connections would also help genuinely spiritual people see what unites them, understand the problems they share, and perhaps confront those problems together for the first time.

A few pages ago, we spoke of the tension between sharia and haqiqa: the outward requirements of revealed religion and its inner spiritual truth. We can shut ourselves inside the outward form and, by rejecting the inner truth, diminish even that outward form. Or we can devote ourselves to the inner truth and thereby preserve the full meaning of the outward practice. We have seen that this second approach lies at the heart of Twelver Shiism and the teaching of its Imams.

But the same tension belongs to what I have called the experience of having a sacred Book. It is familiar to all the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab). Judaism and Christianity, too, have traditions concerned with hidden spiritual meanings, and these have much in common with the seekers of inner knowledge in Islam.

It would be a fascinating undertaking—enormous in scale, with consequences we cannot foresee—to compare the place and history of these inner traditions in Islam and Christianity. We would have to go back to Gnosis, the search for saving spiritual knowledge. We would need to consider the teachings Christ gave his closest disciples, reread the recently recovered Gnostic Gospels with fresh eyes, and ask how certain Gospel passages and sayings, often quoted by Shiite and Ismaili writers, reached them through Gnostic channels or acquired a Gnostic colouring along the way. By “fresh eyes,” I mean approaching Gnosis without a prejudice against it. Ignorance cannot excuse every misunderstanding.

What we usually call “Gnosticism” would then appear as one expression of a much wider religious experience: gnosis, or knowledge that brings salvation. It is knowledge because it involves being initiated into a teaching. It brings salvation because the mystery of higher worlds, concealed beneath the words of divine revelations, cannot truly be disclosed or understood without a new birth in the person who receives it—a spiritual birth, called wiladat ruhaniya in Arabic.

We are still far from having gathered all the surviving writings and evidence of this wider Gnostic religious tradition into an accessible collection.

Yet seekers of spiritual knowledge, wherever and whenever they have lived, share another characteristic: they resist a faith based solely on historical evidence, what Latin calls fides historica. Such faith judges how real something is by whether documents can show that it existed physically in the past—or insists on reading documents as proof of that kind. It demands a securely established place in ordinary chronology, just as it would for any event or person in secular history.

That sort of faith belongs only to the outward person. Mystics have criticised it as fides mortua, a dead faith. There may even be a deep and troubling connection between faith understood in this narrowly historical way, the rise of the view that everything must be explained through history, and the decline of philosophy. Ultimately, there may be a connection between the dominance of this historical faith and the preparation or arrival of what became known as historical materialism.

We have already recalled a teaching repeated by several Shiite Imams: if the revelations of the sacred Book had only this kind of “historical meaning,” the whole Book would have died long ago. More precisely, they give the phrase historical meaning an entirely different sense. For them, it does not mean an outward event locked away in the past, buried with the people who died, and now interesting only to archaeologists. It means something that is fulfilled again and again in living people, right up to the Last Day. It concerns the inward person and events that are entirely real, although they do not occur on the physical level of existence. This is the inner meaning of scripture, and its truth does not depend on outward historical circumstances.

Around this living meaning of the sacred Book, we find spiritual families coming together across different places and periods. On the Christian side, we would need to study the figures known as the Spirituals of Protestantism: Sebastian Franck, Valentin Weigel, and Caspar Schwenckfeld; the circles shaped by Jacob Boehme's teachings on divine wisdom, and later by Swedenborg's Arcana Caelestia; and thinkers such as Oetinger, together with the Christian Kabbalists, whose work cannot be separated from Jewish Kabbalah.

On the Islamic side, we would need a systematic account of how the Qur'an has been interpreted in search of its spiritual meaning. That story begins with the Imams themselves, continues through Ismaili and Twelver Shiite thought, and includes the great Qur'anic commentaries of sages and mystics such as Ruzbihan, Ibn Arabi, Semnani, Haydar Amoli, and Mulla Sadra Shirazi. It reaches as far as the Shaykhi school, which we will meet again in Chapters IV and V. So far, time has allowed me to make only a beginning on this kind of comparative study of spiritual interpretation.9

If we pursued it more deeply, we would begin to see both what the worlds beyond our senses have in common and what their interpretation reveals about the inward human being. We would discover shared features of the inner traditions based on prophecy—and, unfortunately, shared features among their opponents, too. These may be religious lawyers and scholars of the Law, the fuqaha, or figures like the Grand Inquisitor portrayed by Dostoevsky.

We will meet their counterparts again when we consider the return of the Twelfth Imam in Book VII.

By learning to share this understanding of the sacred Book, we could begin to understand the problems we face together and find a language in which to address them. Earlier, I mentioned a small Shiite study circle in Tehran that I had the pleasure of joining, year after year, during my autumn visits. Its central figure was Shaykh Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i, a professor of traditional philosophy at the theological university in Qom.10 The group also brought together some colleagues from Iran's new university, several religious teachers, and a number of their students who represented the traditional culture.

I repeatedly noticed how readily these friends understood the situations and questions arising from an inward reading of the Bible. Some passages by Meister Eckhart and Jacob Boehme, translated into Persian, and even episodes from our legends of the Holy Grail, seemed to speak a language very close to their own. The same could not be said of the ways we in the West try to explain our present situation. Our methods of argument, our social analysis, and our attempts to describe events in the language of cybernetics are not immediately accessible to Eastern friends who still have the privilege of living fully within their inherited culture.

More seriously, our way of viewing the present hardly seems to interest them. To them it is only natural that people should drift towards chaos after losing their spiritual centre—their “polar dimension”—and becoming unable to see any higher or vertical order except as a social relationship of power and domination. Our own questioning and protest are themselves called into question. And that is precisely where a shared problem may begin.

Westerners must accept responsibility for the consequences of a situation no one asked them to create. They must produce their own antidote to it.

But they can do so only if they understand what they have brought about, including disasters of the kind described in the moving testimony I will quote shortly. They must learn to value what they are in the process of destroying, and at last understand why those who remain its guardians value it so deeply.

Sometimes we face problems of translation that seem impossible to resolve. Words such as laicisation, secularisation, materialisation, socialisation, and evolutionism cannot simply be carried over into Persian or Arabic. We have to use longer explanations, give familiar words new meanings, or invent unfamiliar terms. Yet none of these methods produces in our Eastern listeners quite the same feelings and associations that those words awaken in us. This remains true even of friends who seem thoroughly “Westernised.”

The fact that we lack a shared vocabulary for our most urgent problems—and that it can be equally hard to translate the rich philosophical language of Shiite thinkers into our own languages—shows that we lack a common spiritual “past.” I do not mean shared outward events. I mean a shared experience of the inward person and the worlds of the soul: an experience that takes place in the soul's own time, the time of its unfolding story.

That story develops as the inner meanings of the sacred Book come alive within a person. It is not a one-way sequence of events that can never recur. We saw that the Imams refer to this story when they explain ta'wil, the practice of uncovering scripture's spiritual meaning. Western spiritual writers are speaking of the same kind of experience. In this time of the soul, we can bring about something that genuinely happens between us. A shared spiritual reading of the sacred Book can be its starting point.

Unfortunately, our own spiritual thinkers are still little known to these Eastern friends. What they have heard of Christianity comes largely from missionaries and defenders of the faith—or, more overwhelmingly, from the modern ideas that have spread out of post-Christian societies, turning older religious mysteries into worldly doctrines. The Christianity supposedly “driven out of history,” yet kept alive by our spiritual writers in the history of their own souls, remains almost unknown to them. When we introduce it, they welcome it warmly, as the examples above suggest.

But most people still fall back on the tired contrast between Western machines and technology on the one hand, and Eastern spiritual tradition on the other.

That is why I want to end these opening reflections by showing why we sometimes need to reverse this oversimplified contrast, particularly if we are to overcome the same dangers together. I shall set two striking testimonies side by side. The first comes from Nikolai Berdyaev, a representative of the Christian philosophy of Russian Orthodoxy. Our Eastern friends generally know little about that philosophy, although it is much closer to their thinking than our political and social ideologies are. Few people have protested more clearly than Berdyaev against the danger of allowing collective social life to swallow up the life of the spirit.

The second testimony comes from a Sunni Arab public figure. It shows the dead end to which an excessive drive to become Western can lead.

Berdyaev's fearless originality makes him impossible to place in any one school, apart from the tradition of divine wisdom associated with Jacob Boehme, to which he often explicitly declared his allegiance.11 His whole body of work develops the central theme of The Meaning of the Creative Act. It goes beyond an angry protest: it is a revolt against an age “in which sociological consciousness has replaced theology [...]. The domination of social life over modern consciousness weighs like a nightmare; this outward social world conceals and extinguishes every authentic reality.”12

For, as he writes, “In every age, mysticism has discovered the world of the inward person and set it against the world of the outward person.” What mystical experience revealed was that the human being is a microcosm: a whole world in miniature. This is also one of the great themes of Islamic mystical wisdom.

Yet it is precisely what a purely social and supposedly scientific view of human life ignores or rejects. Such a view breaks the human being's connection with the cosmos.

And we should not confuse this connection with space travel. Today's rockets and satellites cannot restore what has been broken. There is a Threshold to cross, and no rocket or satellite can ever cross it. Once the connection is broken, all that remains is a rather pitiful individualism, helpless in the face of collective pressure and demands for conformity. The mystic, by contrast, carries a whole universe within and can stand in balance with the world outside.

This is the paradox of mystical experience: going deeply into oneself is also a liberation from oneself, a movement beyond one's boundaries. For “all mysticism teaches that the depths of the human being are more than human, that a mysterious bond with God and the world lies hidden there. It is within oneself that one finds the way beyond oneself.”13 The bonds that hold us are broken through an inward work, “from within and not from without.”14

That conviction led Berdyaev to insist that “the human being studied by psychology is still only the outward person. The psychological is not the mystical. The inward person is spiritual, not merely psychological.”15 This distinction recalls the old Gnostic difference between those who live by the spirit and those who live only at the level of the soul. It is central to his thought, because it shapes how the mystic responds when living faith is turned into an external object, a system of beliefs.

“Religions,” he writes, “translate into knowledge and fixed forms of being what mysticism experiences and reveals directly. The dogmatic teaching of the universal Churches has been an objective translation of mystical experience as it was immediately lived [...]. Dogmas decline and die when they lose their mystical source, when they concern themselves with the outward person rather than the inward person, when the experience they express is physical and psychological rather than spiritual. Faith based on historical fact is the faith of the outward person, whose spirit has not reached down to the mystical sources. It is faith adapted to the physical level of existence.”16

We can now understand why I suggested an unsettling connection between the demands of strictly historical faith and the coming of an age dominated by historical materialism. The same theme runs through Berdyaev's Essay in Eschatological Metaphysics. “Christ rejected the temptation of the kingdoms of this world in the desert, but in the course of history Christians yielded to that temptation.” For Berdyaev, this is what happened when Christianity directed towards the last things gave way to Christianity adapted to the conditions of external history.17

From that point, the transformation of Christianity into something worldly had begun. We need to grasp this if we are to understand the secular forms of social messianism that appeared in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. We also need it to resist the claim that history possesses a fixed and unquestionable meaning. For such a meaning cannot be understood without a dimension beyond ordinary history—the “polar dimension” mentioned earlier, connecting human beings to a heavenly pole. And it is precisely this dimension that a strictly factual, socially focused view of the world removes from human awareness.

I have stressed this attempt to recover a mystical Christianity, oriented towards the final fulfilment of things, because Berdyaev's work suggests that Westerners may be able to produce an antidote to the damage done when Christianity is reduced to a social system. It is almost a kind of spiritual homeopathy. But what happens elsewhere, where the poison comes from outside and is therefore harder to recognise for what it is?

Islam, too, has always looked towards the final fulfilment of things, especially Shiite Islam. But can Islam now produce its own antidote to imported ideologies that are destroying the spiritual life it once possessed? This is the serious question already raised here, and it stands at the centre of the situation we must face together.

Consider, by contrast, the words of a prominent Muslim from Jordan, part of the Sunni Arab world. They were spoken in an interview some years ago, but I would not change a word, since the situation has, if anything, become more widespread and more severe. He said:

Because I live in the modern world and have received a Western education, I can imagine progress only outside tradition. Many of us in Jordan think this way and try to bring together things that cannot be reconciled. Like our Arab and Muslim brothers everywhere, when we begin to think seriously, we face a terrible inner conflict. Can we separate religion from a social system that scientific and technological progress has condemned, without killing God? In the Islam we know, religion and society are inseparable; neither exists without the other. Can we modernise without condemning ourselves to damnation?18

What makes this testimony so painful is the way a person's whole inner life has been taken over by an ideology to which that person cannot find an antidote, because its basic assumptions come from elsewhere. Here is a Muslim who takes pride in a Western education.

Yet the Western influence visible in his words contains nothing of the resistance expressed by Berdyaev in the passages we have just read. Quite the opposite: it comes from precisely the ideologies Berdyaev was opposing.

The first revealing statement is the slogan “live with your times.” Who will help this bewildered Muslim discover the awareness and strength to live in his own time—not the time imposed by an anonymous collective, but his personal time, the time in which his own existence unfolds? This is the time in which a teaching becomes true and meaningful through his own living commitment to it, not because it belongs to some date in the historical past or to the social arrangements of an earlier age.

Yet Islamic spiritual thinkers explained this distinction beautifully. They spoke of outward, historical time (zaman afaqi) and the time of the soul (zaman anfosi). They knew that a tradition can be passed on alive only in this second kind of time, because there it remains a continually renewed inspiration, not a funeral procession or a register of approved opinions. The life and death of spiritual things are our responsibility. We make them “things of the past” only when we give up on them and refuse the changes in ourselves that would keep them alive in the present.

The task is not to attempt “impossible syntheses.” It is to understand what spiritual thinkers have always understood, expressed in the saying of Imam Ja'far recalled earlier: “Islam began as a stranger, and it will become a stranger again. Blessed are the strangers!”

For spiritual thinkers, the danger of damnation—the danger of “killing God”—has never chiefly lain in separating spiritual life from social life. Strangely enough, they have seen it in confusing religion with a particular social system and treating the two as one. The separation at stake is more radical than merely distinguishing “spiritual power” from “temporal power.” As we observed earlier, as long as we speak of power and authority, we have already begun to turn spiritual life into a social institution. We are already somewhere on the path leading to Nietzsche's cry, “God is dead.” And we have just heard an unexpected echo of that cry on the lips of a Muslim.

So, only a few weeks after the interview appeared, we put a question to ourselves in our small Shiite study circle in Tehran: what would a Shiite have to say? What would someone say who truly lived Islam as Din-e Qiyamat, the religion of Resurrection?

The interview might indeed describe the tragedy of any form of Islam identified entirely with sharia, the religion of religious law and outward practice. But what if sharia is understood as only one half of religion in its fullness? What if the other, essential half is haqiqa: spiritual truth, the saving knowledge that is itself Resurrection (Qiyamat)?

There are profound differences between Arab Islam and Iranian Islam. We need not explore them all here. One of them, however, is the spiritual outlook that, at the time I am writing, helps protect Iranian Islam from being drawn into political passions and extreme racial or national feeling. This is why the universal meaning of Islam as a religion, beyond the boundaries of nations, is experienced and expressed with particular clarity in a country such as Iran.

What is certain is that the Jordanian speaker makes no mention at all of the two sides of religion represented by sharia and haqiqa. His education has probably left him quite unaware of the distinction. On one side is religion understood as Law: left to itself, it becomes no more than a social religion. On the other is spiritual religion, religion lived in truth, whose substance is the spiritual meaning of divine revelation. This meaning does not depend on any particular social order.

Even during the most severe upheavals of public life, a believer can remain faithful to the requirements of sharia, because observing them is a personal matter between that person and God. But this remains possible in its full sense only when outward practice is kept alive by haqiqa, the inner truth. Where, then, does that inner truth come from? What is its source?

As we discussed the interview among friends in Tehran, we came to see that this question goes to the very heart of Shiite spiritual life. It led us back to the foundations of Shiite philosophy and religious experience. What matters most is the role played by its understanding of prophecy and of the Imams. Together, these place Shiism at an equal distance from two positions: a religion reduced to outward rules and legal requirements, and the implications of the Christian doctrine that God became incarnate.

Shiism presents itself instead as a “straight path” (sirat mustaqim). On one side lies an abstract, rigidly unified idea of one God. On the other lies the kind of doctrine associated with the Church and its authority, which can become a worldly ideology: the idea that the divine is embodied in society itself, once theology gives way to thinking about religion solely in social terms.

Equally important is ghayba: the concealment of the Imam, his present invisibility. The hidden Imam points to a divine presence that remains unrecognised, a spiritual community rather than an institution defined by worldly power, and an expectation directed towards the end of time: the Imam's return, or parousia.

This expectation gives meaning to humanity's present condition because it anticipates the condition's end in a transformation of heaven and earth. The very idea of the Imam's concealment rules out turning religion, in its deepest sense, into an institution or a social object. His return, which we will examine again in Book VII, is not simply an event that will arrive from outside on some future day.

The Imam is hidden because human beings have made themselves unable to see him. His future appearance presupposes a change in human hearts. Through the way his followers live and become who they are, they themselves have a part in bringing about that appearance. Until then, the period of the Great Occultation is the time of an unrecognised divine presence. Precisely because this presence remains hidden, it cannot be turned into an object, a thing, still less something that society can take possession of. The time of the hidden Imam is therefore not merely historical time. It is the time of lived existence.

The contrast can now be summed up. Shiite teachings about prophecy and the Imams resist attempts to turn spiritual life into a social system because walayat concerns spiritual initiation and inner knowledge, not the foundation of a Church. The Friends of God, the “people of God,” are guides who lead others into spiritual understanding. They are not an institution empowered to impose dogma.

Visions and manifestations of God through particular spiritual figures do not require the doctrine of an Incarnation in which the divine is brought into ordinary physical history. The Imam's concealment preserves the expectation of a final transformation, as it did in early Christianity. It also preserves a hidden spiritual community—an Ecclesia spiritualis—whose inner order cannot be captured by public institutions and therefore cannot be turned into a worldly one.

The correspondence between the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of walayat makes it possible to recognise a continuing sacred history: a history that unfolds in the spiritual world, rising from one level to another, rather than simply moving along the endless straight line of conventional historical progress. Truth does not depend on where we stand on a timeline. It depends on the height of the horizon from which we perceive it. The Great Occultation is not a period in which we “make history” in the outward sense. It is a form of lived time. The Hidden Imam is the time of Shiite consciousness itself, its continuing link with what lies beyond ordinary history.

These reflections help us see what kind of problems we need to overcome together. Earlier, I mentioned the paradox of Shiism's outward position, beginning with its own political success under the Safavid restoration in the sixteenth century.

We will return to it in Chapter II. The powerful work of Haydar Amoli in the fourteenth century, and of Mulla Sadra Shirazi and his students in the seventeenth, draws on the teaching of the Imams. Such thinkers can help Twelver Shiism confront its own paradox by recognising the present meaning of its spiritual message and of the struggle to remain faithful to that message (see Chapter III).

Let me close this chapter with one striking observation. Twenty years ago, it was unusual to meet a young Iranian intellectual with whom I could discuss the philosophy of Mulla Sadra Shirazi. At the time I am writing, that is no longer exceptional. This is not something that will ever interest statisticians, but something is beginning to take shape. The pages of this book hope to contribute to it, however modestly.

Of course, I know that many Iranians, young and old alike, are deeply committed to the teachings of the great spiritual masters discussed here.

But others, also of every age, have grown used to dismissing these names and ideas. For some, the dismissal springs from ignorance; for others, refusal often hides a longing for what they have lost. I hope this book will at least give them the courage to acknowledge that longing. There is no reason to surrender to the myth of the inevitable “direction of history,” a myth that cannot see as living in the present what it calls the past, because it imagines it has already left that past behind.

We recalled earlier the Imams' teaching that the inward meaning of divine revelation is its true historical meaning. That is because its inward meaning never stops unfolding in the inward person, right up to the Last Day. In this sense, spiritual meaning is historical meaning: it belongs to the history of the soul, and that history keeps it alive in the present.

This is why tradition, by handing on what it protects, creates something new each time—not fashionable new ideologies, but new witnesses. That is certainly different from the usual idea that history belongs to the past.

But is this way of understanding things in the present really less honest or rigorous than the supposedly new methods of historical research? When archaeology, economics, and sociology are used to present the past lives of anonymous masses as the true “subject of history,” are we not still looking into a mirror? Is it not our own assumptions, preferences, and resentments that shape the image we read there in the present—all, of course, in the name of objectivity?

There is an image I am particularly fond of, one that I will return to here. It came to me as I contemplated the dry riverbeds that cut across the high Iranian plateau. Often, in the company of these same friends, we imagined the unforeseeable day when living water would once again fill those channels to the brim.

Then we would ask ourselves: where does the future of a living stream lie, whether it is a river of this world or a stream of spiritual life? At the mouth where the ocean swallows it? In the sandy desert where it disappears? Or at its source? Might its source be its true future?

For when we speak of the life of the soul, past and future are not properties of external things. They belong to the soul itself. It is we who are alive or dead, and we who are responsible for the life or death of these things. That is the secret of the Imams' way of uncovering scripture's spiritual meaning.

Mulla Sadra, for example, understood very well that we know only as much as we love, and that our way of knowing is itself the shape our love takes. Everything that the indifferent call “the past” therefore remains something still to come, to the extent that we love it. Our love is the very source of the future, because it gives the future life. But we must have the courage to love.

PreviousOutline of Books I and IINextII. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

Chapter II Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams

1. The central idea of Imami Shiism

Let us begin with a broad view of the central ideas of Shiite thought and spiritual life. What I sketch here will be developed more fully in later chapters. Elsewhere I have described the history of Twelver Shiism in terms of four major periods, so I will only recall them briefly here.19

The first period is that of the Imams themselves. It begins with the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib (died 40 AH/661 CE), the Prophet's trusted companion and guardian of his secrets. Shiite tradition preserves a great many conversations and sayings that bear witness to this role. The period ends in 329 AH/940 CE, the year that marks the beginning of the Twelfth Imam's Great Occultation.

This was also the year in which Muhammad ibn Yaqub Kulayni died. He had been head of the Shiite community in Ray—ancient Rhages, near present-day Tehran—before moving to Baghdad. There he spent twenty years gathering thousands of hadith, reports handed down about religious teachings and events. He drew directly on their transmitters, including the final two representatives (na'ib) of the Twelfth Imam. His work forms the earliest systematic collection of Shiite traditions still known to us.20

Older and more limited collections had already been made. Kulayni could consult some of them, and a few have survived. But persecution caused enormous losses in the Shiite literature of the early centuries, leaving us with many works whose titles are all that remain. Every hadith, as we know, is traced back to one of the Imams through a sequence of witnesses known as its chain of transmission, or isnad.

The second period runs from Kulayni to the major Twelver Shiite thinker Nasir al-Din Tusi (died 672 AH/1274 CE), who also had dealings with the Seven-Imam, or Ismaili, branch of Shiism. This was above all the age in which scholars compiled the great collections of Shiite traditions, wrote studies devoted to particular questions, and produced major tafsir works—commentaries on the Qur'an.

The third period extends from Tusi, around the time of the Mongol invasions, to the Safavid revival at the beginning of the sixteenth century. We will return to it in Book IV, particularly through the work of Haydar Amoli, to whom this book owes a special debt.

The fourth period begins with the Safavid revival. It includes what I have elsewhere called the School of Isfahan, dominated by such figures as Mir Damad and his students (see Book V). It also takes in the Qajar era (see Book VI) and the thinkers who still represent the traditional schools in my own time. Only those who come after us will be able to say when a fifth period began, and in what sense it deserves the name.

With that brief history in mind, let us turn to the defining features of Shiism. The word shia refers to those Muslims who follow the teaching of the Imams and show them a special devotion. They look to the Imams not only for the ordinary practice of Islam but also for its deepest philosophical teachings and for guidance in understanding the spiritual meaning of the Qur'an.

The Arabic word tashayyu' means to profess Shiism, while tasannun means to profess Sunni Islam. The latter comes from sunna, meaning tradition. Shiites, of course, also use the word sunna. For them, however, it embraces the full body of transmitted teachings attributed to the Twelve Imams.

The central distinction can be stated as follows. Sunni Islam teaches that the Prophet Muhammad (died 11 AH/632 CE) brought the cycle of prophecy to an end and revealed the final religious Law, the final sharia. According to the Prophet's own declaration, no prophet and no new revealed Law would follow him. He is the “Seal of Prophecy” (khatim al-nubuwwa), the “Seal of the Prophets” (khatim al-anbiya). On this understanding, the history of divine revelation has reached its conclusion. Generation after generation, Muslims look back to that final point in the past when the sequence of revelations came to a close.

Shiism also accepts Muhammad as the Seal of Prophecy. But it does not regard humanity's religious history as finished. Here we come to the distinctive Shiite understanding of prophecy, which we will explore in Chapter VI. For the end of the “cycle of prophecy” (da'irat al-nubuwwa) is also the beginning of another cycle: the cycle of spiritual initiation, or walayat.

The word walayat carries the meaning of friendship; the Persian word is dusti. On one side, it refers to the love and devotion that followers feel for the Imams. On the other, it refers to the love and preference that God has shown the Imams from before the beginning of time, setting them apart as God's Friends, those who are close to God and beloved by God (awliya Allah).

Once there are no more prophets (nabi), the title “Friends of God” applies to those who guide their followers—their own “friends”—into the true meaning of the prophetic revelations. In the strict Twelver Shiite sense, this title belongs above all to the Twelve Imams and only secondarily to their followers. Sunni Islam, particularly Sunni Sufism, applies it more widely.

The cycle of walayat opened when the cycle of prophecy closed. Just as Muhammad embodied the “Seal of universal Prophecy,” so the First Imam embodied the “Seal of universal walayat.” The “Seal of Muhammadan walayat,” however, will be revealed only when the whole cycle of walayat reaches its conclusion: at the appearance of the Twelfth Imam. We will develop these ideas further in Chapters VI and VII of Book I, and again in Book VII.

The cycle of walayat is the gradual initiation of humanity into the inward, spiritual meaning (batin) of divine revelation. When the Seal of Muhammadan walayat appears, all these hidden meanings will be disclosed. That will be the reign of religion lived entirely in spirit and truth. The Seal will be the final Imam, the Twelfth, returning into the present as the Imam who announces the Resurrection (Qa'im al-Qiyamat).

So when a Shiite believer looks back to the Prophet, the Seal of prophetic revelation, that believer also looks towards the figure whom the Prophet himself announced as a descendant, another form of himself: the future Seal of walayat. By accepting the message of the final Prophet, the Imam's followers are not imprisoned in a past that has been closed and sealed. They also look forward, carried by the hidden movement of an ongoing spiritual prophecy, towards the one who will come.

What this future figure will disclose is not a new Law or a new sharia. It is the inward, hidden meaning of all the revelations given to humanity, which will thereby be transformed and brought into a new light. The way of experiencing religious life is therefore fundamentally different in Shiism and Sunnism.

Twelver Shiism is also known as Imamism. As we have already seen, the Arabic word Imam originally means “one who stands in front.” The Imam is the spiritual guide. In Iran, the Persian word pishva is also widely used, followed by a number to identify each of the Twelve: pishva-ye yakom, the First Imam; pishva-ye dowom, the Second Imam; and so on.

In the specifically Shiite sense, the title belongs to the Twelve: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin and the first Imam, and eleven descendants of the Prophet through his daughter Fatima (al-Zahra, “the Radiant One”) and Ali. The idea of an Imam as both guide and initiator is inseparable from the idea of Shiism as a path to the deeper knowledge of Islam. The Imam is a guide (hadi) precisely because God has guided him (mahdi).

All Twelve Imams can therefore be described as both guided and guiding. Together they form a complete spiritual whole, a pleroma, and share one and the same essential reality (haqiqa, the Greek ousia).

The Twelve Imams lead their followers towards the hidden, inward meaning (batin) of the revelation proclaimed by the Prophet. Their teachings form a vast body of tradition, and from the time of the final Prophet until the return of the Hidden Imam they remain the source of a spiritual inheritance that cannot be improvised or reconstructed through logical arguments alone. Their persons, understood as supernatural intermediaries, also remain the focus of their followers' devotion.

This, in a few words, is what lies at the heart of Shiism. It gives rise to a characteristic way of thinking, a philosophy that calls itself prophetic philosophy (hikmat nabawiya). This is Shiism's distinctive and indispensable contribution to Islam. Sunni thinkers, in general, have not understood this dimension, and it has been just as little recognised in the West. Some in the West, he suggests, have found it easier to admire the prestige of majority Sunni Islam and avoid questions that might disturb their own assumptions. My Shiite friends in Iran have often asked me what lies behind this bias, which they find so strange.

2. Prophetic philosophy and religion as spiritual initiation

This “prophetic philosophy” is, in a sense, what is at stake in Shiism's spiritual struggle on several fronts. Whether Shiism remains true to itself depends on the outcome. For too long, scholars have taken for granted a conventional picture in which Islamic thought and spiritual life appear in three forms: Sufism; the philosophers described as followers of Greek thought; and kalam, usually called Islamic scholastic theology, although it is more accurately a form of argument devoted to defending religious belief.

But some forms of Sufism reject philosophy and books, while others have created an extraordinary account of the nature of reality, drawing their central themes from the Islamic search for inner knowledge. Likewise, some philosophers reject Sufism, while others embrace it. Then there are the scholars of kalam, the mutakallimun, who generally have no more sympathy for the Sufis and philosophers than those groups have for them.

Complex as this picture already is, it remains misleading because something essential is missing: Shiite prophetic philosophy. Its method is less a matter of debating abstract ideas than of interpreting and revealing meaning. Instead of building arguments from logical abstractions, it seeks to uncover what lies hidden (batin) beneath what is outwardly visible (zahir), and to recognise how that inner meaning echoes through different levels of reality.

When Suhrawardi's Ishraq—his “Eastern wisdom,” or philosophy of illumination (see Books II and V)—had become firmly connected with Shiite thought, Iranian writers often described the relationship in a striking way. They said that Ishraq stands in relation to abstract philosophy as Sufism stands in relation to kalam. That comparison alone tells us a great deal about how these different approaches were understood.

A prophetic philosophy begins with the fact of prophecy. In its understanding of knowledge and the different levels of knowledge, it places prophetic knowledge—the various forms of sacred knowledge—at the summit. That is because its whole account of knowledge grows out of its understanding of prophecy (see Chapter VI below). Its source lies in the teachings handed down from the holy Imams, teachings that often explain the allusions found in a Qur'anic verse. Historically, I do not believe we can trace this kind of thought to any earlier Islamic sources. It even helps explain the structure and language of philosophical systems that have usually been studied on their own.

We can understand, for example, why al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Suhrawardi all place prophetic knowledge at the highest level of what human beings can know.

This kind of philosophy naturally belongs to a religion founded on prophecy, such as Islam. Such a religion centres not on the idea that God enters history through a divine incarnation, but on a message given to humanity by a God who always remains beyond the world. God inspires chosen people to communicate that message. If we want to understand the place of philosophy in Islam, and the kind of spiritual life that can grow alongside it, we must look for the setting in which philosophical reflection truly belongs, rather than one where it feels out of place or is rejected. What, then, is the human situation that this philosophy, by its very origins, has to address?

The Islamic understanding of human beings and their destiny allows for events that are entirely real without belonging to what we ordinarily call history: events that can be placed on a timeline and documented through material records. This understanding also recognizes events of sacred history beyond ordinary time. They are not events that come after history, but events that reach across and beyond it.

Just because they are not historical in the usual sense does not mean they are myths in the usual sense either. The ability to recognize reality in this space between myth and recorded history exposes the limits of certain attempts to explain religion through social psychology. Such explanations often begin by assuming that anything must be either myth or history—and that no third possibility exists.2122

For Islamic spiritual thought, the central event of this history beyond time is recalled in Qur'an 7:171. God asks the spirits of all human beings, before they have taken bodily form on earth: A-lastu bi-rabbikum?—“Am I not your Lord?” Everyone answers yes.

Yet, according to the thinkers we are studying, that shared answer conceals many differences, because each person also chose, before entering this world, the destiny they would follow here. This “prologue in heaven” is a central point of reference for Islamic spirituality, although different writers understand it at different depths.

For Ibn Arabi (d. 638 AH/1240 CE), God was, before the beginning of time, both the one who asked the question and the one who answered it. For Ruzbihan of Shiraz (d. 606/1209; see Book III below), the vision established a bond of love with the eternal Witness (shahid-e qidam), who is at once the one who contemplates and the one contemplated. When human spirits entered their earthly bodies, the love they had known before that passing condition of existence led them to cry out with Moses: “Show Yourself to me.”23

The mystic thus finds a personal Mount Sinai: the place where God will become manifest to that person. For those who seek inner meanings generally, and for Shiite thinkers especially, the verse clearly points to souls existing before their earthly lives, however that earlier existence is understood.24 This may explain the distinctly Platonic flavour of the statement of faith drawn up by Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh (d. 381/991), one of the earliest and most important Shiite scholars. For Muslims more broadly, the verse means that human beings are answerable for a mysterious covenant made with God by God's own will.

That covenant gives earthly life its meaning in Islamic spirituality: life is the test of whether we remain faithful to the promise made with God before time began. The prophets come to remind people of that earlier promise.

But what exactly does it mean, and how can we keep it? The answer is a secret hidden beneath the outward wording of the revelations brought by the prophets. This is why the verse has inspired so much reflection in the tradition of inner spiritual knowledge known as irfan, or gnosis. Such knowledge has always troubled strict interpreters of religious texts and defenders of fixed doctrines. It reveals a level of reality and awareness that they do not accept. And it is knowledge that saves and transforms: it cannot come into being without a process of spiritual initiation and renewal through which a person's deeper self awakens.

From this point of view, a human being is not primarily a sinner, sick with an inherited original sin. A human being is an exile—a gharib (see Book II, Chapter V, and Book III, Chapter I)—whose task is to understand why they are far from home and how they can return. Those who refuse the return lose themselves in a hopeless abyss. Those who seek the way home find it through inner knowledge: by discovering the hidden meaning of the prophetic revelations through ta'wil, the practice of leading their outward words back to their spiritual meaning. This is what makes spiritual rebirth (wiladat ruhaniya) possible.

The need to find both the path and a guide for travelling it lies at the very roots of Shiism. It is also where prophetic philosophy begins. Its spirit could hardly be expressed better than in an image used by the great philosopher Mulla Sadra of Shiraz (d. 1050/1640): “The Qur'anic revelation is the light by which we see, like the sun pouring out its light. Philosophical understanding is the eye that sees that light. Without the light, nothing can be seen.

“But if we shut our eyes—that is, if we claim we can do without philosophical understanding—the light itself will go unseen, because there are no eyes open to receive it.” The apparent conflict between philosophy and theology is overcome from the outset in hikmat ilahiya, or “divine wisdom.” By Mulla Sadra's time, this prophetic wisdom would come to mean, above all, the spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an taught by the Imams.

Revelation and philosophical reflection are thus bound together from the beginning. Philosophy, when understood as prophetic philosophy, cannot be separated from spiritual effort or personal spiritual fulfilment.

We can already see a basic difference between this approach and an understanding of Islam centred on religious law. The law-centred understanding of Sunni Islam and the inner spiritual teaching of Shiite Islam start from the same belief but draw different conclusions from it. Both accept that Muhammad brought the earlier cycles of prophecy to a close. Before him came the great prophets—Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Muhammad was the last prophet to bring a revealed religious law, or sharia: the Seal of the prophets who give laws (nubuwwat al-tashri).

Now suppose prophetic revelations have only their outward, literal meaning. Suppose they amount to nothing beyond a moral and social law. In that case, humanity's religious history has truly come to an end, because there will never be another divinely revealed sharia. We have already heard the Fifth and Sixth Imams declare that if the Qur'an had no meaning beyond its literal words, it would already be dead.

But suppose the text of revelation contains something hidden, something the Prophet, in his role as prophet, was not charged with disclosing (see Chapter VI). Everything changes. Then religious life becomes a waiting for the full meaning of revelation to be revealed at the end of time. That unveiling advances through what Corbin calls the night of hidden meaning. The night began with the First Imam, after the Prophet left this world. It will end only when the last Imam, the Twelfth, who is now hidden, finally appears. His appearance will herald the Great Resurrection (al-Qiyamat al-Kubra).

For Shiism, teachings about the end of time are not merely a vague article of faith or a way to encourage moral behaviour. They are fundamental to its philosophy. A prophetic philosophy is inseparable from an understanding of the last things: it arises from an awareness of what is to come and gives shape to the ways people anticipate it. Perhaps nearly everyone in Islam could agree with the arguments by which the Shiite Imams, from the beginning, explained why prophets were necessary.

But what happens after the last prophet has come, now that no more prophets will appear? This is the urgent question that Shiism raises and seeks to answer. Indeed, prophetic philosophy is needed precisely because there will be no more prophets.

The answer is the walayat of the Imams, which continues after the last Prophet's risalat, his mission of bringing God's message. This is the answer given in the traditions attributed to the Imams themselves. It is also developed by leading Shiite thinkers devoted to divine wisdom, such as Ibn Abi Jumhur (who died after 901/1496). For these writers, what chiefly sets Shiism apart from mainstream Islam is walayat: the Imams' spiritual bond with God and their role as guides to the hidden truth. This is the inner reality of religion—the res esoterica, literally “the hidden matter” (al-amr al-batina).25 The Islam understood through Shiite spiritual awareness therefore calls for initiation into a teaching that leads to salvation. In this sense, it is a form of spiritual knowledge within Islam.

At its heart is a claim that was enough, from the very beginning, to alarm the scholars of Sunni orthodoxy, in its concern for religion's literal forms. Everything outward, everything visible, every surface appearance (zahir) has an inward, hidden reality (batin). The outward is the form in which the inward becomes visible: the place where it appears (mazhar). And the reverse is equally true: every inward reality requires an outward form. The outward is what we can see of the inward; the inward is its spiritual truth, its real nature (haqiqat), its secret, its inner knowledge, and its meaning beyond the senses (ma'na). The outward takes shape in the visible world. The inward has its reality in the unseen spiritual world (alam al-ghayb).

This relationship between outward form and inner reality is reflected in the relationship between the Prophet's mission as God's Messenger (risalat) and the Imam's spiritual mission as a Friend of God (wali Allah). The Prophet brings about the “descent” (tanzil) of revelation: its arrival in the world in the form of words and religious teachings. For Shiism, this necessarily calls for another, complementary task: to lead those revealed words back to their spiritual truth, their original meaning. That return is ta'wil. Its literal sense is “leading back,” and it names the spiritual interpretation of revelation.

This work belongs above all to the Imam's special spiritual gift and guiding role—his walayat. Just as the outward and inward meanings depend on each other, prophecy and the Imam's work of spiritual guidance (nubuwwat and walayat) are interdependent and inseparable. The Shiite understanding of the Imam can therefore exist and make sense only within the spiritual awareness that gives rise to it. It is a basic, guiding image in religious consciousness—one that comes before any evidence drawn from outward experience.

Any other explanation would miss what fundamentally distinguishes Shiite belief in the Imams from mainstream Islam understood chiefly as a religion of law, with its concern for the validity of actions and rituals and its suspicion of attempts to uncover an inner dimension through spiritual initiation. Equally, to discuss inner spiritual traditions in Islam while leaving out Shiism—as Western scholars have often done—is to miss something essential. It ignores the claim that faith (iman) reaches its full meaning only through the Imam's walayat: by recognizing both the Imam's identity and his spiritual role.

Faith also needs ta'wil, an inward understanding (ma'rifat) of divine revelation (see Chapter V). From a Shiite perspective, separating spiritual interpretation from the doctrine of the Imams would amount to turning Shiism into something detached from its own sacred foundation. As we shall see, this becomes especially important when we examine the relationship between Shiism, Shiite Sufism, and forms of Sufism that do not identify themselves as Shiite.

We have already introduced several key ideas about prophecy and the role of the Imams. We will examine them more fully in Chapters V–VII. But a few more points are needed now, especially those that our authors use to describe the Imam's spiritual identity.2627 The Friend of God's guiding role—his walayat—is directed towards knowing the inner meaning of divine revelation. In contrast, the ordinary inheritance left by a prophet (warathat) concerns the outward meaning, the words of revelation as they stand.

We will see in Chapter VI, section 4, what is involved in inheriting spiritual knowledge. The Imam's role in its fullness includes both outward and inward knowledge. To receive the Prophet's spiritual trust (wasayat) is to preserve the continuing line of inner meaning (silsilat al-batin). The worldly caliphate, or outward succession to the Prophet, preserves the line of outward religious law and teaching. But without the inner line, its claim to preserve that inheritance is always uncertain and open to question.

This distinction already shows why the question of the Shiite Imamate is far greater than accounts that reduce Shiism to politics or struggles for power. Ali ibn Abi Talib, the First Imam and the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, became only the fourth caliph in the official history of Islam's outward institutions.

But that does not lessen his standing as Imam. Nor does the earlier position of the first three caliphs—Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman—give them the spiritual authority of an Imam. Neither does holding the caliphate give that authority to later Umayyad or Abbasid rulers. To understand what is at stake in Shiism is to understand that it is not simply a matter of supporting one political dynasty against another. The Imam does not need to be recognized by the general population in order to be Imam. His spiritual gift is invisible to them, as is the spiritual world from which it comes and to which it belongs. His status therefore does not depend on their judgment.

There are even times when the Imamate must remain hidden—as it does during the present period of ghaybat, the Imam's concealment. The worldly caliphate concerns the maintenance of the sharia, the outward inheritance. None of the eleven Imams who came after Ali actually exercised that caliphate.

Yet each was still the Guardian of the Holy Book (Qayyim al-Qur'an). This means something very different from political rule. It is the caliphate in its “true sense,” realized in the person of the Imam. But its complete realization belongs, by its very nature, to the fulfilment of history at the end of time.

A passage that captures the spirit of Shiism especially well will now bring these ideas together. It records something like the closing words of a conversation between the Sixth Imam, Jafar al-Sadiq, and one of his closest disciples, Mufaddal ibn Umar al-Jufi. This is how Mufaddal himself tells the story:

“Our cause is difficult,” the Imam said. “To bear it, people need minds in which the dawn can break, hearts burning with light, healthy souls, and beautiful natures. God has already received the pledge (mithaq) of our Shiite followers. May God faithfully grant paradise to whoever remains faithful and loyal to us. Whoever betrays us and violates our right has already placed himself in hell.

“God has entrusted us, the Imams, with a secret—a secret whose burden He placed on no one else. Then He ordered us to pass it on, and we do.

“But we would have found no one worthy of receiving it, no one able to hold and carry it, if God had not created certain people for that purpose. They were formed from the clay of Muhammad and his descendants—from the very substance of the Prophet and the Imams. They were created from the light of the Imams through the overflowing generosity of divine mercy.

“We pass on to them what God has commanded us to pass on. They welcome it and can bear it; their hearts are not disturbed. Their spirits are in harmony with our secret. They are naturally drawn to a spiritual understanding of who we are, and of their own accord they seek to know our cause.

“But God has also created people who belong to hell. We have been ordered to tell them the same thing, and so we tell them. Yet their hearts close against our secret. They recoil from it, throw it back at us, and deny it as false because they cannot bear it. God has placed a seal upon their hearts. Their tongues speak a portion of the truth and repeat its words, but their hearts reject it.”

Then, Mufaddal relates, the Imam wept. Raising both hands, he prayed: “O my God, let them live as we live and die as we die! Do not let an enemy prevail over them. For if You allowed their enemies to overcome them, there would be no one left in this world to worship You.”28

This passage, so strongly marked by the Shiite spiritual outlook, will echo throughout the pages that follow. It prepares us for the interpretation of Qur'an 33:72 as a verse concealing the secret of the trust God placed in humanity. It also expresses themes found in the First Imam's conversation with his disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad (see Chapter III, sections 2 and 3). It suggests that, in the scene of the covenant before time (mithaq), the yes spoken by humanity did not come from every heart in the same way.

Some hearts already concealed a refusal. Their owners would be the enduring deniers, people whose initiation never came to completion, whose answer was a no disguised as a yes. Their destiny, too, would spring from a choice made before earthly life—one that no human explanation can fully reach.

Finally, the Imam's opening statement matches the beginning of a famous tradition identifying the Imams' secret with the secret of interpreting revelation's hidden meaning. It therefore points towards the mystery of the Primordial Prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya; see Chapter V).

We can now identify two further points that complete the Twelver Shiite understanding of the Imamate. First, why do the Imams form a complete group of twelve persons sharing one spiritual reality, and how do they perform an essential role in revealing God even before appearing on earth? Second, why does this role make the Imamate a necessary part of the eternal religion of prophecy, present throughout every period of the prophetic cycle?

3. The Complete Circle of the Twelve Imams

To understand these two points, we must first consider why the number twelve is held to be complete in itself. The Prophet's reported statements about the number of Imams are taken as proof of that completeness. Because the group of twelve forms a perfect whole—a pleroma, or complete circle—its number cannot be exceeded. That is what gives the mysterious Twelfth Imam his special place.

We must then consider how this pattern appears throughout the universe and throughout sacred history. The Twelve are made manifest at different levels in the coming-into-being of the cosmos and during the successive periods of prophecy. These many forms of manifestation surround the earthly lives of the historical Imams, whose appearances were brief and took place during the first three centuries of Islam.

The number twelve also matters in Seven-Imam Shiism, or Ismailism. There, however, it does not specify a fixed total number of Imams.
