Rather, it refers to the twelve dignitaries, or hujjats, who permanently surround each Imam. So twelve does not establish quite the same basic pattern in the two branches of Shiism. This is an important difference.29 Many traditions state that the Imams number twelve, some attributing this teaching to the Prophet and others to individual Imams.

To show why twelve represents a perfect and complete whole, these traditions point to the twelve signs of the zodiac, the twelve princes or tribes of Israel, the twelve springs that appeared when Moses struck the rock, the twelve months of the year, the twelve hours of the day, and other examples. In this way, Twelver Shiism takes up an entire theology of the Aeon: a sacred order of time and cosmic completeness.

The Imamate also has its origin in the eternal Prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya), before and beyond all its appearances in our world. That is why the relationship between the Prophet and the Imam—between Muhammad and Ali ibn Abi Talib—is unique. With the Prophet of Islam, the Imamate was openly revealed.

But it had already been “revealed in secret” alongside each of the earlier prophets who brought religious laws, as we shall see. The prophets' chief mission had always been risalat: delivering the divine message in its outward, literal form. The Imams' task was to guide people into the hidden spiritual meaning of that revelation through ta'wil and tahqiq, the search for its true reality. They lead people towards spiritual understanding. More than that, they are themselves that inner meaning (see Chapter V).

This is because Shiite reflection on the Imams sees their existence before earthly life as the first manifestation of God: a heavenly reality beyond ordinary humanity, created rather than divine in itself, but serving as the Face through which God becomes known to human beings. People turn towards that Face when they turn towards God, because God in His own being remains inaccessible to them: the unfathomable depth, the divine Silence, the hidden God (Deus absconditus). This idea of the divine Face is central to Shiite theology. It is not the result of later speculation; it is already expressed in sayings attributed to the Imams themselves.30

We shall see in Chapter VII that the Imam, understood in this way, makes it possible for human beings to know God's oneness (tawhid).

However hard we try, we can turn only towards the Face of God as revealed (Deus revelatus). By recognizing this, we avoid two opposite errors: tashbih, making God resemble a human being or other created things, and ta'til, treating God as so unknowable that we are left with no living knowledge of Him. From this Shiite standpoint, anyone who rejects the Imam repeats the error of Iblis. One path leads to tashbih, a misunderstanding of God's names and attributes; the other leads to ta'til, which tries to protect God's absolute otherness but merely replaces a naïve, human-like picture of God with an abstract one.

The Twelve Imams, together with the Prophet and his daughter Fatima—Fatima al-Zahra, “the Radiant,” “she who shines like flowers,” and the mother of the Imams' line—form the complete circle of the Fourteen Pure Ones (Chahardeh Ma'sum in Persian). Their manifestations, or appearances through which God becomes known, take place at different levels of the universe: lahut, jabarut, malakut, and nasut (see Chapter V).

We cannot explore all the comparisons here, for they need fuller study. But the group has striking similarities to groups of twelve and fourteen found in Coptic Gnostic texts.3132

The Apocalypse of Adam, for example, speaks of fourteen Aeons of light, forms in which the Illuminator appears. In Shiite language, we might call them the visible forms (mazahir) of the eternal Prophetic Reality. Manichaean spiritual teaching interprets a prayer offered by Seth, Adam's son, to the “fourteen great Aeons of light.” Seth, as the “Imam of Adam,” is also an important figure in Shiite inner teaching.

The same Manichaean tradition speaks of the “fourteen vessels” on which Jesus travelled down into this world. The likeness between the Twelfth Imam—the fourteenth of the Pure Ones—and the fourteenth Aeon of light is especially striking. In the Apocalypse of Adam, the fourteenth is a stranger, a being from elsewhere: a boy born under mysterious circumstances, carried away to a place no one can reach, and brought up and nourished there.33

The Twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Qa'im (“the One Who Will Rise”) or al-Mahdi (“the Rightly Guided”), is also said to have been born mysteriously. He disappears while still a child, on the very day his young father, the Imam Hasan Askari, leaves this world (260 AH/873 CE; see Book VII).

We shall hear the Prophet Muhammad speak of him in words recalling those of the prophet Zarathustra about the saving figure called the Saoshyant: “I am in him, and he is in me.”

The Twelfth Imam, the fourteenth of the Pure Ones, is the Hidden Imam of our own age. According to this understanding, he lives in a world beyond the senses, invisible to human beings, until his future appearance brings the present cycle of the world to an end. The time in which we live is the time of his concealment, the ghaybat. As the Imam who is awaited (Imam muntazar), he has been identified by several Shiite writers, including Haydar Amoli, with the Paraclete whom Jesus promises in the Gospel of John.34

We shall return to this, because the connection between the Shiite understanding of Islam and the promised Paraclete raises an important question for a wider study of the world's religions—a field of thought that may yet develop in the future. Since devotion to the Twelfth Imam lies at the heart of Twelver Shiism, the final book of this work will be devoted to him. For the same reason, we could not go any further without introducing him here.

As we have said, numerous Shiite traditions, or hadiths, are cited in support of the complete group of twelve. Shiite interpreters also find support in Qur'anic verses, while a cosmic understanding of divine wisdom reveals further patterns that we will consider later. Here we can do no more than touch on a few of the many traditions.

In one tradition, the Prophet declares: “There will be twelve Imams after me. The first is Ali ibn Abi Talib; the twelfth is the One Who Will Rise (al-Qa'im), the Mahdi—the Rightly Guided, and therefore himself the Guide (al-Hadi). Through him, God will bring the East and West of the earth under His rule.” Other traditions compare their number to the months of the year, the springs that Moses brought from the rock at Horeb, or the chiefs (nuqaba) of Israel.

Addressing Ali, his own spiritual successor (wasi), the Prophet says: “Ali, the Imams, rightly guided and guiding others, your descendants who are perfectly pure, will be twelve in number, counting you among them. You are the first. The last will bear my own name, Muhammad. When he appears, he will fill the earth with justice and harmony, just as it is now filled with wrongdoing and violence.”

Another tradition recalls what the Prophet was shown during the ecstatic night of his ascent to heaven. He saw twelve lights on the supports of the Throne. Within each light was a line of green writing bearing the name of one of the twelve Imams.35 The same image returns in the story of an emerald tablet brought down from heaven by the angel Gabriel to Fatima Zahra, or brought to the Prophet and given by him to his daughter. We might remember here the emerald tablet of the Hermetic tradition.

Written on Fatima's tablet in letters of gold that shone like sunlight were the names of the Prophet and his twelve Imams. One of the Prophet's Companions, Jabir al-Ansari, who was among the earliest Shiites, was even allowed by Fatima to copy it. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir (d. around 115/733), is said to have confirmed the account. In the sacred narrative, then, this testimony was given well before the line of twelve Imams had reached its historical end.36

These many traditions develop and explain what Shiism sees in the Qur'anic verses it regards as divine confirmation of its beliefs. Two connected ideas are especially important. The first is ismat, the purity and freedom from fault granted to the Imams by God. The second is nass, God's designation of the Imam, which means that his spiritual place cannot be assigned or taken away through human election. Two Qur'anic verses are particularly significant here.

The first is Qur'an 3:54, in the verse numbering Corbin uses, which refers to the challenge known as mubahala. Muhammad offered this solemn test to the Christians of Najran and their bishop in 10 AH/631 CE. Each side would call upon God to give a sign settling their disagreement about who Christ was. As is well known, the Christians ultimately declined to take the test.

But the scene prepared for it was extraordinary. On the “red dune,” the Prophet had a large piece of black cloth hung between two trees trimmed to form posts, creating a kind of canopy. He stood beneath it with his daughter Fatima—al-Zahra, “the Radiant,” also called al-Batul, “the Virgin”—behind him. On his right stood her husband and cousin, Ali, the First Imam. On his left stood the two young Imams, Hasan and Husayn.

These four members of his family, together with the Prophet himself, were the five people he put forward as participants in the sacred test. Together they are known as the Five People of the Cloak (Ashab al-Kisa). This is the same cloak that the Hidden Imam will wear when he appears, giving the image a remarkable power.37 Shiite belief understands these five people, joined by a sacred bond, as a manifestation of God. For Shiite theologians, the Qur'anic wording leaves no doubt that the Five share one essence (ousia), one spiritual reality (haqiqat).3839

Another verse makes the same five people sacred, and through them the succession of Imams down to the Twelfth. It is not descent by blood alone that makes each of the Twelve an Imam. What matters is ismat, purity granted by God, together with nass, God's explicit designation of that person. Qur'an 33:33 says: “God wishes to remove all impurity from you, members of the Prophet's household, and to make you entirely pure.” Again, the five are gathered under the Prophet's cloak. On this occasion he prays: “My God, these are the members of my house. My brother Ali is the prince of the Imams, his sons are the finest of my descendants, and my daughter is the sovereign of women.40 The Mahdi will come from our family.”

One of the Companions, again Jabir al-Ansari, asks: “Messenger of God, who is the Mahdi?” The Prophet replies: “There will be nine Imams descended from Husayn. The ninth will be the Qa'im, the One Who Will Rise. He will fill the earth with harmony and justice, just as it is now filled with tyranny and violence. He will struggle to bring people back to the spiritual meaning (ta'wil), just as I struggled to reveal the outward words (tanzil).”

That final sentence explains why, as we shall see at the end of this work, the Twelfth Imam stands at the centre of the whole cycle of spiritual initiation—the cycle of walayat—that began when the cycle of prophecy came to a close. Here we meet a paradox that is characteristic of Shiite thought and is already present in the Prophet's statement that twelve Imams would succeed him. How can twelve be enough to cover all the time remaining until Yawm al-Qiyamat, the Day of Resurrection? From the beginning, the line of twelve Imams cannot be compared with, or set in competition against, any worldly dynasty. It belongs to another order of reality.

On the one hand, the earth can never be without an Imam, even an invisible, hidden one. Without him, the earth would lose its connection with heaven. The Imam is its spiritual centre; if he ceased to exist, humanity could not continue to exist. Whether the great majority of people know of this centre or not makes no difference. The Imam must therefore always be present.

On the other hand, the complete circle of twelve is already established. Twelve is the perfect number: fewer would leave the Imamate incomplete, and more would break the very completeness that gives it meaning. The Twelfth Imam must therefore exist now, and must have existed in this world from the moment the Eleventh Imam departed it.

Yet the cycle of spiritual guidance through walayat is not over. The Twelfth Imam's final appearance is still awaited. He must therefore be both already present and still to come—someone who has existed in the past and whose appearance belongs to the future.

This double relationship to time defines his existence today. It is a presence between times: invisible and enduring, from the beginning of his “Minor Occultation” in 260 AH/874 CE until the end of historical time and the dawn of a new Aeon, the age of the Perfect Human Being.4142 Such a presence cannot be an ordinary physical presence at a location in the visible world. It requires another world, beyond the senses, between the world we know and the highest spiritual reality, with its own kind of time (see Chapter IV, section 5). This lasting presence is what makes the idea of a Hidden Imam necessary, along with the doctrine of concealment, or ghaybat.

Shiite thinkers devoted to divine wisdom have reflected on it at great length. It protects the central idea of Twelver Shiism from being reduced to a worldly institution or a political and social programme (see the whole of Book VII).

Besides the verses of the Qur'an and the teachings attributed to the Prophet and the Imams, Shiite doctrine is supported by a larger vision of how the universe came to be and how sacred history unfolds. Within Shiism, these ideas preserve a much older tradition of inner spiritual knowledge. Unlike what happened in the West, philosophical thought here was not confined by a more or less arbitrary boundary between inherited religious teaching and speculative reasoning.

The only aim worthy of such thought was a complete understanding of divine wisdom, a theosophia in its fullest sense. Qur'anic verses and traditions provide material for thinking about the universe. In return, philosophical accounts of the universe continually refer back to those sacred sources. Their meeting reveals the second great feature of the Imamate mentioned earlier: its place as an essential part of a universal religion of prophecy, present throughout every period of the prophetic cycle.

Consider, for instance, a saying attributed to the Sixth Imam, Jafar al-Sadiq: “Night has twelve hours, day has twelve hours, and the year has twelve months. The Imams number twelve, and Ali is one hour among the twelve.” Our authors have no difficulty seeing this as a reference to the cycle of spiritual initiation, or walayat, whose length and stages correspond to those of a cosmic day and night.

In another tradition, the Prophet recites Qur'an 85:1: “By the heaven with its twelve fortified mansions”—the signs of the zodiac. Then he asks his listener: “Do you think God Most High is swearing by the astronomical sky and its constellations? The heaven spoken of here is my own person. And the twelve fortified mansions, the twelve zodiacal signs, are the twelve Imams who will come after me.”43

Here the doctrine of the Imams reaches beyond earthly life to the scale of the universe itself. As we have seen, the historical persons of the twelve Imams are understood as earthly manifestations of the spiritual powers through which the cosmos comes into being.

Shiite divine wisdom is therefore, at its heart, a teaching about how God becomes manifest. This is why Shiite thinkers so readily recognized ideas they saw as originally their own in the immense writings of Ibn Arabi, and made his work part of their own tradition. They did, however, refine his account of the oneness of being (wahdat al-wujud). The Shiite commentators on Ibn Arabi, especially Haydar Amoli, offer a revealing example. Haydar was quite willing to criticize teachings of Ibn Arabi that conflicted with Shiite doctrine, above all the identity of the “Seal of the walayat” (see Book IV, Chapter I).

Yet the central idea on both sides remains the same: the different levels of the universe correspond perfectly with one another, linking visible worlds with spiritual worlds. That is why the twelve Imams, from the first to the last, are said to make manifest every religion and every perfection, both spiritually and visibly.44

This statement by Ibn Abi Jumhur comes from a view of the universe in which the different levels of existence form a very complex order. That order also determines the different levels of meaning that spiritual interpretation uncovers in the Qur'an (see Chapter V). Let us reduce this picture to its simplest outlines, leaving aside the variations between accounts.45

At the eternal origin of all manifestations of God stand twelve heavenly princes, or primordial Imams. They occupy the highest heaven of twelve dwelling places, each seated on his own throne. They know the secrets of the Preserved Tablet (Lawh Mahfuz), not because they have learned them from elsewhere, but because this knowledge belongs to their very being. In their turn, they establish seven representatives or leaders (nuqaba), corresponding to the ruling Intelligences of the planetary spheres described by philosophers. These seven leaders are assisted by guardians or “temple-keepers” (sadana), some of whose roles correspond to the heavenly souls (animae caelestes) that philosophers say move the spheres.

This entire order revolves in service to the twelve original heavenly princes. Twelve orders of angels serve as messengers between the worlds and correspond to them. Angels, stars, and heavens all appear as different manifestations (mazahir) of the one reality of the Primordial Human Being (Insan, the Anthropos). This primordial human reality is the source of everything that exists. Under its different names, it is the first being brought into existence by the God who forever remains beyond existence itself.

If we consider the twelve heavenly Imams in their original role in the creation of the universe, angels and heavenly spirits become the forms through which they are made manifest in their respective worlds. But if we consider the Imams as they appear in human form on earth, their spirits receive inspiration and higher knowledge from those angelic spirits.

In short, the worlds together are many different manifestations of a single primordial reality, which appears on earth in the Fourteen Pure Ones: the twelve Imams, the Prophet, and Fatima, his daughter and the source of their family line.

The correspondences are easy to see within this traditional picture of the cosmos. The order and completeness of the visible worlds depend on the seven heavenly bodies, the seven heavens, and the twelve zodiacal constellations. The order and completeness of the spiritual cosmos are governed by the seven central figures, or poles (aqtab), who are prophets, and the twelve Imams. The spiritual orders described in Sufism have their origin in this pattern. It also helps us understand the role of the Twelve in both the cycle of prophecy and the cycle of spiritual initiation.

By this same pattern of correspondence, each prophet who was not only a nabi but also a messenger (nabi mursal), sent to reveal the Book of a new religion and begin a new period of prophecy, was followed by twelve Imams, his spiritual heirs (awsiya). Each messenger was a manifestation of the same prophetic reality that finally appeared in its fullness in the “Seal of the Prophets.” In the same way, the Imams belonging to the different prophets were manifestations of one and the same reality of the Imamate. They were not reincarnations of one another.

Speaking of Ali, his own direct spiritual successor, the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have said: “Ali was sent secretly with every prophet; with me he was sent openly.”46 The saying speaks through the person of Ali of an eternal Imam. If we remember that the Imam's spiritual role is to lead people into the hidden meaning of revelation, we can begin to see the importance of another fact: Ismaili spiritual teaching gives this “eternal Imam” the name of Melchizedek.47 This shows how deeply the Shiite understanding of the Imam is rooted in the idea of a universal religion of prophecy. Here we can see that idea unfolding, although the chain by which it reached the all-embracing inner vision of Shiism—one that takes in the whole of sacred history—is still far from clear.

There are seven great prophets among the messengers (nabi mursal): Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, and Muhammad. Their number corresponds to the seven planetary spheres.48 In this scheme, the seven are called the poles. Just as the movements of the planets are marked out against the heavens of the twelve zodiacal signs, the seven periods of prophecy, each beginning with one of these figures, are marked by twelve successive spiritual heirs (awsiya), or Imams.

No prophet dies without appointing a spiritual successor. That successor does not take over the office of prophet; he carries on the work of the Imamate. Adam appointed his son Seth; Noah appointed his son Shem; Abraham appointed Ishmael; Moses, after Aaron's death, appointed Joshua; and Jesus appointed Shamun al-Safa, or Simon Peter.

But Muhammad reminded his followers that every one of these prophets had been betrayed by his own people. He also warned that his own community would betray its promise of loyalty to the man he named as his spiritual heir, Ali ibn Abi Talib. This painful picture has a powerful place in Shiite consciousness. It is how the tradition understands what it sees as the great failure of the Sunni majority: abandoning the Imamate, which Shiism regards as the heart of Islam understood as a spiritual religion.

We have already seen how difficult it is to translate the full meaning of awliya, the “Friends of God,” and walayat.

We shall meet the difficulty again. A great Twelver Shiite Sufi master of the seventh/thirteenth century, Sad al-Din Hamuyah (d. 650/1252), explains that these terms appeared only with the religion of Muhammad, although the spiritual role they name had existed throughout the earlier periods of prophecy. In those earlier times, people who held this role were still called nabis, prophets in a more general sense, rather than messengers sent with a revealed Book. We shall return to these distinctions in Chapter VI, section 2.

This teaching implies that with Islam—and, in this understanding, with Shiite Islam in particular—the inner meaning of religion reached its full expression.49 It is also the meaning given to the following saying when applied to the twelve Imams: “The sages of my community correspond to the prophets of Israel.” Our authors can name in detail the twelve spiritual guides who marked the successive stages of each earlier prophetic period.

But this is one of the most difficult subjects in Shiite accounts of prophecy and the Imams, whether Twelver or Ismaili. The lists include both biblical and non-biblical names. Their sources still need careful investigation, and the rendering of many names into Arabic has changed them so much that identification is often uncertain.5051

Among the Imams associated with Adam's period, for example, we recognize Seth, Abel, and Enoch. In Noah's period we find Shem, Arpachshad, and Japheth, as well as the Arabian prophets Salih and Hud, who are named in the Qur'an. In Abraham's period the names include Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Job, Zeno, and Daniel the Elder. For Moses, they include Aaron, Joshua, and Uzayr. For David, Solomon and Asaph.

In the time of Jesus, the line begins with Shamun al-Safa (Simon bar Kepha, or Peter) and ends—through a series of names different from those of the canonical Christian group—with Bahira, also called George. He is presented as the Nestorian monk who assured Muhammad that his calling to prophecy and his visions were genuine, after Muhammad, troubled by doubt, was brought to him by his wife Khadija.

This repeated appearance of the complete group of twelve throughout sacred history is essential to understanding the story of the Twelfth Imam. It is a continuing spiritual pattern, not a belief in reincarnation. It helps explain the prophetic dreams said to have been given to the Twelfth Imam's mother while she was still a Christian. The twelve “Imams of Christ” do not have quite the same role as the twelve Apostles in Christianity. They do not live at the same time. Instead, they hand on the message from one generation to the next until a new prophet is called—the last Prophet.

We shall encounter them again in the story of the visionary betrothal of the Eleventh Imam and Princess Nargis (see Book VII).

Finally, we come to the Twelve Imams belonging to Muhammad's period. The Second and Third Imams are brothers, both sons of the First Imam and Fatima. From the Fourth Imam onward, the line passes from father to son. According to Shiite tradition, all died as martyrs. From the Fourth Imam on, the means of killing them is consistently said to have been poison.

I. Ali al-Murtada, Amir al-Muminin (“Commander of the Faithful”), husband of Fatima and cousin of the Prophet. Born in Mecca between 600 and 605 CE; assassinated at Kufa in 40 AH/661 CE. His shrine is at Najaf.

II. al-Hasan al-Mujtaba (“the Chosen One”). Born in Medina in 3 AH/624 CE and died there in 49/669. His grave is in al-Baqi, the cemetery of Medina; Baqi means “a place thick with trees.”52

III. al-Husayn, Sayyid al-Shuhada (“Prince of the Martyrs”). Born in Medina in 4/625; killed as a martyr in the tragedy of Karbala in 61/680. His tomb is at the shrine of Karbala, which, together with Najaf, is among the chief places of Shiite pilgrimage. As we have already seen, he and his brother Hasan were still young boys when they joined the Five People of the Cloak. They were then called “the princes of the young people of paradise.”

IV. Ali Zayn al-Abidin al-Sajjad (“Ornament of the Devout,” “He Who Is Constantly at Worship”). Born in Medina in 36 or 38 AH/656 or 659 CE; died in the same city in 92 or 95/711 or 714. His grave is in al-Baqi. He is credited with a work of spiritual teaching known as the “Psalter and Gospel of the Prophet's Family.” Shiite writers have produced many commentaries on it, and it has remained a book of everyday devotion among pious Shiites.

V. Muhammad al-Baqir (“He Who Opens” or “Splits Open,” meaning one who makes knowledge accessible). Born in Medina in 57/676; died there in 115/733. His grave is in al-Baqi. The many sayings attributed to him are especially rich in teachings about inner spiritual knowledge. In certain scenes borrowed from the infancy gospels and adapted in some Ismaili texts, he takes the place occupied by Jesus in the original stories.

VI. Jafar al-Sadiq (“the Truthful,” “the Loyal”). Born in Medina in 80 or 82 AH/699 or 702 CE; died there in 148/765. His grave is in al-Baqi. He taught many pupils and disciples, and a very large number of traditions come from his teaching. Like that of his father, his work was decisive in the development of the different branches of Shiite thought.

VII. Musa al-Kazim (“He Who Controls Himself”). Born in Medina in 128/745; died in Baghdad in 183/799. His tomb is at the shrine of Kazimayn, near Baghdad. Twelver Shiites recognize him as the Seventh Imam. His older brother, Imam Ismail, who died young, gave his name to the Ismaili Shiites, for whom the Imamate continued through Ismail's descendants. Here the Shiite family divides into the Twelver and Seven-Imam branches.

VIII. Ali al-Rida (“He with Whom God Is Pleased”). Born in Medina in 153/770; died at Tus, in Khurasan, in 203/818. His tomb is at the famous shrine in Mashhad, one of the most important places of pilgrimage for Iranian Shiites. We have already seen how the Abbasid caliph al-Mamun, son of Harun al-Rashid, named him his intended successor. The Imam's early death—probably not an accident—ended that plan.

But what could have come of it in any case? The Imam had accepted only under pressure. From the Shiite point of view, there could be no compromise with the direction in which the caliphs' politics had taken Islam. The Imams had to remain what they were: witnesses to a world beyond this world, a different order of reality.

We can still hear the testimony of Imam Rida and of his father, Musa al-Kazim, in the substantial collection in which Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh (d. 381/991) preserved their main teachings and sermons.

IX. Muhammad al-Jawad al-Taqi (“the Generous,” “the Devout”). Born in Medina in 195/811; died in Baghdad in 220/835. His grave is at the shrine of Kazimayn. With him begins the moving and tragic final group of Imams, all of whom died in the prime of life.

X. Ali al-Hadi al-Naqi (“the Guide,” “the Pure One”) was born in Baghdad or Medina in 212 or 214 AH (827 or 830 CE). He died in Samarra in 254 AH (868 CE), in the military camp where the Abbasid caliph and his police had kept him a prisoner for twenty years. A number of teachings attributed to him carry profound meaning. His tomb is in the shrine at Samarra.

XI. Hasan al-Zaki al-Askari (“the Upright One,” “the One Held in the Military Camp”) was born, perhaps in Medina, in 231 AH (845 CE), and died in Samarra in 260 AH (874 CE). He is a moving figure, and we will return to him at length towards the end of this book. Like his father, he is buried at the shrine in Samarra, an important place of Shiite pilgrimage.

XII. Muhammad al-Qa'im, al-Mahdi is the most mysterious of these figures. He is called the One Who Rises (Qa'im), the Rightly Guided One (Mahdi), the Awaited One (Muntazar), the Proof or Guarantor of God (Hujjat), and the unseen master of the present age: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Born in Samarra in 255 AH (869 CE), he disappeared on the very day his father died, 4 Shawwal 260 AH (24 July 874 CE). The entire final book of this work will explore this disappearance, known as the Occultation, what it means, and how it will end.

Leaving aside their titles of honour, the Fourteen Immaculate Ones bear only seven personal names: Muhammad, Fatima, Ali, Hasan, Husayn, Ja'far, and Musa. The meaning of these Names beyond earthly life is one of the great themes of Shiite spiritual philosophy. The order in which the Fourteen briefly appear in our world is not seen as an accident of history. Their earthly succession reflects the order in which they first came into being, before time, in the fullness of the spiritual world—the order in which their beings of light answered the mysterious question, A-lastu bi-rabbikum? (“Am I not your Lord?”). That question resounded in a world before Adam and before anything visible had appeared on earth.

Their brief lives in history therefore cannot show us the whole of who they are. Most of those lives were obscure to the people around them, and marked by grief, sorrow, and hardship.

We must also see their other dimension: a spiritual depth hidden within the fragile, passing body. It still speaks to us through the teachings they gave their disciples, who asked them to explain the meaning of divine revelations. Each of these figures has a fuller identity, revealed from world to world and from one person's awareness to another, that goes infinitely beyond what could appear during a short earthly life. Each of the Twelve Imams deserves a book devoted to this fuller reality. The sources are abundant, and the task would be immense.

Some diagrams show the timeless arrangement of their different ranks. We find them in the writings of scholars of divine wisdom, such as Haydar Amoli, who saw these patterns in their own visions. We also find them in popular Shiite religious art. One familiar Iranian devotional image places the Twelve Imams around the edge of a circle, with the Prophet Muhammad at its centre.

Fatima, her face veiled and her head surrounded by the sun's radiance, connects the Prophet to the line of Imams. Sometimes she appears directly between the Prophet and the First Imam; sometimes she stands a little to the right. The Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam, is shown as a young boy. He marks one end of the line that also includes the Prophet, Fatima, and the First Imam.

These images, which make the invisible figures present to the eye, arise from the deepest feelings of religious devotion. A religion reveals something of its most private secret in its sacred images and its prayers. That secret can never be fully expressed in human words. We would like to make the inner music of Shiite prayer perceptible here, but the subject would require a substantial book of its own.

Because the Imam is “absent,” he cannot personally lead the community's formal prayers in the mosque. Believers can therefore also pray in their own private places of worship. Shiite Islam has developed an extensive body of prayers for personal devotion, known as du'a. This literature contains treasures of religious feeling and insight into the inner life of faith. It includes greetings addressed to each of the Twelve Imams according to the yearly, weekly, or daily calendar, as well as prayers that allow the believer to visit the Twelve—or, more precisely, all Fourteen Immaculate Ones—in the mind and spirit. Later, in Chapter V, we will return to one of these spiritual pilgrimages, the al-Ziyarat al-Jami'a. It begins:

Peace be upon you, members of the House of Prophecy, where the prophetic message has its dwelling, where the angels come one after another, where divine revelation descends…

But we cannot pass over another prayer, widely regarded as the Twelver Shiite prayer above all others. It is attributed to the great philosopher and theologian Nasir al-Din Tusi (d. 672 AH/1274 CE), who played such an important part in protecting the Shiite community when the Mongols captured Baghdad. The prayer is therefore known as the Davazdeh Imam-e Khwajeh-ye Nasir, or “The Twelve Imams of Khwajeh Nasir.” I see no decisive reason to reject this traditional attribution.

In the introduction to the prayer, Tusi himself tells the story of its composition. He had wished to offer a scientific treatise he had written to al-Mu'tasim, who was to be the last Abbasid caliph of Baghdad (640–656 AH/1242–1258 CE).

But the caliph found a tribute to the Twelve Imams at the beginning of the book, tore the manuscript apart, and threw it into the Tigris. Tusi decided that it would be wise to put some distance between himself and the caliph. He left for Samarkand, arriving while preparations were under way for the Mongol expedition that would bring the Abbasid caliphate to an end. During his journey, he dreamed that the Prophet and the First Imam appeared to him and urged him to compose a prayer praising the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.

We will encounter a similar story in Book V, involving a prayer that Mir Damad heard in a visionary dream at the mosque in Qom.

The full prayer, conceived as a spiritual pilgrimage, is too long to reproduce here. Our ellipses show how extensively we have shortened it. Among the passages omitted are the references to each of the Fourteen Ones' shrines—the burial places the worshipper visits in the imagination (as noted above). Our aim is simply to convey the rhythm of the prayer. Each passage has two movements: a changing invocation addressed to God, followed by a response voiced together by the worshippers.53

I. O God, honour and welcome the Prophet; sustain him and bless him… the Lamp that gives light, the shining Star… the Prince of Messengers, the Seal of the Prophets… Honour and peace be upon you, O Messenger of God, O Imam of Mercy, O intercessor for the community, O God's Witness before His creatures, O our prince and our lord… Intercede for us before God.

II. O God, honour and welcome the purest prince, the victorious Imam; sustain him and bless him… the manifestation of wonders and miracles… the blazing Meteor… the Centre of the Circle of Difficulties… the victorious Lion of God… the Imam of East and West… O brother of the Messenger of God, O husband of the Virgin… O God's Witness before His creatures, O our prince and our lord… Intercede for us before God.

III. O God, honour and welcome the glorious Lady; sustain her and bless her—the beautiful, the utterly pure, the wronged, the generous, the noble… who suffered so many sorrows in so short a life… Queen of Women, the Dark-Eyed One, Mother of the Imams… daughter of the greatest of prophets… the Immaculate Virgin, the deeply devout… Honour and peace be upon you and your descendants, O Fatima the Radiant, O daughter of Muhammad, God's Messenger… O God's Witness before His creatures, O our Lady and our sovereign… Intercede for us before God.

IV. O God, honour and welcome the chosen prince, the Imam of Hope; sustain him and bless him… who knew suffering, hardship, and pain, both in their visible and hidden forms… Honour and peace be upon you, O Hasan, O son of the Messenger of God, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of Fatima the Radiant! O God's Witness before His creatures… O prince of the young people of Paradise… Intercede for us before God.

V. O God, honour and welcome the prince who renounced worldly pleasures, the Imam of Prayer; sustain him and bless him… adornment of pulpits and holy places, the One Tried by suffering and sorrow… Honour and peace be upon you, O Husayn ibn Ali! O martyr, O wronged one! Son of the Messenger of God, son of the Commander of the Faithful, son of Fatima the Radiant… O prince of the young people of Paradise… Intercede for us before God.

VI. O God, honour and welcome the father of the Imams and Lamp of the Community; sustain him and bless him… the One Who Knew Sorrow, the One Who Brought the Tradition to Life… Honour and peace be upon you, O Ali ibn Husayn, O al-Sajjad (foremost in worship), O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

VII. O God, honour and welcome the Moon of Moons, the Light of Lights, Guide of the Chosen and Prince of the Just; sustain him and bless him… a surging Ocean and a precious Pearl… Honour and peace be upon you, O Muhammad ibn Ali, O al-Baqir (the one who penetrates the depths of knowledge)… O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

VIII. O God, honour and welcome the faithful and utterly truthful prince; sustain him and bless him—the wise, the steadfast, the patient, the compassionate, the guide along the path, the one who gives his Shiite followers a generous draught of pure wine… Honour and peace be upon you, O Ja'far ibn Muhammad, O al-Sadiq… O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

IX. O God, honour and welcome the generous prince, the patient Imam, the one who knew how to master his anger; sustain him and bless him… the one surrounded by the brightest radiance of nobility… Honour and peace be upon you, O Musa ibn Ja'far, O al-Kazim, O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

X. O God, honour and welcome the purest prince, the wronged Imam, the martyr who died by poison; sustain him and bless him… the sage who knows the hidden knowledge, the full moon in a star-filled sky… companion of souls… Honour and peace be upon you, O Ali ibn Musa, O al-Rida, son of the Messenger of God… God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

XI. O God, honour and welcome the prince of justice, the noble-hearted, the generous; sustain him and bless him… the one who knows the secrets of the Beginning and the Return, guide to all people, refuge of his friends on the day when the caller raises his cry… the Imam in the tradition of Ahmad, the Light of Muhammad… Honour and peace be upon you, O Muhammad ibn Ali, O al-Taqi al-Jawad, O son of the Messenger of God… O God's Witness before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

XII and XIII. O God, honour and welcome the two noble and perfect Imams; sustain them and bless them… twin suns, twin moons, twin lights… heirs to the two holy sanctuaries… both helpers of the human race… twin signs of right guidance… both of whom knew hardship and sorrow, both masters of generosity and goodness… Honour and peace be upon you both, O Ali ibn Muhammad and O Hasan ibn Ali! Upon you, O al-Naqi al-Hadi, and upon you, O al-Zaki al-Askari! Sons of the Messenger of God… God's Witnesses before His creatures… Both of you, intercede for us before God.

XIV. O God, honour and welcome the one who gathers into himself the Prophet's calling, the fierce courage of the Lion of God, the perfect purity of Fatima, the patience of Hasan, the bravery of Husayn, the devotion of al-Sajjad, the memorable teachings of al-Baqir, the traditions of Ja'far, the knowledge of al-Kazim, the arguments of al-Rida, the generosity and devotion of al-Jawad al-Taqi, the revered dignity of the two Askaris, the hiddenness of divine concealment, the One Who Rises (Qa'im) in truth… the Word of God… God's Witness, the One Who Triumphs by God's command… Imam in secret and Imam openly revealed, the one who drives away sorrow and grief… the generous, the noble-hearted, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, unseen lord of this age and representative of the All-Merciful, Imam of human beings and jinn… Honour and peace be upon you, O heir of Hasan Askari, O Imam of our time, O awaited One Who Rises, O guided one who guides others! Son of the Messenger of God… Witness of God before His creatures… Intercede for us before God.

This is how Shiite hearts pray. At the end of the present work we will meet the last three Imams again, especially the moving figures of the Tenth and Eleventh, the two Askaris. Although the Abbasid government held them captive in the military camp at Samarra, they were preparing the way for the mysterious Twelfth Imam's brief appearance in this world. One of the surviving texts will then allow us to hear the distinctive tone of the prayers he inspires in those who make a spiritual pilgrimage to him.

As we have already said, just as his ancestor Muhammad is the “Seal of the Prophets,” the Twelfth Imam is the Seal of the Muhammadan walayat: the final and fullest expression of the spiritual bond through which God's friends lead others into the mystery of divine manifestations. The Prophet and the Imam reveal the same original Light and the same Supreme Spirit (Ruh A'zam). The Prophet brings the outward message; the Imam discloses its inner meaning.

Walayat is that inward reality—the spiritual truth contained within prophecy—while prophecy is its outward and visible form. Just as every prophet was a manifestation (mazhar) of the Seal of the Prophets, so every friend of God and every person initiated into the spiritual life manifests, in some measure, the one who is and will be the Muhammadan Seal of God's Friends. In the chapters that follow, we must explore this whole group of ideas more deeply.

4. The Paradoxes Faced by Ismailism and Twelver Shiism

Even this brief account has allowed us to glimpse some of the defining features of Twelver Shiism: its central ideas, the direction of its spiritual life, and what we might call its focus on the Imam. What I can say here is necessarily only a beginning, a foundation for further work. And to give a rounded picture of Shiite thought and spirituality—without leaving out a vital part of Iranian Islam—we would now need to turn to its other main branch. This is the tradition sometimes described as the “Seveners,” but more commonly called Ismailism.

As we have seen, Ismailism takes its name from its Seventh Imam, Ismail, the eldest son of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 148 AH/765 CE), who died before his father. The two great branches of Shiism part ways at the Seventh Imam. In Ismaili teachings about divine wisdom and the Imams, seven, rather than twelve, becomes the central number. I have outlined elsewhere the main differences between Ismailism and Twelver Shiism, so I will not repeat that discussion here. Both traditions still deserve a comprehensive study of their deepest ideas, and I hope to devote separate works to them.54 For now, I want simply to recall why the Ismaili religious tradition matters so much to the spiritual history of Iranian Islam.

To begin with, any serious study of Shiism must return to its origins during the Prophet's own lifetime. It must therefore start before the movement divided into its two principal branches (alongside smaller branches, such as the Zaydis of Yemen). Such a study would need to bring together the traditional teachings of the Imams accepted by both principal branches. Together, these teachings make up an enormous body of material. Preserving and collecting them was above all the work of Twelver Shiites. Meanwhile, between the fourth/tenth and fifth/eleventh centuries, Ismaili thinkers produced their great syntheses of divine wisdom. These belonged to the Fatimid period, and some of the most important authors were Iranian: Abu Ya'qub Sijistani, al-Mu'ayyad Shirazi, Hamid al-Din Kirmani, Nasir-e Khusraw, and others.

During the same period, Twelver Shiites—often living under extremely difficult conditions—were chiefly occupied with gathering the traditions of their Imams. They arranged these teachings systematically around the major subjects that would become standard in Shiite religious thought. Their patient care made possible a later achievement. When conditions improved for Twelver Shiism, the great Iranian theologian of the Safavid period, Muhammad Baqir Majlisi (d. 1110 AH/1698–99 CE), was able to work with a whole team of assistants to assemble this vast collection. In its older, stone-printed edition, it filled no fewer than twenty-six parts in fourteen large folio volumes. At the time of writing, a new printed edition was being prepared in Tehran.

For various reasons, some traditions (hadith) were not included. Even so, the collection brings together the teachings of the Prophet and the Twelve Imams: the full body of sacred tradition (sunna) recognised by Twelver Shiism. It is not merely the basis for interpreting the deeper meaning of revelation. It is also an encyclopedia of spiritual knowledge. Its subjects include God's oneness (tawhid), prophecy, the Imams, the universe, human nature, and what happens at the end of time. It also explains religious rites and the practice of the sacred law (sharia).

In short, it addresses both the inner meaning (batin) and the outward form (zahir) of religion.

We have already seen how central this distinction is to Shiism. Batin means what is inward, hidden, or spiritual: the deeper meaning. Zahir means what is apparent or outward: the expressed words, the visible form, the literal meaning. The two correspond to the distinct roles of Prophet and Imam.

Twelver Shiism has sought to keep them in perfect balance. The Prophet and the Imam are two lamps lit from the same Light (we will return to this in Chapter VI). The inner meaning cannot exist for us without the outward form that carries it. What a symbol means can reveal itself only through the symbol itself. This was also the position of Ismaili teachers in the Fatimid period.

On this subject, we possess a long letter from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq to his disciple Mufaddal al-Ju'fi, who was disturbed by the extreme views of certain fellow believers. The Imam did not condemn their search for hidden knowledge. He condemned one particular, fundamental mistake.55 Knowing the inner meaning of prayer, pilgrimage, fasting, and other religious practices does not give us permission to stop practising them. Spiritual knowledge allows the deeper truth (haqiqat) to shine through the rites prescribed by the sacred law (sharia). It makes the very words of the law transparent to their inner meaning.

But that can happen only while both the outward practice and its inward truth remain together.

Break that connection, and spiritual freedom turns into a rejection of all discipline. The living world of symbols is destroyed; in one sense, Adam's mistake is repeated. This is why Imam Ja'far so strongly insisted on preserving the balance between zahir and batin, and why Twelver Shiism would continue to regard that balance as essential.

Yet human history has constantly threatened this balance, precisely because it runs against the grain of ordinary worldly affairs. This conflict is what I mean by the spiritual struggle of Shiism. We have seen that Shiism's deepest secret lies in walayat: the special bond of divine love and devotion that gives the Twelve Imams their spiritual responsibility to preserve and pass on the inner meaning of revelation. Walayat is therefore described as the “inner meaning of the prophetic mission” (batin al-nubuwwat).

But this leads to an unsettling question. Could the greatest danger facing a religion devoted to hidden spiritual truth be the very thing that seems to promise its success—a victory in the world of politics? Its ultimate triumph belongs, by its nature, to the end of time. If a religion whose hope points beyond ordinary history must adapt itself to the demands of government and public life, will political success bring about a deep crisis in its spiritual teaching?

Ismailism and Twelver Shiism each faced this paradox, though under very different conditions. For Ismailism, the test came through the success of the Fatimid dynasty in Egypt, between the tenth and twelfth centuries. For Twelver Shiism, it began at the opening of the sixteenth century, when the young Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty, restored Iran's national unity, and established Twelver Shiism as the state religion.

How did Ismailism respond to this trial? This is not the place to examine the gap between the lofty spiritual philosophy found in Ismaili books and the practical necessities of Fatimid rule in Cairo. It is fair to say, without oversimplifying matters, that Fatimid political policy did not in itself favour placing the inner meaning of religion at the centre of attention.

After the death of the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir bi'llah in 487 AH (1094 CE), a bitter crisis split the Ismaili community into two branches. The so-called western branch continued the earlier Fatimid tradition. The eastern branch emerged from the reform proclaimed at Alamut, the famous Ismaili stronghold in the mountains southwest of the Caspian Sea. This was, more particularly, Iranian Ismailism.

What distinguished this reformed Iranian tradition was its willingness to tip the balance decisively towards haqiqat, the inner spiritual truth, and away from sharia, the law governing outward religious practice. It therefore also gave the Imam precedence over the Prophet. This was the meaning of the proclamation of the “Great Resurrection” (Qiyamat al-Qiyamat) at Alamut on 8 August 1164. Recently, a few devoted individuals have been able to mark its eight-hundredth anniversary,5657 making up for the neglect of an age so absorbed in official, outward history that it scarcely notices the events of spiritual history, which escape its control and its usual categories.

Put very simply, the solemn proclamation at Alamut of the personal religion of the Resurrection (Din-e Qiyamat) announced the end of the rule of sharia.

The spirit of the Alamut reform thus stands in sharp contrast to the political Ismailism of the Fatimids. It was, in a sense, a reaction against it. If we compare the surviving documents with the earliest Ismaili writings, we cannot help feeling that the reform recovered something of the spirit of an original, uncompromising Shiism—an understanding of the Imam that existed before the Fatimid dynasty.

Another sign of this spirit appeared after the Mongols destroyed the Alamut organisation and its fortified centres in Iran. Iranian Ismailism went underground and became closely blended with Sufism. Even today, it is regarded, to some extent, as a Sufi tariqa, or spiritual brotherhood. Here, devotion to the Imam unfolds into an experience of mystical love, with the Imam as its centre. Twelver Shiism knows this experience too, for its spiritual life draws upon the same sources.

Consider, for example, the way the Qur'an's Verse of Light (24:35) is interpreted. It speaks of an olive tree that is “neither of the East nor of the West.” In mystical interpretation, this becomes a tree growing at the summit of an inward Mount Sinai. The mountain is the spiritual person, who relives the experience of Moses. And the olive tree represents the Imam: the Soul of the soul, the soul's eternal Beloved.58

As this suggests, the flourishing of mystical love is not what separates Ismaili spirituality from that of Twelver Shiism. On both sides, walayat could lead to the same flowering. What gives Twelver spirituality its particular character is the paradox it had to face in order to remain true to itself. More precisely, we shall find that it confronted two related paradoxes.

First, Twelver Shiism has a different understanding of the Imam and of the Imam's relation to the present world. As we have already observed, its complete spiritual company of Imams is fixed at twelve from before the beginning of time. The idea of the Hidden Imam is therefore built into the very meaning of the Imam in Twelver belief.

The Twelfth Imam's spiritual rule stretches across the interval between his past presence and his future return. He is invisibly present within the time of this world, from the moment he disappeared from human sight in 260 AH (874 CE) until the day he appears again. His rule continues on a spiritual plane beyond the reach of the senses, and its daily effects unfold in the hidden depths of human awareness. His position is not comparable to that of the Fatimid Imams, descendants of Imam Ismail, who held political power in Cairo for two centuries—from the rise of Ubaydallah al-Mahdi in 909 to the death of al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah in 1130.

For the same reason, Shah Ismail (1487–1524), the founder of the Safavid dynasty, cannot be compared with the Fatimid Imams. Acting with all the fervour of youth, Shah Ismail acted in the name of the invisible Imam. He restored the Shiite community's right to live openly—its right to bear witness to its faith in this world.

But he was not himself the Imam. The same distinction has applied ever since to every Iranian ruler who has governed a Shiite state.

The ruler's task is to secure for believers the time of their waiting, until the Imam appears again. Becoming a state religion inevitably changed Shiite life from what it had been during the years of secrecy.

Yet the belief that the Imam is essentially invisible makes spiritual life more demanding in a way that differs profoundly from a tradition in which the Imam can be encountered, generation after generation, as a living person in the physical world. By treating the ghaybat—the Imam's concealment or invisibility—as essential to his role, Twelver Shiism places the Imam's reality on an exceptionally high spiritual horizon.

We must go further, because some Western writers have introduced a serious misunderstanding by speaking of “Shiite legitimism,” as though the Imams were simply the rightful claimants in a dynastic struggle. Their cause is not a claim by one earthly dynasty against another. As we have already said, the dynasty of the Grail is no more a rival of an earthly dynasty or of the succession to the Apostolic See. Reducing the matter to competing claims for power misses the point entirely.

Rivalry is possible only between things that exist on the same level. Here we are dealing with two different worlds. The malakut, the spiritual kingdom, stands too far above the world of our political struggles to compete with it.

We can learn something important about this from Qazi Sa'id Qummi (d. 1103 AH/1691 CE), an outstanding scholar of divine wisdom in the Safavid period. In his enormous commentary on a work by Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh, one of the earliest Shiite teachers, he writes:

The tradition firmly establishes that God's Messenger was given a choice between being a servant and being a king. He chose to be a prophet who was a servant (abd nabi), not a prophet who was a king (malik nabi). There can therefore be no outward, worldly kingship (saltanat zahira) inherited from him, no rule of the kind exercised by the powerful of this world (imarat al-jababira). If he himself possessed no such kingship, how could anyone who succeeded him inherit it?

So, if the Prophet has a successor, that succession must necessarily be religious (khilafat diniya). Its purpose is to help believers prepare as well as possible for the journey and the Return. This spiritual kingship (saltanat ma'nawiya) belongs to one who is constant in devotion, one who can truly be called the very soul of the Prophet—as the Prophet himself said of Ali, Hasan, and Husayn.59

Nothing could be clearer. This statement expresses, in a particularly direct way, the religious understanding of spiritual Islam held by the Shiite scholars to whom we must turn if we want to understand their tradition.

The Imam's role as a spiritual king, and his essential invisibility in the present condition of the world, both follow from the idea of walayat. That idea will keep returning throughout this work. We must now bring out another part of its meaning, which will prepare us to understand the first of our two paradoxes.

In Shiite writings, the word mahabbat, meaning “love,” often appears alongside walayat, or even takes its place. It describes the devoted love that believers feel for the holy Imams. More precisely, accepting the Imams' walayat is inseparable from recognising the Prophet's mission (nubuwwat), just as recognising that mission is inseparable from affirming God's oneness (tawhid). The profession of faith (shahadat) is therefore, in its fullest form, a threefold declaration. Without all three parts, someone may be a Muslim (muslim), in the sense of professing Islam, but is not yet a true believer (mu'min) in the Shiite sense.60

In the devotion shown to the “Holy Family,” then, Shiite Islam reveals itself as a religion of love. This is strikingly different from the mainly legal character often associated with Islam, and which does, to a degree, correspond to the general approach of Sunni Islam.

But Shiite teachers rely on their most explicit traditions to make an even stronger claim: without the loving intention and devoted service contained in walayat, no good deed can receive God's acceptance.

In this respect, Shiism—which has so often been presented as the opposite of Sufism—was already following the path of love before Sufism came to be identified with it. Yet this immediately raises a serious question. If many deeply devoted Shiites have indeed expressed misgivings about Sufism, what was the relationship between Shiism and Sufism at their beginnings?

One of the hardest questions Sufism had to face was whether love—the word itself, as well as the feeling—could properly describe the relationship between a human being and God. We will encounter this question again in Book III, when we study Ruzbihan. The answers given by different thinkers varied widely.

Here, however, we must make an essential point. Shiism insists, through its understanding of what cannot be said about God, that God's oneness (tawhid) places the divine reality absolutely beyond our grasp.61

But it is precisely the teaching about the Imams that keeps this belief from falling into two opposite traps. One is to say that God is so unknowable that nothing meaningful can be known or said about the divine. The other is to imagine God too easily in human terms. Both, in different ways, distort our understanding of God.

Shiism avoids these traps by recognising the pre-eternal spiritual reality of the Imams as the place where God's Names and Attributes become manifest. In the Imam, the believer contemplates the revealed “Face” of God. We introduced this idea of the divine Face in Chapter I, Section 3, and will return to it. From its beginnings, then, and before Sufism had even worked through the problem, Shiism had found a way to understand the love that can exist between a human creature and a God who, in himself, remains beyond all reach.

All this is contained in walayat, understood as the inner meaning of the prophetic message, and in the Imam's role as the guide who leads us into the inner world (batin). But by “inner world” I do not mean something merely private or subjective, as opposed to something objective and real.

That may be difficult to explain today. There is a kind of disbelief that still calls itself Christian yet speaks contemptuously of “inward and subjective religiosity.” Its advocates are so absorbed in their “engagement” with the affairs of this world that they have never taken the time to understand what they dismiss. For the spiritual thinkers we are studying, the inner world means the spiritual reality of worlds beyond the senses. Far from being less real than the outer world, this spiritual reality surrounds and contains it.

Qazi Sa'id Qummi gives this surprising idea particular emphasis. In the circles of the spiritual worlds, unlike those of the material world, the centre surrounds the circumference. To “leave” what we normally call the outer world is not merely a subjective experience. It is, in the fullest possible sense, an experience of reality—however difficult that may be to convey to someone determined to think of themselves as “modern.”

Even so, Shiism has not always been free, throughout its history, to express openly the essential character I have just sketched. We said earlier that it too had to face a trial and a paradox resembling those faced by Ismailism under the Fatimids.

Yet the trial was bound to take a different form. We have already seen why, and we shall return to the matter: the Twelver understanding of the Imam and his spiritual authority is shaped above all by the Twelfth Imam and the belief that his concealment (ghaybat) is necessary.

For a long time, Shiites were forced to practise their faith in varying degrees of secrecy. With the restoration of Iranian sovereignty under the Safavids, however, they could at last live openly. Such a change brings a powerful temptation to settle comfortably into this world. And the more comfortable our place in this world becomes, the less likely we are to give our full attention to the questions that matter most to thinkers concerned with spiritual wisdom.

Perhaps this helps explain the paradoxical growth, within Shiism, of fiqh, the study of religious law, at the expense of irfan and hikmat ilahiya: inner spiritual knowledge and divine wisdom, both taught by the Imams themselves. Yet the tradition of the hukama and the urafa—the sages and those devoted to inner knowledge—has never been broken, right down to our own day. It remains something distinctive in Islam. We will return to this vital part of Shiism's spiritual struggle.

At first sight, then, the situation might seem quite simple. On one side stand those devoted to the spiritual life, who remain faithful to what they see as the whole of Shiism: both its outward practice and its inner meaning. Broadly speaking, these are the urafa and hukama, the mystics and the philosophers of divine wisdom. In Book II, we shall see how Suhrawardi distinguished different levels among them.

On the other side stand those who, for one reason or another, distrust anything they regard as “philosophy.” They devote themselves to fiqh, religious law, almost as though it were the only truly Islamic field of knowledge. These are the fuqaha, the scholars of the Law. Their fellow Shiites have more than once accused them of a profound inconsistency: they claim to teach the Imams' religion while setting aside an essential part of the Imams' own teaching.

But the real situation is more complicated than this division suggests. Much of the difficulty arises from the uncertain relationship between Shiism and Sufism at their beginnings, one cause of which we have already touched upon.

In Sunni Islam, the broad pattern is easier to recognise. Over the centuries, Sufism and the Sufis have stood, in contrast to the scholars of religious law, for the daring possibilities of inner religion and the seeming contradictions of a faith rooted in love. In Shiite Islam, matters are not so simple. From the very beginning, walayat has stood at the heart of Shiite teaching. As a result, that teaching already includes everything needed for a religion of love directed towards a divine manifestation: the revealed Face of God, who in himself is beyond all knowledge, the Person who can “answer on behalf of” the unreachable God.

As a point of orientation, this same Face guides the mystic on an ascent through the spiritual worlds that it reveals. As the spiritual centre, the invisible Imam gathers around himself an entire order of spiritual beings who, like him, remain hidden from the eyes of this world. All these ideas can also be found in Sufism and its spiritual philosophy. Indeed, Sunni Sufism can sometimes give the impression of being a kind of Shiism that no longer dares to call itself Shiite.

And yet this is precisely why someone who lives the fullness of Shiite faith has no need to become a Sufi as such. Shiism already offers a tariqa, a spiritual path, as we suggested in Chapter I, Section 3 (pp. 18 onward). In other words, Sufism (tasawwuf) does not embrace the whole of mystical life in Islam. That brings us back to the question raised earlier: what, at their beginnings, was the relationship between Shiism and Sufism? Or, to put it another way, what were the beginnings of spiritual Islam?

Simply asking the question clearly helps us avoid confusion. The existence of Shiite Sufism does not, by itself, answer it. Nor should we assume that a Shiite theologian who has reservations about Sufism—even strong ones—must belong to the legal scholars who oppose mysticism. Far from it. Many Shiite spiritual thinkers speak the same language as the Sufis without being Sufis themselves. They belong to no Sufi tariqa.

Mulla Sadra Shirazi, one of the greatest Iranian thinkers of divine wisdom, even found it necessary to write a book against the Sufis of his own day. At the same time, some of his colleagues accused him of being a Sufi. Sufism itself takes many forms. Some Sufi traditions have developed an extraordinary understanding of spiritual reality, tested and confirmed through lived experience. Others dismiss this kind of philosophical understanding altogether. In some, devotion to the Imams is central. In others, the figure of the Sufi master (shaykh) tends to take the place of the Imams' transcendent spiritual presence.

We can therefore speak of a double paradox. First, there is the paradox of religious-law scholars who have lost sight of the full meaning of Shiism and its inner spiritual foundation. This problem grew worse after the Safavid period, though its signs were visible earlier, just as the great schools of thought of the Safavid age had themselves been prepared by previous generations. Second, there is the paradox of forms of Sufism that have forgotten their own origins.

Caught between these two, many Shiite spiritual thinkers had to struggle on two fronts at once. This was true of Mulla Sadra Shirazi and many others, right through to the Shaykhi school. Earlier still, it was especially true of Haydar Amoli, who lived in the eighth/fourteenth century. In his great body of work, he brought together the problems faced by Shiite spiritual thinkers and understood them with remarkable clarity (see Book IV). That is why we shall turn to his writings so often in the pages ahead.

The full complexity of this situation is anything but obvious. To see it, one must spend many years not only with books, but also with people.

What is at stake is nothing less than our understanding of Islam, together with an entire view of human destiny. It is striking that the very features that seem essential to Shiite spirituality, and which we have only briefly outlined here, have so far escaped the notice of Western readers and most Sunni Muslims alike.

In the coming chapters, then, we shall ask Haydar Amoli how he understands the Shiite texts that use Adam's story to express the human condition. Seen in this light, certain conversations between the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and his chosen disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad take on a new meaning. They seem already to foreshadow the entire destiny of Shiism. They also stand in sharp contrast to the “impossible syntheses” we heard described earlier, in the painful admissions of a Sunni Arab figure from Jordan.

In short, Haydar Amoli, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, and later the teachers of the Shaykhi school help us understand both the positions at issue and what is still at stake in what we have called the spiritual struggle of Shiism.

Chapter III The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism

1. The Position of Shiite Spiritual Thinkers

Twelver Shiism has often seemed to stand in opposition to the world around it. It has faced fierce hostility that has rarely let up. This hostility was directed against the First Imam himself, and it marked the tragic lives of his eleven descendants.

Yet the Imams warned their followers from the beginning that their cause would be difficult. To remain faithful to it, they would need “hearts tested by faith.” As a distinguished shaykh once told me, “Never forget that only a handful of people remained faithful to our Imams. It will be like that until the end of this age.” In Shiite understanding, the tradition bears witness to the full spiritual meaning of Islam's prophetic message. For that reason, it could not make peace with the world's ambitions and designs.

Our purpose here is not to write a political history. We only need to understand why so many traces of Shiite life disappear from the historical record. This was especially true after the Seljuk Turks entered Baghdad in 1055, ending the influence of the Persian Shiite Buyid dynasty. For centuries, Shiites lived discreetly, observing strict rules about keeping their beliefs and teachings hidden. Even today, we may have difficulty deciding whether a particular writer was Shiite.

We can sense an admission between the lines, but it was something the author could not safely say openly.

An anonymous Persian treatise from the seventh Islamic century (the thirteenth century CE) expresses this frustration with remarkable force. Its author writes:

Suppose someone asks why the teachings of the Sunni legal scholars, the fuqaha, have spread so widely, while the teachings of the holy Imams—the Ahl al-Bayt, the members of the Prophet's household—have not. Here is the answer. When Muawiya, the first Umayyad ruler, seized power over the Muslim community, he gave free rein to his hatred of the Commander of the Faithful, the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib. He wrote to his governors, ordering them to put to death anyone who followed Ali's religion. ... People even cursed Ali from the pulpits of the mosques. ... The same hatred pursued the Imam's descendants, making it difficult for them to teach or gather students.

We are told that when Sufyan al-Thawri visited the Sixth Imam, Jafar al-Sadiq, the Imam said to him: “Sufyan, the Abbasid police are looking for you, and the ruler has his eye on you. Leave quickly!

“But understand that we are not sending you away.” And when Abu Hanifa, the founder of the Hanafi school of Sunni law, had to refer to the Commander of the Faithful in his lessons, he would say only, “The shaykh said this ...”62

Things did not improve when Umayyad rule ended and the Abbasids came to power in 132 AH (750 CE). The Imams had to remain inside their homes and practise taqiyya: discretion, or the careful concealment of teachings that could put them in danger. No one could freely come to help them or receive a riwaya, a transmitted teaching, from them. ... Meanwhile, every opportunity was given to the legal scholars who opposed the Imams. Their hatred and ignorance brought them honours.

Each was given a province (wilayat) in which he could spread his teaching as he pleased. All this is well known. Let anyone with wisdom reflect on it. If something of the Imams' teaching is still found everywhere today, despite all these obstacles, surely that proves that God protects the religion of His Messenger, the community of our Imams, and their knowledge.63

This bleak picture gives us some sense of what Shiites endured at the hands of the religious establishment backed by political power. The Tenth and Eleventh Imams lived virtually as prisoners in the military camp at Samarra, about a hundred kilometres north of Baghdad. Both died while still young.

Yet they too had fearless students, to whom they passed on their teaching, as the great encyclopedia of Majlisi, mentioned earlier, shows.

The anonymous thirteenth-century writer ends on a note that captures something essential in the Shiite outlook: what we might call desperatio fiducialis, a despair that still trusts. He lived during the upheaval of the Mongol invasions, in the age of the Shiite philosopher and theologian Nasir al-Din Tusi and the Shiite Sufi master Sad al-Din Hamuyah.

In the following century came the writings of Haydar Amoli and Rajab Borsi. Later still, in the century before the rise of the Safavids, came the work of Ibn Abi Jumhur, whom we have already met. If further proof were needed, this history would offer another example of the saying that “the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the faithful.”

But when we speak of the spiritual struggle of Shiism, we are not thinking primarily of this open conflict, in which everyone can easily identify who belongs to which side. We mean something subtler: a struggle against a danger arising from within. This danger is harder to recognise because, as we have just seen in the preceding pages, it takes shape at the very moment when everything outwardly seems to be going well.

From the outside, one might hardly expect danger to grow out of a success as striking as the rise of the Safavids in Iran. It did not, at least, begin with Shah Ismail himself. He was a Sufi, surrounded by Sufi companions. At fifteen, after entering Tabriz in triumph, he boldly had the prayer recited in the great mosque in the name of the holy Imams, despite the hostility of the city's Sunni population.64 At that time, the Safavid family had many ties with the Nimatullahi family, descended from Shah Nimatullah Wali of Kerman, one of the great masters of Shiite Sufism (died 834 AH/1431 CE).65

But the situation changed profoundly under Shah Abbas the Great (1587–1628). We are not concerned here with the history of his reign. What matters is what happened to people devoted to the spiritual life. Mulla Sadra Shirazi's personal remarks in his books—and the reasons he wrote several of those books—tell us enough about that. We shall return to him in Book V.

The Safavid revival brought an extraordinary flowering of thought, unlike anything else then found in the Islamic world. Several schools arose whose influence can still be felt today. Their leading figures included Mir Damad, Sadra Shirazi, Mohsen Fayz, Rajab Ali Tabrizi, and many others, followed in turn by generations of students.

But this does not mean their lives were easy. Mulla Sadra tells us why he spent about ten years in seclusion in a small village hidden high in a valley near Qom: the hostility of the fuqaha, the legal scholars, and their refusal to engage with hikmat (philosophical and spiritual wisdom) or irfan (inner spiritual knowledge).

We now encounter the paradox we began to describe a few pages ago. Shiite spiritual knowledge had survived centuries of persecution and concealment.

Yet with Shiism's worldly success, it faced a new kind of trial. Human affairs took their familiar course. Alongside the exceptional achievements of the great sages, the hukama, there grew an increasingly powerful religious establishment centred on law. It became more and more concerned with the practical details of religious rules, legal judgments, and individual cases, and increasingly suspicious of philosophy, divine wisdom, and mystical experience. Strictly speaking, it is difficult to talk about a clergy where there is no Church.

Yet the fuqaha and the akhunds—the religious scholars and teachers—have sometimes filled that role so thoroughly that the consequences are still felt today.

Mulla Sadra is not our only witness. The lack of understanding later shown towards the Shaykhi school offers another example; we shall discuss it in Book VI. I can say that even today, in Iran, the dominance of fiqh (Islamic religious law) and the fuqaha is a frequent subject of quiet conversation among the hukama (sages) and the urafa (those devoted to inner spiritual knowledge). How did things reach this point? How did the study of religious law come to occupy so much ground?

Of course, the study of law forms part of every philosopher-theologian's education. The problem arises with legal scholars who claim that all theological knowledge can be reduced to fiqh. In doing so, they cut away part of the Imams' own teaching and prevent Shiism from making its spiritual message known.

But keeping that message alive and passing it on has nothing to do with whether a particular Muslim society decides to introduce a civil legal code in order to “adapt to the modern world.” When the whole of Islamic learning is narrowed to the study of religious law, the result is a dead end.

This is no doubt a familiar pattern in the social history of religion, and not only in Islam. The rejection of spiritual insight, or gnosis, grows out of a rigid reliance on reason that often conceals an unwillingness—or an inability—to recognise what lies beyond it. The result is the situation we described earlier: Shiism is almost forced to hide from itself. Its own tradition of inner spiritual knowledge must retreat from official Shiism in order to survive intact.

Yet from the beginning, Shiism understood itself as the inner meaning of the prophetic message (batin al-nubuwwa). In the moving words of Imam Jafar, it was the religion of the strangers, the ghuraba, within Muhammad's community. That worldly triumph should have produced an official Shiism that in turn makes strangers of the Imam's own strangers—this is what gives the “spiritual struggle of Shiism” its meaning.

It is for Shiism itself to carry that struggle through and overcome the predicament described by the Jordanian public figure in the interview we discussed earlier (pp. 32 onward). The age of outward triumph has already passed. Only those who understand the Imam's call will be able to meet the immense questions raised within Shiite Islam, as elsewhere, by the influence of the West. And this is not simply a problem facing traditional Islam in what is called the modern world. It faces everyone, wherever they live, who still senses that human beings have a spiritual destiny beyond this earthly life.

Iranian Islam has never lacked people willing to take up this struggle, generation after generation, right down to our own time. Earlier, we said that Shiite spiritual thinkers had to fight on two fronts. Haydar Amoli's writings show that one of these fronts was itself divided in two, because Sufism could be understood in two very different ways. It could be seen as a witness to Shiism within the Sunni world, or as a movement that had broken away and forgotten its beginnings.

To understand this, we must return to a particular kind of Shiite spiritual thinker.
