Such people use much the same specialised language as the Sufis, and their teaching about divine wisdom is familiar enough that many non-Shiite Sufis can readily find their way through it. They too have dreams and visionary experiences. Yet they do not belong to Sufism as an organised movement.

This was precisely the situation that led Mulla Sadra, on one side, to confront legal scholars who dismissed spiritual wisdom and, on the other, to write a treatise against certain Sufis of his day.66 These Sufis professed a kind of pious refusal to seek knowledge. They scorned books and rejected philosophical reflection as a spiritual practice. In the end, this attitude could become a kind of spiritual licence: the opposite error to that of the legal scholars. Instead of giving all importance to the outward form of religion, they readily claimed to possess its inner meaning (batin) without needing its outward form (zahir).

The mystical philosophers of the Shaykhi school also criticised Sufism. One of their objections concerned the way some Sufis understood wahdat al-wujud, the idea that “being” has one meaning wherever we encounter it.

But their criticism was directed above all at Sufi orders (tariqat), their collective practices, and the authority given to the Sufi shaykh or master. For these Shiite thinkers, Shiism itself, understood in its fullness, is already the spiritual path in the highest sense. A separate Sufi master therefore seems to take the place of the one spiritual guide a Shiite should acknowledge and follow: the Hidden Imam, who cannot be seen by the senses but is present to the heart. We might compare the role of a Sufi shaykh here with that of a guru in India.

These thinkers shared the view Haydar Amoli had expressed much earlier: that Sufism first arose within Islam through Shiism, but lost its true nature when it broke away from the Shiite Imams.

Indeed, it is as though Sunni Sufism transferred the teaching about the Imams onto the person of the Prophet alone, leaving out whatever did not fit Sunni belief. Take the Sufi idea of the mystical Pole, the Qutb: it is essentially the idea of the Imam. In Shiite Sufism, the Imam remains the Pole of poles, because he is the Seal of walayat, the highest spiritual guidance and closeness to God. In Sunni Sufism, the Qutb takes the place occupied by the Imam in Shiite thought.

We can already see signs of this relationship during the third and fourth Islamic centuries (the ninth and tenth centuries CE), when the great works of Ismaili spiritual philosophy began to appear. The question becomes even more pointed when Sunni Sufis present themselves as bearers of a message from the Hidden Imam.

Consider al-Hallaj. He cannot simply be separated from the people whose technical language he adopted: no one borrows a set of words without taking something of its meaning.

Yet it seems that people tried to distance him from them in order to discredit those very people. The more sharply he is separated from them, however, the more this seems to support the Shiite judgment of his case.

We should also remember Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous alchemist. According to a long-established tradition that has never been decisively disproved, he was a disciple of Imam Jafar al-Sadiq. From early on he was known as the Sufi. Jabir's alchemy cannot be separated from his Shiite ideas: the Imam plays the same role in the spiritual world that the Stone or the Elixir plays in the world of Nature. One of Jabir's most difficult works may even contain the earliest developed expression of a genuinely spiritual theme: the Stranger, the one who comes from elsewhere, the spiritual exile (gharib) who has travelled from distant shores.

In Shiite spiritual thought, the model for this Stranger is Salman the Persian (Salman Parsi), also called Salman the Pure (Salman Pak). He was a pilgrim searching for the true Prophet. Born into the chivalric tradition of the Zoroastrian religion, he passed through Christianity before finding what he understood as pure, spiritual Islam. Alone and without family, he became the adopted son of the Imam.

Salman's story is also the story of everyone addressed by Imam Jafar's celebrated saying. We must quote it again, because it serves almost as a guiding motto: “Islam began as a stranger, and it will become a stranger again, just as it was at the beginning. Blessed are those within Muhammad's community who become strangers—the ghuraba.”67

As we already know, these words rule out any simple equation between religion and society. The Imam is not calling people to a merely social religion. By blessing the spiritual exile, he calls that person to refuse compromises with the accepted values and structures of this world. Instead, the world itself becomes the setting for a quest for another world. It becomes the place of a journey towards what is already invisibly present within it: the world of rebirth and Resurrection, which the Imam announces.

If we want to use today's fashionable language, we might say that this is the only true way for the spiritual pilgrim, as a witness to what is absolute, to be “present in the world” or “committed” to it. This is the spiritual Islam whose existence went unnoticed not only by the Jordanian figure whose moving testimony we discussed earlier, but also by the many people whose thinking that testimony sadly represents today.

Imam Jafar's saying, by contrast, describes a person's encounter with the last things—death, resurrection, and the life beyond—as something that can be lived now, in the present. Choosing spiritual exile in order to follow the Imam is a decisive break. It ends a kind of captivity: the safety offered by the walls society builds around individuals to protect them from a direct religious experience. Once those walls are broken, a person suddenly becomes conscious of ghurbat, of being in exile. Suhrawardi will give this discovery unforgettable form in a story we shall examine in Book II.

The Imam's words call his follower into walayat: a devoted love for the pure figures through whom God makes Himself known. Their light draws the person out of the loneliness of exile. It also exposes all the falsehoods that have disguised the reality of that exile and encouraged a comfortable compromise with this world. This is why Haydar Amoli still speaks directly to Shiite spiritual life today. His work awakens readers to a threefold spiritual struggle, a struggle on three fronts, which they must face if they are to answer the Imam's call and remain faithful to Shiism in its fullness.

We already know two of these three fronts. The first is the struggle with Sunnism insofar as it is treated as a religion concerned only with sharia, the outward religious law. In this form, its legal authorities refuse to let the law come alive through its inner spiritual truth. The disagreement is clear enough. It becomes clearer still when “modernising the sharia” turns religious law into a merely social religion.

The second struggle is more painful, because it takes place within Shiism itself. Here the urafa and hukama—spiritual seekers and sages who remain faithful to the whole teaching of the holy Imams—find themselves opposed by legal scholars who profess Shiism outwardly but have forgotten its calling. They have forgotten the Imams' teaching about the inner meaning of revelation, through which the prophetic message is deepened and transformed.

Finally, there is an even subtler struggle with a certain kind of Sufism that has forgotten its own roots. By turning away from Shiism, forgetting where walayat begins, and losing sight of who is its Seal, it mistakes the source of spiritual authority. And by giving too much attention to particular techniques at the expense of irfan, genuine spiritual understanding, it risks sinking into a pious darkness that can no longer answer people's questions or meet their deepest hopes.

As we shall see in Book IV, Haydar Amoli's great work has precisely this aim: to persuade the legal scholars that mystical knowledge (irfan) is necessary, and to bring back those Sufis who have become, in a sense, lost witnesses to Shiism within Sunni Islam. Only then can the original relationship between Sufism and Shiism be restored.

For Haydar Amoli, the very survival of spiritual Islam depends on this. Writing in the fourteenth century, he had already seen with extraordinary clarity the problems that would become increasingly urgent as Shiism developed in Iran. And the way he stated those problems still matters to anyone who understands what is at stake in this threefold struggle: the divine trust placed in human hands.

2. The Divine Trust Given to Humanity

At heart, the question is this: if we remove the batin—the hidden, inner, spiritual meaning—from Islamic teaching, do we remove something without which the whole teaching loses its meaning? And is the teaching of the Shiite Imams precisely this inner dimension of Islam, an essential part of what it means for a religion to have a revealed holy book?

For the Imams themselves are understood to embody the inner reality of the Muhammadan Word, the eternal prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya). From the beginning, then, the full reality of a revealed Book requires both zahir and batin: its outward meaning and its inner meaning.

This explains why Haydar Amoli takes the same position as Shiite sages and spiritual seekers everywhere. He challenges two groups at once. On one side are Shiites who reject the spiritual knowledge found in Sufism because they have forgotten its Shiite origins. On the other are Sufis who attack Shiism because they have forgotten those same origins.

Both groups act as though they do not know that the teachings of the holy Imams contain the secrets of the highest forms of knowledge. Both have set this side of the teaching aside, insisting that the Imams were concerned only with outward religious matters: the observance of the law, religious rites, and legal judgments.

Some have even suggested that, if the Imams possessed a secret teaching, they never passed it on to anyone. Certain Shiite legal scholars have argued this way in order to deny that any inner teaching exists. Certain Sufis have done so in order to disown their own beginnings, forgetting that without Shiism and the Imams, their philosophy of divine wisdom would not exist. We shall examine the relevant texts in Book IV, section 1.

The Imams were not merely interpreters of the sharia. Or rather, it was through the way they interpreted it that they became guides along the spiritual path (tariqat) and teachers of its deepest truth (haqiqat). Shaykh Ahmad Ahsai and the Shaykhi school, from the eighteenth century to the present, have argued for nothing different. Their spiritual struggle follows the same direction as Haydar Amoli's.

The Twelve Imams are understood as primordial manifestations of God. Before appearing on earth, they exist as spiritual beings who take part in the very coming-into-being of the worlds (as we saw in Chapter II). These are not merely speculative ideas invented by later thinkers. They are stated in the earliest transmitted teachings, the hadith, including those collected in Kulayni's Kitab al-Hujja.

Just as Christian interpretations of the Bible cannot ignore the place of Christ, Shiite interpretations of the Qur'an necessarily centre on the Imam. The teaching about the Imams contains the secret of both God and humanity—that is, the secret of the relationship between them. According to this vision, the relationship could only be established through “people of light,” the figures designated as prophets.

The manifestation of the Twelve Imams—or, more exactly, of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—takes place as a descent through successive worlds. Each stage is like a new form in which the divine Word appears, much as in the Acts of John, where the Word appears in different forms.68 A complete interpretation of the revealed Book must therefore take account of all these levels of existence, from the highest down to the world of earthly human life. We shall return to them in Chapter V.

Many sayings traditionally attributed to the Prophet and the Imams make the same point. They explain hints found in Qur'anic verses and show, in this understanding, that Islam and the Qur'anic revelation require an inner teaching: a higher truth that remains hidden. We could also examine the many sermons (khutbas) attributed to individual Imams. In these sermons, however, it is really the eternal Imam who speaks, and each of the Twelve Imams is an earthly expression of that one reality, for they all share a single essence.

One of the most striking examples is the famous Sermon of the Declaration (Khutbat al-Bayan).69 Here the Imam identifies himself with the Perfect Human Being (Anthropos teleios). In doing so, Shiite teaching about the Imams connects with the ancient spiritual image of the Heavenly Human, found in earlier traditions of inner knowledge.70 The sermon contains seventy statements. Repeated one after another with growing force, they are said to have carried the audience into a trance when the First Imam delivered them at Kufa. Here are just a few:

I am the Sign of the Almighty. I am the First and the Last. I am the One Who Is Revealed and the One Who Is Hidden. I am the Face of God. I am the Hand of God. I am the Side of God. I am the one called Elijah in the Gospel. I am the one who holds the secret of God's Messenger. ...

This vision of the Imam as a manifestation of God leads Shiite writers such as Haydar Amoli to find in the Qur'an itself a command to exercise discretion: taqiyya, or kitman, the duty to keep certain truths concealed.

We must be clear about what this means. It is not simply the practice of saying something while silently meaning the opposite. It certainly offers a means of protection, and the reasons Shiites needed that protection are easy to understand. But above all, it follows a demanding principle of spiritual honesty.

If the Qur'an teaches this honesty, that is because there is both an outer and an inner meaning to religious truth. It is fitting that the instruction itself should be expressed in a veiled form. This is the inner sense of verses that speak of a trust which must be returned only to someone entitled to receive it.

One verse in particular says: “God commands you to restore the trusts placed in your hands to those to whom they belong” (4:61). Haydar Amoli explains that all God's secrets (asrar Allah), all the hidden truths of divine wisdom, are trusts placed in the hearts of God's friends (awliya). To disclose them to someone unprepared to receive them is to break both the religious law and God's command. This is why the Imams themselves told their followers to observe taqiyya.

The idea of an entrusted secret also brings us to the story of Adam, the earthly human being, and to the drama that begins with him. The very possibility of revealing a secret to the wrong person—and of disobeying the instruction to pass it on only to its rightful heir—takes us to the heart of the holy Book and of spiritual wisdom. One Qur'anic verse is so important that the whole reason for an inner religious teaching can be said to depend on it. For the verse joins the mystery of God to the mystery of humanity, as though they were one and the same mystery. God declares:

We offered the trust of Our secrets to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. They all refused to carry it; they all trembled at receiving it. But the human being accepted the burden, for he is violent and ignorant. (Qur'an 33:72)

To understand this verse, we must answer two questions.

First, what is the trust? What secrets does it contain? Second, what do the human being's violence and ignorance—or lack of awareness—mean here? The questions cannot be separated. What sort of secrets could a person have accepted only by being violent and ignorant? And how could those very qualities lead that person to betray the trust? This violence and ignorance have a troubling double meaning. Shiite interpretation finds in them the drama from which the human condition, as we know it now, arose: the secret of humanity's present destiny.

To do this subject justice, we would need to bring together all the Shiite traditions and all the sayings of the Imams that touch, directly or indirectly, on this verse. That would require an entire book.

Let us give only the briefest outline. The Imams repeatedly explain the verse by saying, “That secret was our walayat.”

But walayat, their spiritual authority and closeness to God, is itself part of a threefold acknowledgment: of the oneness of the one God (tawhid); of the prophets' outward mission (nubuwwat); and of the inner mission of God's friends (walayat). The burden humanity accepted was this threefold testimony (shahadat).

Yet this threefold testimony—especially its second and third parts—assumes the existence of a humanity made entirely of light: a higher, heavenly humanity that existed before Adam and the earthly human race. That is why the full meaning of the Qur'anic verse can be understood only within the whole Shiite vision of how the worlds began and how prophecy came into existence. Within that larger vision, Adam's violence and ignorance have two sides. One brings him praise; the other brings about his downfall. Recognising both sides allows us to see how the different Shiite explanations of the verse fit together.

Let us try to make these closely packed ideas a little clearer.

We must keep in mind two sayings, one attributed to the Prophet and the other to the Imam: “I was already a prophet ...” and “I was already a wali, an Imam, when Adam was still between water and clay.” In other words, they existed before Adam had even been formed.

According to this teaching, before the humanity descended from earthly Adam, there was already another humanity. Its existence reaches unimaginably further back than anything the sciences could call prehistory. This is a humanity of pure light, like the seraphim: beings untouched by any fall, immaculate and free from error, unlike earthly human beings. They form the complete company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones (Chahardeh Masum).

Our texts, including the commentaries of Qazi Said Qummi, give them revealing names: the supreme humanity, the humanity of the heights (al-bashar al-awali), the archangelic humanity (anas aqliyun), the people of light (bashar nuriyun), and others. In their longing and the rapture of their love (walah wa hayaman), these beings of light surround the sublime Throne: the invisible Temple that serves as the model for every temple in every universe.71 Many sayings of the Prophet and the Imams refer to this existence before earthly humanity. The idea shapes the whole Shiite account of the origin of the worlds and of human nature.

Among these sayings is an exceptionally long conversation between the Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, and his disciple Jabir al-Jufi.

We can give only the main outlines of this magnificent hadith.72 It begins with the teaching we have already encountered: the Prophet and the Imams were the first beings created. At that time, there was no heaven or earth, no place, no night or day, no sun or moon, no Adam and no earthly humanity.

The Fourteen Immaculate Ones came forth as Fourteen Lights—fourteen beings of light, or aeons. Their relationship to their Lord's light is like the relationship between the sun's rays and the sun itself. The picture even recalls the emerald vision in the Book of Revelation. The Fourteen Lights surround the Presence that words cannot describe, like fourteen green canopies: “Around the throne was a rainbow that looked like an emerald” (Revelation 4:3).

From this complete company of Fourteen Lights, the worlds come into existence in the following order: first the Place of places, then the cosmic Throne, then the heavens and the angels, then the air and the spirits or jinn, and finally Adam, the earthly human being. At every stage in the creation of the worlds, the threefold testimony (shahadat) appears again, in one mysterious form or another. It affirms God's absolute oneness (tawhid), the prophets' mission (nubuwwat), and the Imams' role in guiding people towards the inner truth (walayat). This is because every stage of creation has its own manifestation of the Fourteen Lights.

The creation of the worlds and of humanity ends with a solemn enthronement of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. God addresses them:

It was for your sake that I created what I have created. You are the chosen ones whom I have placed between Myself and My creation. Through you I have hidden Myself from all My creatures other than you. I have made you the means by which they come into My presence, and through you every request is addressed to Me. For everything is destined to perish except My Face (see Qur'an 55:26–27), and you are My Face. You do not perish, and neither will those who choose you as their friends.73

This solemn passage is a good example of what is called a hadith qudsi: a sacred saying in which God speaks in the first person, as He does in the Qur'an. Its form becomes understandable within the wider Shiite teaching about how prophetic knowledge is received, which we shall examine in Chapter VI.

What the saying tells us is that the Fourteen beings of light are the original figures through whom God is made known. They make divine manifestation itself possible. For the God who is beyond all reach, “creating the world” means becoming known. And He can be known only through these figures, because whichever way we turn, they are the divine Face we encounter.

Human beings can know God only through His Names and Attributes; the Fourteen provide the forms in which those Names and Attributes can be recognised. This is why they are called Hujjat—the surety, the proof, the ones who stand as witnesses. The Fourteen Immaculate Ones stand for the God whom nobody can see or reach. That is why they are His imperishable Face. Later, in Chapter VII, we shall see that this is the very secret of why the Imam stands at the centre of Shiite spiritual life.

Many other traditions confirm this account. Some were collected by Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh.74 They describe the Prophet and the Imam as two primordial Spirits who form a single Light: a unity with two sides, expressing the two dimensions of the Haqiqat Muhammadiya, the eternal Muhammadan Reality.

The implication is that the higher humanity belonging to the Muhammadan Word, or Muhammadan Light (Nur Muhammadi), existed before Adam and the human race descended from him. The meaning of this higher humanity becomes clearer when God decides to create earthly Adam. The Creator takes a portion of this Light and kneads it together with a portion of the “clay” of Illiyyun, the highest level of paradise. This substance of light is then placed within Adam.

It becomes the divine side (jihat haqiqiya, the lahut) of the prophets' being, alongside their human, created side (jihat khalqiya, the nasut). Through the first, the prophets receive from God. Through the second, they communicate with human beings. The light placed in Adam passes from prophet to prophet until the last stage in the cycle of prophecy. With Abd al-Muttalib, the common grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad and Imam Ali, this one light divides into two halves. One appears in Muhammad as the Seal of Prophecy. The other appears in Ali as the Seal of walayat, the completion of the Imams' spiritual authority and guidance.75

Of course, this light is not passed on through any process taking place in the physical body.

We must understand its transmission in terms of the “subtle body,” the spiritual form of a person rather than the body of flesh. It points towards the only sense in which Islamic teachings about the prophets could accept the idea of “incarnation.” It also recalls a very specific idea from early Christianity, particularly Jewish Christianity and the Ebionites: the “True Prophet,” who moves swiftly from one prophet to the next until reaching his final resting place. For Christians, that resting place is Jesus; in Islam, it is Muhammad.

With these ideas in mind, we can begin to see what secret was entrusted to Adam, the human being, and how the very lack of awareness that allowed him to accept such a responsibility also led him to betray it.

The holy Imams repeatedly taught that the secret entrusted to humanity was their walayat76: the special relationship with God that makes them the “friends of God” (awliya Allah) and the guardians of God's cause (al-amr al-ilahi). Their mission runs alongside and completes the mission of the prophets (nobowwat). They guide those who choose them as their friends and teachers towards the hidden, spiritual meaning of the revelations given to the prophets.

To take the Imams as friends is to love them. The sources call this devotion walayat or mahabbat, often using the two words interchangeably. In loving them, their followers direct their love towards the divine Face made visible through them.

We can now see why, in Shiism, Islam as a prophetic religion is also a religion of love. Those who take the Imams as friends are saved from perishing, because the divine Face does not perish.

This love is also why the believer's testimony to walayat is the necessary completion of a threefold declaration of faith (shahadat). First comes the testimony to the One: God beyond all being, beyond words and beyond anything we can say about Him.

Second comes the testimony to the prophetic mission through which God reveals His Names, qualities, and acts to humanity. Third comes the testimony to the Imams and their walayat. The believer's loving devotion to them is part of faith (iman) itself, because it recognises the Imam as the guide who reveals the hidden meaning of those divine Names, qualities, and acts.

This is why Shiite teachers agree that these three testimonies belong together. The declaration of God's oneness (tawhid) relates to the declaration of the prophetic mission in the same way that the prophetic mission relates to the declaration of the Twelve Imams. Or, looking from the other direction, walayat stands in relation to prophecy just as prophecy stands in relation to God's oneness.

None of the three can be separated from the others. The believer's testimony to the Twelve Imams is the response, deep within the heart, to God's own love for them. It completes and seals the whole declaration. Without walayat—without the loving devotion carried by that word—faith is not merely empty; it is not faith (iman) in the fullest sense at all.77

This threefold testimony has, in a mysterious sense, been written into every universe, at every level where God becomes manifest. For it concerns the first Principle and two movements that begin and end in that Principle: the movement by which creation comes forth, and the movement by which everything returns to its source. These are mabda' and ma'ad, origin and return.

The same pairing appears throughout religious life. There is tanzil, the descent of revelation, and ta'wil, the spiritual interpretation that leads the revealed words back to their original, higher meaning. There is shariat, religious law, and haqiqat, the spiritual truth at its heart.

There is nobowwat, the mission of the prophets, and the Imamate, the mission of the Imams. At each level where the divine becomes manifest, the beings belonging to that world were asked to make the same threefold commitment (mithaq). This continued all the way down to the world of human beings on earth.78

Shiite scholars also agree on the meaning of the scene of the first Covenant, described in Qur'an 7:171, where God asks humanity, in a realm beyond ordinary history, “Am I not your Lord?” (Alastu bi-rabbikum?). At the same moment that Adam's descendants were asked to recognise God's oneness, they were also asked to accept the messages of the prophets still to come and the spiritual guidance of their Imams.7980

Humanity answered “yes,” but the scholars acknowledge that not everyone gave that answer in the same way. As we have already seen, Adam's humanity held within it the pure light of all the prophetic messages to come. It is this light within Adam that answers “yes”; it is the part of him that speaks. The story of sacred history makes the point when the Prophet tells the Imam, “You and I were the first to answer yes.”

Humanity accepted the terrifying burden before which the heavens, the earth, and the mountains had trembled (Qur'an 33:72). And what did humanity accept? The very secret of God's appearances: the mystery of how the Unknowable reveals His Face while remaining hidden within the figures through which He is revealed. This is what makes the bond between the Imams and the hidden meaning of revelation permanent.

Here, too, a remarkable way of reading scripture opens up. In Shiite spirituality, it develops something comparable to the Renaissance Platonists' theme of the dignity of the human being (De dignitate hominis). To accept the burden of such an overwhelming secret, the human being had to be both reckless and unaware.

Yet in this setting, both words become terms of praise. Haydar Amoli speaks of magnificent secrets here, of matters whose depths cannot be measured. He devoted an entire treatise to them, The Treatise on the Trust (Risalat al-amana), though unfortunately we have not yet managed to find a manuscript.

We can, however, recover something of its argument from the Shiite commentaries inspired by the same Qur'anic verse (33:72).

What, then, are this recklessness and ignorance shown by the human being in accepting God's trust? The recklessness is an act of courage directed against oneself. Adam, standing for humanity, accepts the divine secret by setting aside his own separate self before God's absolute Self. He chooses to know nothing that is other than God—not even to acknowledge that anything other than God exists.

At this point, the mystery of humanity meets the mystery of God. The secret of declaring God's oneness is to deny independent reality to everything that is not God, and to know that only God truly is. Haydar Amoli calls this oneness at the level of being, or ontological tawhid. Theological tawhid—the belief that God is one—is only its first stage. If we stop there, we risk falling into what he sees as a kind of idolatry in our very idea of God.

When something goes beyond its proper limit, it can turn into its opposite. That is what happened with Adam's recklessness and ignorance. At first they were a heroic daring, a magnificent unawareness, without which he could never have carried God's secrets. In that sense, they truly were qualities to admire. By gathering all his spiritual strength—his Minuta—Adam lifted a burden greater than his strength should have allowed.

Someone asked him—who it was, the symbolic story does not say—“You thought yourself stronger than you were. Didn't you know how crushing the burden would be?” Adam replied, “I knew nothing apart from God.”81 That was how he could bear the hidden truth, the secret of those to whom God had said, “You are My Face.”

Qazi Sa'id Qummi describes this state of knowledge through an arresting image. In a spiritual circle, unlike a physical one, “the centre surrounds the circumference.” The mind, as the centre, embraces all the lights that make up its knowledge.

Hence the saying: “Knowledge is a single point; it is the ignorant who turn it into many.” That multiplicity appears when we begin to recognise something other than God. For Qazi Sa'id Qummi, this is the ignorance hinted at by Qur'an 33:72.8283

As long as Adam remains unaware that anything other than God can truly exist, his magnificent unawareness gives him the strength to carry the weight of the divine secrets. He is a bearer of God, a theophore.

But the moment God is no longer enough for him, he begins to recognise something outside God—and by recognising it, he sets it apart as something other. The figures through which God appears are not God Himself. So why, Adam begins to ask, should he need them to reach God? And if he no longer needs them, why should he not reach the hidden truth directly, without the outward form that makes it visible and known?

Once he has set up this world of “otherness,” he too is something other than God. Why, then, should he need anyone else? His once-magnificent unawareness turns into a dizzying pride in himself. He becomes blind to the claims of others and wants to take for himself everything that belongs to them. This is the fall that sacred history tells through symbols.

The divine secret spoken of in Qur'an 33:72 was the walayat of the Imams.

We can now understand why it was represented by the tree in Paradise that Adam was forbidden to touch or dishonour. In his interpretation of this verse, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq says that Adam was shown the divine, more-than-human nature of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones, shining in the blazing glory of the Throne. Adam wondered: could there really be a humanity greater than his own, created “in heaven” before him?

Yet their light—the light of that heavenly humanity—was precisely the trust he had accepted and promised to protect. When they appeared in the human world, these beings were to come from his own descendants.

But Adam was no longer content with that role. He wanted to possess for himself what had been entrusted to him. Overcome by ambition, he tried to go beyond his proper place and claim immediately the rank that would only be made visible at the end of his line, through the one called the “Seal of walayat.”

That was what it meant to touch the forbidden tree and break the rule that sacred secrets must be disclosed only to those ready to receive them. The tree symbolises both the walayat of the Imams, whom Adam wanted to replace, and their knowledge: the knowledge of that humanity made of light (bashar nuriyun). Adam wanted to reach it before his time, though he lacked both the strength and the capacity to bear it. In the words of Qur'an 33:72, he was “reckless and ignorant.”

Qazi Sa'id Qummi explains the problem with unusual depth. The person who knows and the things that person knows must exist at corresponding levels. What we know becomes actual within us, much as food becomes part of the person who eats it. By touching the forbidden tree of Knowledge and “eating” its fruit—the things it offered him to know—Adam forced that knowledge down to his own level. And in doing so, he himself “descended from Paradise.”84

What makes this interpretation so striking is the connection it draws between Adam's disobedience and the violation of hidden spiritual knowledge. Shiite spiritual knowledge is the inner meaning of prophetic revelation. It had been rejected and persecuted by those whom the tradition calls “the reckless and the ignorant,” so its teachers could hardly fail to see the importance of this story. Adam's transgression is really a movement backwards: a fall to a lower kind of knowing, where the ability to understand symbols is lost.

There is no longer any sacred knowledge connecting the human mind with worlds beyond this one, and no awareness of spiritual realities beyond the senses. By casting off the divine secrets he had accepted, and betraying the trust placed in him, humanity becomes agnostic about these spiritual realities. In this sense, Qur'an 33:72 binds together the mystery of God and the mystery of humanity.

Just as striking is the agreement between Ismaili and Twelver Shiite interpretations of Adam's fault. Both see it not as a drama of the flesh, but as a drama of human knowledge. In Ismaili sacred history,85 Adam was appointed prophet and Imam at the start of our present “cycle of concealment” (dawr al-satr). Conditions in this cycle are entirely different from those of the earlier “cycle of disclosure” (dawr al-kashf). Even the rules of knowledge have changed. Human beings can now perceive spiritual things only by understanding the links and correspondences between visible things and invisible realities.

But knowledge through such correspondences—the ability to recognise symbols—depends on the partnership of two sides: shariat and haqiqat, the outward religious law and its inner truth; the written words and the spiritual knowledge they express; the visible form and the hidden meaning.

At Iblis's suggestion, Adam tried to gain a kind of knowledge beyond his reach. He wanted to grasp the hidden spiritual reality directly, stripping away the outward form through which that reality shines and makes itself known. Some fashionable theologians today speak of “demystifying” and “demythologising,” without fully realising what they are doing.

Adam was trying to seize, by force, a knowledge that belongs essentially to the Resurrection, and that only the final Imam of the cycle, the Qa'im, is appointed to reveal. Because that knowledge exceeded his capacity, it slipped away from him. All he found was his own nakedness: the darkness within him, his own ignorance. He tried to strip the hidden meaning bare, but what he exposed was his inability to know it.

To lose the language of symbols is to lose the garment of God's Word, which had surrounded him like a robe of light and driven out his inner darkness. What could remain? Only the memory of the symbols he had lost. And that is what it means, in the story, for the human being to cover his nakedness with “leaves from the garden.”

We can therefore understand what Shiite spiritual interpretation, and Haydar Amoli in particular, hear in the Qur'anic commands to remain faithful to a trust. They hear a command on which their own spiritual tradition depends: “Believers, do not betray God and His Messenger by betraying the trusts placed in your care, when you know what you are doing” (8:27). We have seen what this trust is.

We can now understand that it can be betrayed in two different ways, both leading to the same result.

The first is to try to take it by force: to strip away the outward covering through which the hidden meaning becomes visible, and to abandon the duty of guarding sacred secrets. That hands the secret over to people who are not ready for it.

Unable to understand it, they can only distort it and do violence to its meaning. They confuse spiritual resurrection with social revolt, for example. Their efforts no longer even approach the point at which the idea of being born anew—a spiritual birth (wiladat ruhaniya)—can begin to make sense.

The second way is simply to deny that the trust exists. And the first betrayal makes this denial much easier: once the hidden meaning has been stripped of its true character and distorted, it becomes all the easier to reject. Such outright rejection takes many forms, from the devout refusal of the scholars of religious law and their social successors to acknowledge spiritual knowledge, to the narrow view of the world held by technical experts who recognise only what can be measured and used. The first group reduces knowledge of spiritual realities to the level of natural or social facts.

The second refuses to recognise spiritual knowledge at all. It is easy for them to agree.

When the hidden meaning is rejected, the outward meaning (zahir) also suffers a radical loss. Religious law (shariat) cannot remain true to itself without spiritual understanding (irfan and haqiqat). It makes no sense to speak of an “orthodox” Sufism if that means Sufism without inner knowledge. Left entirely on its own, the visible world no longer points beyond itself to the invisible. It becomes a still life, a dried-out husk, an empty chrysalis.

Religion reduced to law and social rules, and nature reduced to what technical science can investigate and exploit, are two faces of the same decline. Turning spiritual life into something purely secular and social goes hand in hand with the drive for power of a useful but spiritually blind science. This is why Western technology can threaten traditional Shiite Islam only to the extent that Shiite Islam has already abandoned or betrayed the divine trust entrusted to humanity.

That trust weighs even more heavily on Adam now that he carries it with longing and repentance, having recovered it only after a long search. One of Imam Ja'far's conversations includes a beautiful symbolic story. It strongly recalls the famous Hymn of the Pearl in the Gnostic Acts of Thomas, and may help us understand the pearl as a symbol, and the search for the pearl as a spiritual journey.

We will encounter another echo of the same theme in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Western Exile (Book II).

The Imam asks one of his disciples, “Do you know what the Black Stone is?”—the stone set into a corner of the Kaaba in Mecca. He explains that the Black Stone had once been an angel, given to Adam as a companion in Paradise to remind him of his promise, his covenant (mithaq).

More precisely, this was the angel who carried the entrusted secret at the very centre of Adam's being. For the events described by the Qur'anic verses of the Covenant (7:171) and the Trust (33:72) take place in the malakut: the angelic world of the soul, which is itself the hidden, spiritual side of the world we see.

When God turned towards Adam again in response to his repentance, He changed the angel into a white pearl and sent it out of Paradise towards Adam as he travelled down the road of exile. Adam did not recognise it at first. To him, it looked like an ordinary stone. Through repentance, he had to peel away the covering that hid the pearl. Then it took its original form, spoke to him, reminded him of his promise, and awakened the memory of his homeland of light. Adam wept.

Once again, the angel was hidden, this time in the form of a precious stone. Adam carried it on his shoulder all the way from Ceylon to Mecca. Whenever he grew tired, the angel Gabriel, who travelled beside him, took the weight and carried it for a while. That is how Adam's angel—the hidden, spiritual meaning at the heart of Adam—came into this world. The Black Stone was placed in one corner of the Temple at the centre of the world, just as the angel was at the centre of Adam's being.86

The entrusted secret, the angel hidden within Adam, is the weight of the divine mysteries that Adam carries after rediscovering the pearl of spiritual knowledge. So great is that weight that Gabriel, the angel of Knowledge and Revelation, must help him bear it.

This is why the Shiite Imams repeatedly gave the teaching we have already encountered: “Our cause is difficult, and its burden is heavy. No one can bear it except an angel of the highest rank, a prophet sent by God, or a believer whose heart God has tested for faith.”

As we will see in Chapter V, this saying introduces their whole teaching about hidden spiritual truth. The believers who have passed the test are those Shiites who answered the first Covenant with an unreserved “yes,” those who, in the words of the tradition, “were created from a ray of the light of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.”

Imam Ja'far speaks of them again in the long hadith we quoted earlier (p. 52): “Our cause is difficult,” he says. “To uphold it, we need minds in which dawn is breaking, hearts burning with light, healthy souls, and beautiful natures. God has already received the pledge of our Shiite followers [...]. O God, let them live our life and die our death. Do not let the enemy overcome them. For if You let the enemy overcome them, there will be no one left in this world to worship You.”87

These are the witnesses who carry Shiism in its fullest sense and keep the chain of spiritual knowledge alive in this world (silsilat al-irfan). They can bear the entrusted secret and take up the cause of the Imams because they are the believers “whose hearts God has tested for faith.” This is why there were never more than a handful of true followers around the Imams. It is to people like these that we hear the First Imam refer in a conversation with his disciple Komayl.

3. Conversations between the First Imam and Komayl ibn Ziyad

I have in mind two conversations between the First Imam and Komayl ibn Ziyad, one of his most distinguished disciples and companions. For our purposes, the first is an introduction to the second. Few texts show more clearly what “spiritual struggle” means in the Imam's teaching, what is at stake in that struggle, and what kind of spiritual courage it requires.

In the first conversation, Komayl asks, “What is gnosis—direct spiritual knowledge?88” The Imam tests him with a question of his own: “What business do you have with gnosis?” He explains why it could harm them both if he poured such a secret from himself into Komayl: a vessel cannot hold more than its capacity allows, and the Imam has been commanded to put each thing in its proper place.

Komayl appeals to that very responsibility. “Can someone like you,” he asks, “disappoint a person who comes to you with a question? With your knowledge of the highest spiritual realities, and your ability to judge what each person is ready to understand, could you deny the questioner what is rightfully his? Could you leave him unable to reach his goal simply by refusing to answer? Surely not. God's command says, ‘Do not turn away the one who asks’ (Qur'an 93:10). You must answer, guided by the Prophet's instruction: ‘When you speak to people, speak to each according to their understanding.’”

The Imam grants his request and begins:

Imam: “Gnosis is the unveiling of the sanctuaries of divine Majesty, though there is nothing you can point to and show.”

Komayl: “Tell me more.”

Imam: “It is the disappearance of everything uncertain, and the quiet assurance of what is known with certainty.”

Komayl: “Tell me more.”

Imam: “The veil is torn away, and the secret has prevailed.”

Komayl: “Tell me more.”

Imam: “A light rises from the dawn before time began. It shines in the temples of tawhid”—that is, within those who profess God's true oneness. (A note in the margin of one of our manuscripts adds that this light is the eternal Imam.)

Komayl: “Tell me more.”

Imam: “Put out the lamp. Morning has come.”

After that, the Imam fell silent.

This conversation alone shows us that the Imams' teaching, the source of Shiite wisdom, is quite different from three familiar approaches: the reasoning through argument practised by Islamic scholastic theologians (mutakallimun), the methods of proof used by philosophers working in the Greek tradition (falasifa), and the attitude of pious ascetics who take little interest in spiritual knowledge. It is a distinctive kind of teaching, one that tends to be overlooked when Islam is discussed in the West.

We have even come to mistake Shiism for a “religion of authority,” in the Western sense of that phrase, because we have largely lost our understanding of what spiritual initiation involves.

Notice that the Imam does not impose a fixed formula of belief. Our authors describe the knowledge he teaches as knowledge inherited by the soul ('ilm irthi; see Chapter VI, section 4). The soul is entitled to this inheritance, and receives it, to the extent that it is capable of understanding it.

The true heir is the one who can understand. No amount of clever argument can win this inheritance by force. The person's level of understanding is what gives them the right to receive it and makes them someone to whom the sacred trust can be handed over. That, precisely, was Komayl's reason for asking the Imam to answer him.

The conversation is certainly difficult, and it has inspired long commentaries.89 Haydar Amoli, who discusses it at length in the second part of the major work we will examine later (Book IV, Chapter I), makes just one observation when he first quotes it. The key to the entire exchange, he says, lies in its final words: “After that, the Imam fell silent.”

For Haydar Amoli, the silence means that Komayl has been brought to the point on the spiritual path where he can see for himself. There is no longer anything to be gained by asking questions in the language of logical argument. Compared with the sun, argument is only a lamp. In the end, inner revelation and mystical experience cannot be fully expressed or shown to another person—as the Imam had hinted from the very beginning.

Haydar Amoli draws two lessons from this. First, it is through silence that a person seeking spiritual knowledge reaches the goal of the search, through an experience that brings the person as close to God as is possible.

Second, although the Imams revealed these divine secrets (asrar ilahiya) to their closest and most accomplished disciples, nobody is permitted to disclose them to people who are unprepared or unable to receive them. Here again we meet the solemn duty to guard the entrusted secret. Who, then, are the people who have protected and passed it on from one generation to the next?

A second conversation between the Imam and Komayl takes place in a setting of deep solitude.90 The Imam takes Komayl by the hand and leads him out of the city into the desert. There he lets out a deep sigh and says:

“Komayl ibn Ziyad, hearts are vessels, and the best are those with the greatest capacity. Remember what I am about to tell you.

“People fall into three groups. There are the sages whose wisdom comes from God ('alim rabbani), the true masters of divine wisdom. There are those who receive their teaching and are guided towards deliverance. And there is the ordinary crowd, who follow every agitator and turn whichever way the wind blows. They are not illuminated by knowledge, and they have no solid pillar to lean on.

“Komayl, knowledge is worth more than material possessions. Knowledge watches over you, whereas you must watch over your possessions. Spending wealth reduces it; sharing knowledge makes it grow.91 [...] Knowledge judges, while wealth is judged.

“Komayl, the store of material wealth will perish. But those who possess spiritual knowledge remain alive with a life that lasts through the ages. Their bodies disappear, and others whose hearts are like theirs take their place.”

Then the Imam points to his own heart and continues:

“Here is knowledge in overflowing abundance! If only I could find people strong enough to carry it. Sometimes I meet someone with a quick and subtle mind, yet I cannot trust him. He uses religion to advance his worldly interests. He uses God's gifts as an excuse to rise above God's servants, and uses his learning to gain power over God's friends.

“Or I meet someone who obediently follows the religious scholars but has no inner vision of his own. As soon as he meets the first difficulty, doubt enters his heart. No, neither of these men deserves my trust or can be entrusted with my spiritual knowledge. At other times, I meet someone who can never get enough pleasure and willingly lets his bodily desires lead him, or someone obsessed with gathering and hoarding wealth. Neither could ever serve as a guardian of religion. They are more like the flocks grazing in a field. Does this mean that spiritual knowledge must die whenever those who carry it die? Certainly not!

“The earth is never without people who uphold God's testimony on God's behalf, whether they do so openly or remain hidden and completely unknown. Thanks to them, God's signs and the understanding of their meaning are never lost. How many are there? Where are they? I swear by God, they are very few, but their standing is exceedingly high. Through them, God preserves the signs and proofs of the divine presence in this world until they can pass them to people like themselves and plant their seeds in kindred hearts.

“For these people, spiritual knowledge reveals itself all at once, in the full truth of inner vision. They know the joy of certainty. What people weakened by an easy life find difficult, they find easy. What frightens the ignorant is familiar to them. Their bodies live in this world, but the spirits within them remain connected to the highest dwelling. Komayl! These are God's representatives on earth, calling people to the true religion. How I long to see them!”

Set this solemn statement by the First Imam beside the words of Imam Ja'far quoted at the end of the previous section. Across the generations, the Imams of Shiism teach the same essential lesson. These statements, and many others like them, establish three things.

First, Shiism is, at its heart, the inner meaning of Islam. Second, this inner teaching is the very teaching into which the Imams initiated their disciples, and which those disciples passed on. Third, people's different responses to this teaching—whether they receive it or reject it—divide them into three groups.

The best explanation of the First Imam's statement to Komayl ibn Ziyad comes from other sayings of the Imams on the same subject. I will mention only a few, but the whole body of these teachings is of decisive importance. They show that Shiism has a calling to introduce people to a deeper teaching, to Islam's inner dimension. They therefore challenge two groups: Shiites who would rather ignore this inner meaning, and Sufis who refuse to recognise the source and foundation of their own spiritual knowledge.

The witnesses described by the Imam, who uphold God's cause from generation to generation without the wider world even knowing they exist, form a spiritual community. Its order is based not on public rank or social position, but entirely on the qualities of a person's inner life. It cannot be reduced to a worldly institution or social structure.

The “representatives of God on earth” are, first of all, the eleven Imams who succeed the First Imam. Beyond them are others who continue an unseen spiritual line around its mystical centre, the Hidden Imam, until the end of our present age. Without them, humanity could not continue to exist, whether it knows this or not. Here, at last, we reach the meaning of Shiism's spiritual struggle and what is at stake in it.

Among the sayings that explicitly explain why Shiism has this inner dimension, one deserves particular attention. We have quoted it several times already because, with slight variations, it returns again and again. It appears in several collections, and the Imams themselves stressed its exceptional importance: “Our cause is difficult. It places a heavy demand on those who accept it. It can be borne only by an angel close to God (malak moqarrab), a prophet entrusted with a mission (nabi mursal), or a faithful believer whose heart God has tested through faith.”92

The disciple who reports this saying from Imam Ja'far goes on: “Imam Ja'far added: Among the angels, some are close to God and others are not. Among the prophets, some are entrusted with a mission and others are not (see Chapter VI below). Among believers, some have been tested and others have not. Our cause was presented to the angels, but only those close to God accepted it. It was presented to the prophets, but only those entrusted with a mission accepted it. It was presented to believers, but only those whose hearts had been tested accepted it.”

The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, had already made the same point to one of his close companions: “Do you not see how difficult our cause must be, when God chose to entrust it only to angels close to Him, prophets sent on a mission, and believers whose hearts had been tested?”93 A commentator from the Safavid period explains the purpose of these accounts: no one can fully embrace this cause without a burning desire for it, complete acceptance of it, and a perfect love for the Imams' immaculate purity (ismat).94

The Sixth Imam, Ja'far, makes another statement to a close companion, repeating the word sirr—“secret”—with striking insistence. To appreciate its meaning, we need to remember that sirr does not refer only to something concealed. It can also name one of our subtle inner faculties: the innermost awareness, beyond ordinary consciousness.

We will return to this saying in Chapter V, alongside the previous one, when we examine how the Qur'an's deeper meaning is understood through spiritual insight. The Imam says: “Our cause is a secret hidden within a secret (sirr mastur fi sirr), the secret of something still concealed, a secret that only another secret can teach. It is a secret upon a secret, itself hidden by a secret.”

Or, in another form: “Our cause is the truth, and the truth of truth (haqq al-haqq). It is the outward meaning, and the inner meaning of the outward meaning (batin al-zahir), and the inner meaning of the inner meaning (batin al-batin). It is a secret, the secret of something still concealed, a secret hidden by another secret.”

We should also reflect on these lines attributed to the Fourth Imam, Ali Zayn al-Abidin (d. 95 AH/714 CE):

I hide the jewels of my knowledge, For fear that an ignorant man, seeing the truth, would crush us. Lord, if I revealed a single pearl of what I know, They would say, “So you worship idols!” And some Muslims would believe it lawful to shed my blood. They condemn as monstrous the most beautiful thing shown to them.

Whether the Imam himself spoke these words or Shiite tradition later placed them in his mouth, they offer unmistakable evidence of how that tradition understands Shiism's inner teaching and the struggle to preserve it.

This is why the discipline of taqiya—the duty to keep certain teachings private—is so strict. As we saw earlier, it follows directly from the idea of a truth entrusted to someone's care. Imam Ja'far goes so far as to say: “Whoever does not practise taqiya”—whether through carelessness or rejection of the inner teaching—“has no religion.”

In the Book of Shiite Beliefs (Kitab al-itiqadat), the great Shiite theologian Ibn Babuyeh (d. 381 AH/991 CE) writes: “The duty of taqiya must not be set aside until the Imam who announces the resurrection (al-Imam al-Qa'im) appears. Through him, religion (din) will be revealed in its entirety, so that from East to West it will be one and the same religion, as it was in the time of Adam.”

This already answers those who deny that Shiism has an inner teaching. If, as some have claimed and still claim, the Imams taught nothing beyond explanations of religious law (sharia) and ritual, the command to keep their teaching secret would make no sense. Haydar Amoli points out that these are precisely the things one may—and should—proclaim openly from mosque pulpits. Clearly, they cannot be what the Imams mean in the sayings quoted above.

In his second conversation with Komayl, the First Imam divided humanity into three groups. Several sayings of the Sixth Imam make the same distinction: “We, the Imams, are the sages who teach; our Shiites are those whom we initiate; everyone else is foam carried along by the flood.” There are therefore three groups. The first consists of the divine sages, the alim rabbani, those who fully embody divine wisdom. Strictly speaking, the title belongs to the Imams, though it can also be extended to sages who have become like them.

The second group consists of believers “whose hearts have been tested,” who receive and pass on this teaching.

Finally comes the great mass—not simply people who have not been initiated, but those who deny or stubbornly reject the very possibility of spiritual knowledge. Imam Ja'far expressly says that there is no fourth group.

Haydar Amoli's generous attempt to bring Shiites and Sufis together, and to help both understand who they are and what they owe to one another, follows naturally from this distinction.95 Everyone must decide where they belong. Those who call themselves Shiites but deny the Imams' inner teaching because they cannot bear even the idea of it, and those Sufis who practise a spiritual path while ignoring its source and foundation, cannot claim to belong to the second group, much less the first.

The second group is made up of believers whose hearts have been tested: people who accept the full weight and consequences of the threefold profession of faith (shahadat). Openly or unseen, they keep God's testimony alive on earth. Through them, this remains a world that God looks upon—a world that still matters to God. Among them is a smaller circle entrusted especially with passing on the Imams' secrets and keeping them alive in the hearts of tested believers. Of these the First Imam said: “Where are they? How many are there? I swear by God, they are very few, but their standing is exceedingly high.”

This circle forms a hidden spiritual hierarchy, an idea fundamental to Twelver Shiism. In Corbin's account, non-Shiite Sufism probably borrowed it from Shiism, because the hierarchy's very existence, structure, and continuity depend on a permanent spiritual centre: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Unless we understand this unseen community, we cannot understand the nature or stakes of Shiism's spiritual struggle. It also changes the way we understand the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. More than that, it shows how the Shiism of the Twelve Imams can offer its spiritual message quietly amid the turmoil of our world: not by compromising with a supposedly unstoppable course of historical change, but by bearing witness to another world and reminding us that such a world exists.

4. The Invisible Spiritual Hierarchies

From one generation to the next, a small number of chosen people pass on a task that remains unknown to almost everyone. It is not the kind of work that appears in official reports or can be uncovered by a social survey. These people form spiritual hierarchies mentioned in certain traditions whose origins and precise meaning remain somewhat mysterious.

Around them gather those who are Shiites in the fullest sense: people who receive their teaching and share their task. They belong to the second of the three groups described by the Imams, the believers “whose hearts God has tested through faith.” They have the strength to uphold the Imams' cause, however difficult, in a world that may know nothing of it.

This teaching is so central to Shiism that the Shaykhi school, as we shall see in Book VI, gives it a particularly far-reaching interpretation. Seeking to preserve or restore the complete teaching of the holy Imams, the Shaykhis present it as the fourth pillar of Shiite doctrine. The first is God's oneness (tawhid); the second concerns prophecy; the third, the Imams and their spiritual role; and the fourth, the Shiite community itself, understood in a deeper sense.

We can best describe it using a familiar Western expression: an Ecclesia spiritualis, a spiritual community. Its hierarchy is invisible and its members remain unknown. Their place within it depends entirely on their inner spiritual qualities.

Our authors see this hierarchy as something borne out by experience. Some people, after all, are more spiritually developed than others, nearer to God, or further advanced in knowledge, spiritual awareness, and devotion. A hierarchy of different degrees therefore exists among them. Such outstanding individuals were present even in the time of the Imams and have continued to appear since: Salman the Persian, Abu Dharr, the two men named Jabir, Mufazzal, and the four successive deputies (na'ib) of the Hidden Imam during the “Lesser Occultation,” the first period of his concealment.

Shiites recognise such figures as intermediaries and guides acting on the Imam's behalf. Even during the “Greater Occultation,” the period in which we now live, they may be granted access to the Imam's presence. Such meetings involve a way of perceiving that goes beyond the physical senses.

But observing that some people possess greater spiritual gifts does not explain why this hierarchy exists. Its deeper structure follows the order in which beings come forth from the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat muhammadiya), the primordial reality first brought into existence, which we have already discussed at length and will return to below. This reality reaches its complete expression in the company of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.” The final figure in that company, considered in the order in which divine realities become manifest, is the Twelfth Imam, now hidden. Our entire work will end by returning to him (Book VII).

For now, the essential point is that every part of these spiritual hierarchies—their purpose, their structure, their way of existing, and the way they act—centres on the Twelfth Imam and his unseen presence. He is the “pole of poles,” their central support and the key to understanding them. This is also connected with the great spiritual cycles: the cycle of walayat, the Imams' spiritual guidance, following the cycle of prophecy (see Chapter V and Book VII). The relationship between the unseen hierarchies and the Twelfth Imam is so complex that it would require a book of its own. Here I can give only the briefest outline.

In some sayings of the Imams, the hierarchies appear in a simpler form than in later traditions. Imam Ja'far, foretelling the inevitable concealment (ghaybat) of the Imamate, speaks of thirty chosen companions, the Nuqaba, or spiritual leaders. Across the generations of the Greater Occultation, which began in 329 AH/940 CE, they enjoy the privilege of meeting and keeping company with the Hidden Imam. During the Lesser Occultation (874–940 CE), the most spiritually advanced Shiites could still gain access to him. Since the Greater Occultation, this privilege belongs only to the thirty Nuqaba.

Their meetings raise a question: where does the Hidden Imam live? The traditions sometimes speak of the mysterious valley of Shamrikh near Yemen and sometimes of the mystical city of Hurqalya. In either case, the setting belongs to a hidden spiritual region called the “eighth climate.” The mysterious Green Island, visited by a pilgrim whose story survives in Shiite tradition, belongs to this same region (see Book VII).

This is the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: a subtler counterpart of the world we perceive with our senses. It stands between our physical world and the purely spiritual world, which is entirely separate from it. Through this imaginal world, the Imam can be present to our world while remaining invisible to its inhabitants. His thirty chosen companions exist and act in a similar way. They too are hidden from human eyes.

Hence their name, rijal al-ghayb: the people of the unseen world, the hidden ones, the Invisibles. Their number never changes. When one dies—or, more exactly, when that person's presence in this world finally ends—another takes the vacant place. They are therefore also called Abdal, those who replace one another. Elsewhere, I have tried to show why the imaginal world is indispensable for understanding the spiritual life we are studying here.96

Another text from roughly the same period, written by a disciple of Imam Ja'far, calls these spiritual figures Abdal by name. It is a prayer composed by Dawud, a grandson of the Second Imam, Hasan Mujtaba, and a companion of the Fifth and Sixth Imams. The Shiite religious calendar recommends reciting it on the fifteenth day of Rajab, the seventh month of the lunar year. In practice, it is better known through Dawud's mother, under the title “the devotional practice of the mother of Dawud” (amal Umm Dawud).

It is an especially beautiful prayer, embracing the whole family of sacred history. It sends greetings in turn to the three great archangels, those who support God's Throne, the guardian angels, Adam and Eve, Abel and Seth, every prophet named in the biblical and Arab traditions, Jesus and his twelve Imams (from Simon to George), the Prophet Muhammad and his twelve Imams, the Abdal and the Awtad, the members of every family descended from the Imams, and all devout people. It ends: “Honour, my God, all those angels and prophets whom I have named, and all those whom I have not named.”97

An even earlier text, a saying attributed to the Fourth Imam, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, already describes different ranks within the spiritual hierarchy. In a conversation with Jabir ibn Yazid al-Jufi, the Imam names seven matters that a faithful Shiite must know through spiritual understanding (marifat): the meaning of the profession of God's oneness; the meanings of God's Names and Attributes; the prophets, who are the abwab, or doorways between God and humanity; the Twelve Imams; the “Supports” or “Pillars” (Arkan); the Nuqaba; and the Nujaba (see also p. 198 below).98

Below the Imam, this gives us three ranks:

  1. The four Supports (Arkan). These are four figures who remain the same through every age, with no replacements. They are generally identified with the prophets taken from this world by God without passing through death: Enoch (also identified with Idris or Hermes), Elijah, Khidr, and Jesus. They live on without dying, sustained by the continuing presence of their spiritual centre, the Imam.
  2. The thirty Nuqaba. These are the spiritual leaders already mentioned.
  3. The forty Nujaba. These are the spiritually noble ones.

The last two groups together number seventy. Their numbers remain fixed, but new members take the places of those who leave this world. Both their numbers and their duties are connected with the idea of God's Names descending through the different levels of being, each Name presiding over a particular universe. This is a very complex body of spiritual thought, which we cannot examine in detail here (see Books III and VI below).

Shiite theologians also know of teachers who place a further, constantly renewed group below the Nujaba: 360 righteous and wise people, corresponding in number to the degrees of the heavenly sphere.

Yet the clearest statements attributed to the Imams themselves do not seem to mention this additional group. Other differences exist as well. In a conversation with Mufazzal al-Jufi, for example, Imam Ja'far explains the hierarchy in detail. Every Imam, in every age, is accompanied by forty chosen spiritual companions: twenty-eight Nujaba and twelve Nuqaba, including the Abdal and the Awtad. Their total, forty, matches the number elsewhere assigned to the Nujaba alone.99

These early teachings attributed to the Imams help us understand the more elaborate versions found elsewhere. An Ismaili account, for example, says: “Our masters have declared: out of humanity we chose four thousand; out of those four thousand, four hundred; out of those four hundred, forty; out of those forty, four; and out of those four, one alone, who is the pole (qotb). The stability of the world rests upon him. The world cannot exist without him for a single instant; without him it could not continue to exist.”100

Another version says: “God has on earth three hundred distinguished people (a'yan)”—the Arabic word can mean both “eyes” and people as precious as one's own eyes. They are the eyes through which, in Ruzbihan's words, ours remains a world that God looks upon.

The account continues: “Three hundred whose hearts correspond to Adam's heart”—the Nuqaba, or spiritual guides—“forty whose hearts correspond to Moses' heart”—the Nujaba—“seven whose hearts correspond to Abraham's heart”—the seven Abdal—“four whose hearts correspond to the archangel Gabriel's heart”—the Awtad, or pillars—“three whose hearts correspond to the archangel Michael's heart”—the three Afrad—“and one whose heart corresponds to the archangel Seraphiel's heart, the pole of poles (qotb al-aqtab).”101

This one supreme example of “seraphic” humanity is always the Imam—in our own time, the Hidden Imam.

We will find the same pattern in Ruzbihan (Book III), though the order of the Nuqaba and Nujaba is reversed. To trace the full development of these hierarchies, we would then need to follow them through the work of Ibn Arabi and his many commentators.

The numbers here must, of course, be understood as symbols. They express relationships within the cosmos and the rhythm by which the different levels of existence are ordered (tartib al-wujud). Still, Shiite authors—especially the Shaykhis—tend to retain three ranks, like a three-part entrance (rawaq) leading to the threshold of the Imam: the four Supports (Arkan), the thirty Nuqaba, and the forty Nujaba, as named in the saying of the Fourth Imam.

That is why the thirty Nuqaba may be identified with the Awtad, the “tent pegs” that hold up the earthly world or the cosmic tent; with the Abdal, who replace one another; and with subordinate spiritual “poles,” since they carry the Imam's gifts to other people. They are also the rijal al-ghayb, the people of the unseen, or Invisibles. Entirely pure and devoted to divine service, they are kept hidden by God from the eyes of oppressors until the Last Day (Yawm al-Din).

The idea of this hidden spiritual hierarchy is so deeply bound up with Shiite thought that, when we encounter it elsewhere—for instance, in Sufi texts outside Shiism—we can recognise an understanding of the Imams that has been carried over into Sufism without openly identifying itself as such. This may have escaped attention until now because Shiite sources have been so widely neglected.

For our purposes, what matters most is how Shiism—and particularly the Shaykhi school—has understood these hierarchies by taking the concealment (ghaybat) of the Imam seriously and following the idea through to its consequences. In this reading, Shiism stands as a defence against every attempt to turn spiritual life into a social institution, to confuse it with social organisation, or to make compromises that threaten its independent reality and its priority over worldly concerns.

The Hidden Imam ordered his last appointed deputy (na'ib) not to name a successor. From then on, the Imams' followers would look to sages who preserved and passed on their teaching, among whom the members of the hidden spiritual hierarchies could be found, though without being publicly known. When Ali al-Samarri, the last deputy personally appointed by the Hidden Imam, died in 329 AH/940 CE, the Greater Occultation began. His final words were: “From now on, the matter belongs to God.” Those words express the whole spirit of Shiism. From then on, the Hidden Imam became the central figure in Shiite religious awareness. The history of that awareness is, in a sense, the history of his unseen presence (see Book VII).

Accordingly, when the Shaykhis discuss the sages who carry this teaching forward, they stress that the Imam directed his followers towards the existence of a kind of person. He did not identify particular individuals by name. This is no church hierarchy. Its members are distinguished only by their inner spiritual worth and the degree of their closeness to the Imam. Who they are remains the Imam's secret. No member can therefore publicly announce that they belong to it or be identified by outward signs.102

We might apply to each of them the rule that governs the knights of the Grail: “His strength is sacred so long as he remains unknown to all.” They are hidden from ordinary sight for the very reason that the Imam is hidden. Above all, the Imam is concealed today because human beings have concealed him from themselves.

Human awareness has become unable to know or recognise him, to perceive how he exists and acts, or to recognise the “place” in which he dwells. The same inability hides those who are, as it were, members of his own being and who together make up his very Name. His final appearance will not be some outside event suddenly imposed on the world. It will mark the completion of a transformation in human consciousness.

A beautiful passage by Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani (d. 1288 AH/1870 CE) brings the point together:

When you have reflected in the way I have explained, you will understand why it is not possible today to know who the Nuqaba and Nujaba are. We are not permitted to ask for their individual names or identities. Nor are they permitted to answer. For they are the sacred Name of the Imam of this age, and during the time of his concealment (ghaybat) his name must not be spoken. Many sayings forbid the mention of their names.

They are the Hidden Imam's real and living Name because a person's name expresses what that person is. What a person is can be understood as their light, and that light as the radiance they give out. The Imam's radiance is his Shiites (shia-ye u), his followers. It is therefore wrong to name these people or seek to discover who they are.

Through a special act of divine kindness, someone may happen to recognise one of them. That person was capable of receiving such knowledge, and God granted it. If God does not make them known to someone else, that person plainly lacks this capacity and has no right to demand it. Yes, this is God's clear and deliberate arrangement for our time: people should recognise that this whole category of persons—the Nuqaba and the Nujaba—exists, acknowledge their role, and feel a bond of solidarity with them.103

In the same way, we know that there is a Hidden Imam (Imam gha'ib). We must acknowledge his existence and his spiritual role and remain in communion with him, even though we do not know him in his physical person.104

This passage is characteristic of a form of Shiite spirituality shaped by the idea of the Hidden Imam, with all that this idea can mean to a mature religious consciousness. There is nothing here resembling a Church, with its clergy and its authority to decide doctrine. Nor does it resemble certain modern “esoteric” organisations that claim an unbroken line of spiritual succession (successio apostolica) and appeal to mysterious documents as proof of their official legitimacy. Above all, there is nothing that allows religious reality to be confused with a social system—a confusion whose painful consequences we have seen in the testimony of a Sunni Muslim.

The standing of these spiritual hierarchies is perfectly expressed in a sacred saying (hadith qudsi): “My Friends (Awliya'i) dwell beneath my tabernacles; no one knows them except me.”105 When one of these people passes from earthly life into another life, someone else takes that person's place.

But this succession remains the Imam's secret. From a Shaykhi perspective, we could say that nothing is more deeply hidden than the structure of the Shiite community. And nothing offers a stronger defence against attempts to subject divine reality (res divina) to worldly ambitions and the desire for power.

At the same time, because this hidden teaching looks towards the final fulfilment of history, it also works against every attempt to freeze religion into fixed doctrines. The final age began when the mission of the “last prophet” came to its close. It will not end until the final Imam appears. He will lift every veil from the secrets that God's Friends have spent this cycle of spiritual guidance (da'irat al-walayat) and concealment helping receptive souls to understand. Ultimately, they are awakening those who can grasp the meaning of the trust that Adam agreed to carry.

To follow Adam in his turning back to God, his “repentance,” and to accept the threefold profession of faith (shahadat) is to reverse the movement of Adam's “descent from paradise.” It means taking part in a spiritual struggle against the urge to rush blindly forward. Today that urge has many names. It likes to call itself “irreversible,” all the more insistently because it does not really know where its supposed “progress” is taking it.

Of course, Shiite spiritual philosophy, like other traditional paths of divine wisdom, has never ignored the idea of an “evolution” embracing every form of life and the whole history of humanity.
