But here the movement goes by another name, because its direction is understood in terms of both its source and its goal. It belongs to a history beyond ordinary history—a metahistory. Without such a dimension, talk of the “meaning of history” is only a metaphor. One principle governs these Shiite thinkers, and others as well: “Nothing rises to heaven except what has come down from heaven.”

The only human beginning we can truly imagine is one that corresponds to our understanding of the end. In other words, the story we tell about our origins is inseparable from what we believe human life is ultimately for. That remains true today.

But unlike the prevailing ideas of our time, the sacred history of humanity and the world is, in this traditional understanding, cyclical. It has an arc of descent (nuzul) and an arc of return or ascent (su'ud). Its direction is vertical—like the soaring lines of Gothic architecture. It is not the story of a supposedly irreversible, straight-line advance from an unimaginably distant past, based on the unsupported assumption that humanity must have begun at a level lower than its own present state. It is a story of gradually turning back, returning, and rising towards what the original descent placed beyond our reach. Here I refer readers to the beautiful pages by Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani, translated elsewhere, on the meaning of this “world in ascent.”106

5. What Is at Stake in Shiism's Spiritual Struggle—and Why It Still Matters

By now, I hope, what is at stake has become clear. We can look at the question in two ways. The first concerns what Shiism is in itself and where it stands within Islam.

The second concerns the spiritual and religious condition of our time as a whole. In drawing these threads together, I am returning to the concerns raised in Chapter I of this book.

The first question takes us back to the Shiite spiritual figures discussed at the beginning of this chapter. Haydar Amoli, a thinker of exceptional quality, analysed their position in the eighth Islamic century (the fourteenth century CE). As I have noted, his account continued to apply in later periods and has lost none of its relevance in our own time.

The sayings of the holy Imams quoted here, together with those still to come, make one thing clear: a form of Shiism that wished to be nothing more than an outward religion of law (sharia) would contradict its own nature. It would cut away an essential part of the Imams' teaching. When the Imams speak of the “secret” entrusted to those capable of bearing it, they are speaking of gnosis: direct spiritual knowledge. Shiite teaching is, in a distinctive sense, the spiritual knowledge at the heart of Islam. Shiism itself is the continuous line through which that knowledge is passed on (silsilat al-irfan).

That is enough to settle the dispute between the divine sages and mystics (hukama rabbaniya and urafa) on one side, and those who would reduce Shiism to the legal rules taught by religious jurists (fuqaha) on the other. The “difficult cause,” the burden that the Imams place on believers whose hearts have been tested, is contained in the three parts of the profession of faith (shahadat). The recognition that God is one is inseparable from acknowledging the prophetic message. In the same way, acknowledging the Prophet's message loses its force if one does not also acknowledge the Imams as its inner meaning and spiritual continuation.

An inner meaning cannot exist on its own, entirely detached from the outward form that gives it expression.

But the reverse is just as true. Strip an outward religious form of its inner meaning—of its power to point beyond itself towards another reality—and it becomes a lifeless body, an empty shell. We have heard the Imams insist that without this deeper meaning the Qur'an would long ago have become a dead book. Revelation would be reduced to a museum of theological curiosities, which is precisely how it already appears to someone who rejects the possibility of religious knowledge.

For a long time, people have tended to see Islam only through its Sunni majority. When they contrast a religion centred on religious law with a spiritual path that crosses the threshold into invisible worlds, they naturally turn to Sufism.

But the relationship between Shiism and Sufism has received very little attention. When it has been discussed, the two have generally been described as incompatible. Is that not a hasty judgment, born of unfamiliarity with Shiite spirituality? Reading the words of the Imams forces us to reconsider the whole question. That is what Haydar Amoli, a Shiite thinker of the fourteenth century, had already done (see also Book IV, Chapter I).

The passages we have studied help explain why Amoli can make this seemingly startling claim without intending a paradox: “The Sufis are those who deserve to be called Shiites in the true sense (al-shia al-haqiqiya), and believers whose hearts have been tested (mu'min mumtahan).” Later Shiite Sufis would repeat his statement. The reverse seems to follow: if true Shiites are Sufis, then those Shiites who reject Sufism can be called Shiites only in a figurative sense (majazi). Perhaps.

But what exactly does it mean to reject Sufism?

Here we immediately think of a kind of Shiite spiritual teacher already mentioned, and to whom we will return. These mystics practise the kind of spirituality associated with Sufism and use its language, yet belong to none of the Sufi orders. Some even have serious reservations about them. We have already noted several reasons: the excessive importance sometimes attached to the personality of the Sufi master, despite the inevitable limits of any individual; certain practices; and certain theories about the nature of being which, when poorly understood by followers, can encourage moral carelessness or self-indulgence.

There is no doubt that some Shiite mystics belong among the believers “whose hearts have been tested,” the second group named by the Imams, while not being Sufis in the usual sense. Haydar Amoli's claim must therefore have a far wider meaning than it first appears to have. Otherwise, we would be driven into a still stranger paradox. Was he including Sunni Sufis as Shiites without their knowing it—even though many had fiercely attacked Shiism? Was he trying to bring back these “lost children” of Shiism, as his life's work seems to suggest?

I think a basic principle of spiritual life can help us understand the problem. What distinguishes Sufi Islam from an Islam centred on religious law is that it is a religion of divine love. As we noted earlier (pp. 81 onward and 101 onward), this raises a formidable theological question: how can we speak of love, or even use the word, while remaining faithful to the absolute oneness of God (tawhid)? We shall see in Book III how painfully Ruzbihan wrestled with this question in both his thought and his life.

But something that has rarely been recognised is obvious to anyone who has lived Shiite spirituality from within: Shiism, as a religion of walayat, the Imams' bond of spiritual closeness and guidance, is itself the religion of love in Islam, in a particularly full and essential sense. At the deepest level of divine being—the divine Ground (Kuhh al-dhat, comparable to Meister Eckhart's Grund)—God is so far beyond human reach that the idea of a mutual relationship of love seems impossible.

But love can turn with confidence towards the figures through whom God becomes manifest, the forms of the revealed God (Deus revelatus). Those figures are precisely the eternal spiritual realities of the Imams, in whom the divine Names and Attributes are made present (see Chapter VII below).

That is why the threefold profession of faith matters so much in practice. From the beginning, it makes Shiism both a guide and a foundation for the longings that find expression in Sufism. At the same time, Shiism's understanding of the Imams protects those longings from going astray, particularly from the dizzying temptation to identify oneself with God as God remains beyond revelation.

This is why Haydar Amoli and thinkers like him are not troubled by the observation that most Sufis are Sunni Muslims—to such an extent that many people instinctively associate Sufism with Sunni Islam. In his view, the presence of Sufism within Sunni Islam answers a need that does not arise in the same way within Shiism. He is also keenly aware of the spiritual dangers Sufism has faced in a Sunni setting, where its deepest aspirations have been separated from both their roots and their fulfilment.

This leads us to a central idea in Shiite spirituality, one that reaches beyond the familiar opposition between the Islam of the legal scholars and the Islam of the Sufis. I have already put it this way: Twelver Shiism, when lived in its entirety, is already a spiritual path, a tariqat. The Shiite believer “whose heart has been tested through faith” is already, in that broad sense, a Sufi, without needing to join a Sufi order. Such a person is already a “Shiite in the true sense.”

But here the word Sufi reaches beyond its usual meaning. We should translate it instead as “mystic” and recognise that Shiite Islam has great mystics who are not necessarily Sufis in the narrower, organised sense.

Take Muhammad Baqir Majlisi, the great theologian of Safavid Shiism to whom we owe a monumental collection of Shiite sayings. He objected strongly when people called his father, Muhammad Taqi Majlisi (d. 1660), a “Sufi.” He was not entirely wrong. His father was not a Sufi in the narrower meaning of the term, yet he was unquestionably a genuine mystic. This is more than a fine point of wording. Understanding the distinction matters if we want to find our way through Shiite spiritual life.

The conclusion, then, is that a Shiite who lives the faith fully, a believer “whose heart has been tested,” must personally follow the spiritual way (tariqat) of the Twelve Imams. Such a person's spiritual life encompasses much of what people in the West generally call Sufism, without necessarily sharing the weaknesses that have exposed some Sufi practices, organisations, and forms of expression to criticism from Shiite spiritual teachers—even in the time of the Imams themselves.

At the same time, the Imams' teaching, lived as a personal reality and guarded as a sacred trust, already protects the Shiite seeker from another danger: a rigid, merely literal religion. Such literalism strips outward forms of the inner meaning that gives them life, cuts them off from the spiritual worlds to which they point, and finally opens the way to confusing religion with society. Reject the Imams' secret, which is itself the spiritual path of Islam, and little remains beyond the rites of a social religion. Then a form of scholarship that has itself become secular will explain and justify those rites solely by the role they play in society.

And so we return to where we began: the troubling question raised by the Jordanian participant whose testimony I described earlier. In our study group in Tehran, we had asked: “Is there no way out? What answer could a Shiite give?” The answer, I believe, is already contained in the First Imam's conversations with Komayl ibn Ziyad, as well as in the many other sayings of the Imams we have examined—and could easily have multiplied.

But consider those who reject haqiqat: the inner truth whose meanings rise beyond the outward words and appearances, through one spiritual world after another, and thereby give this visible world its meaning. The worlds are joined by an axis leading to their heavenly centre. Those who dismiss these inner meanings will also dismiss the idea of a purely spiritual community held together by that truth, invisible yet real. What happens to such people when the outward order of a traditional society begins to fall apart? Because they have identified religion with that social order, their very understanding of religion falls with it.

That is the grave question facing us today: is there still, hidden within Islam, a spiritual strength capable of carrying forward the future of a purely spiritual Islam? For Shiism, answering that question should simply mean answering the Imams' continual call. Its threefold profession of faith gives it a calling to show, through its very existence, that Islam is more than the outward letter of religious law (sharia), just as social life is not identical with religious reality.

This is the final choice posed by Shiism's “spiritual struggle.” One path is surrender: spiritual life is absorbed into social structures, drawn into the ambitions of those who seek power, and made to serve authorities that either have no idea what “spiritual” means or destroy its meaning all the more effectively because they once understood it. For the person who can truly profane or blaspheme is not the unbeliever, but the believer.

The other path is faith in the divine incognito—God's hidden presence—even in what we might call desperado fiducialis, a despair that still holds fast to trust. It is faith in a divine hiddenness that persists as a challenge and finds its clearest expression in the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Here religious reality cannot be turned into an object, forced into an objective system, or absorbed into social or collective life (see Book VII). A believer inspired by such faith will find a way to resolve the problems that arise today from remaining faithful to the requirements of religious law. That believer's spiritual struggle will end in victory.

It is significant that two expressions familiar from certain Western spiritual traditions—the divine incognito and the Ecclesia spiritualis, the spiritual community—should help us convey Shiism's message. They also bring us to the second way of considering our subject, which I proposed at the start of this section. Their distance from the major intellectual fashions of our day tells us something about the unprecedented crisis affecting Christian theology in the West.

After twenty centuries of Christianity, we can now hear Christian theologians denouncing what they call a confusion between Christianity and “systems of religious redemption.” They say these other systems take human beings out of this world and its history, open a window onto a world beyond that can explain this one, and show a path towards recovering a lost human nature. They claim to find in the Bible something that twenty centuries of Christianity had never thought to look for there. They present it as a safeguard against faith becoming what they now call an “escape to heaven.”

For such thinkers, the question is no longer how to defend belief by appealing to the limits of human power. Human capacities, they tell us, have no limits. The powers of homo progressivus, humanity in constant progress, are driving homo sapiens towards ever greater social organisation, collective systems, all-embracing control, and the absolute rule of technical experts ... “How can we avoid killing God?” our Jordanian Muslim had asked in anguish. Some Christian theologians answer by going even further than Nietzsche's declaration. They claim that Christian faith is defined by a confrontation between triumphant human power and the helplessness of a Creator who has been overcome. This, apparently, would be the true revelation of God's transcendence.

Perhaps this is indeed what a certain “demystifying” theological argument reveals.

Yet it is striking how closely that argument agrees with the most radical rejection of religious knowledge. It would be so much simpler, and more candid, to say so. I ask only whether some Western readers might be willing to attempt an experiment: set the results of these dazzling exercises in post-Christian theology beside a direct reading of the Qur'an in Arabic, or beside a few of the Imams' sayings of the kind quoted in this book. Perhaps those who try will hear an inner summons as powerful as the voices of a Last Judgment ...

Anyone to whom such an experiment means nothing may find it perfectly natural to hear that belonging to the Prophet's religion is incompatible with life in a modern state, and that Islam is therefore doomed. Such people can imagine nothing except dragging Islam into the ruin they foresee for themselves.

But believers “whose hearts have been tested” will surely turn the question around: what if the judgment falls the other way?

“How many are they? Where are they?” the Imam asked. Their identity remains God's secret. They are “very few,” but their existence is enough, because they will not be swept along by the flood—the flood that bears so many different names today. And the more of them there are, the less of the “foam carried by the flood” of which the Imam also spoke.

That is why, in answer to fashionable theological movements that condemn everything they call gnosis without clearly understanding what spiritual knowledge is (see pp. 25 onward), we must say that it matters now more than ever. For anyone who knows through spiritual insight, as for the Qur'an itself, the cry “God is dead” is meaningless. The absurd, by definition, is what has no meaning. It would be absurd to imagine that divine truth depends on some particular moment in History, or that the truth revealed in a sacred book depends on the date when it appeared among the outward facts and passing circumstances of the world. We have heard the Imams themselves say as much.

Spiritual events—the entirely real events of sacred history—do not belong to the past in the way that outward, material events do. Because they do not take place within that kind of time, later outward history cannot make them obsolete. They belong to the time of the soul (see Chapter IV, Section 5, and Book IV, Chapter II). In that time they are both present and still to come.

The word “irreversible,” so often repeated without much thought, loses its force. In Semitic languages, the completed form of a verb does not simply correspond to the past tense in our languages. Depending on the context, it may be translated as past, present, or future. Even the events of the final fulfilment of history are described in this completed form.

There is a relentless urge today to force spiritual events into material History—to make them “take place” in the ordinary record of visible facts—because we have grown unable to recognise the reality of events that cannot be entered into a public chronicle. Sacred history offers a different way of understanding them. Its events belong to outward history only as a ray of sunlight passing through stained glass belongs to the building it illuminates. Their truth raises those who witness them towards worlds in which their presence endures, complete and still present.

This is precisely what the experience of a sacred book presupposes. It is also why the question of secularisation may ultimately turn on how we understand the sacred book itself. Secularisation begins with a refusal of haqiqat, a refusal to recognise the full depth and range of the book's meanings. The Imams' way of uncovering those meanings restores that fullness. Seen in this light, the deepest insight of Shiism comes more clearly into view.

Chapter IV The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book

1. The Sacred Book and Its Interpretation

In the preceding pages, we have often spoken of what I have called the “phenomenon of the Sacred Book”: what makes it distinctive, what makes it a complete reality in its own right, and how it gives Shiism its particular character. For Shiism is defined by the way it interprets the Book. The holy Imams are the guardians and guides of that interpretation; they are at once the keepers of the treasure and the treasure itself. Its inner principles open up entire worlds of meaning—worlds in which Nietzsche’s cry that “God is dead” would announce only the spiritual death of the person who utters it.

We are dealing with spiritual realities that have their counterparts in every religious community gathered around a Sacred Book—the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab). The questions they raise have parallels from one tradition to another.

Yet the traditions have not all reached the same degree of clarity about those questions, or studied them with equal care. This matters enormously. I therefore want to sketch the connections among these shared lines of inquiry, however briefly. My hope is that an Iranian reader interested in Western discussions, and a Western reader who wants to connect the interpretation of the Qur’an with questions already familiar to them, can both take part in the same conversation. These few preliminary remarks will help us understand the inner dimensions of religion and spiritual interpretation, which we will discuss in Chapter V, as well as the Shiite understanding of prophecy, which follows in Chapter VI.

The Qur’anic expression Ahl al-Kitab literally means “People of the Book.” Strictly speaking, it describes a religious community that possesses a Sacred Book—a community whose very existence arises from that Book. Its religion rests on a text believed to have “come down from Heaven,” revealed to a prophet who was sent to teach it to the people entrusted to him. Alongside Muslims, the People of the Book are, above all, Jews and Christians. Zoroastrians have, to some extent, been granted the same standing because of the Avesta. The group known as the “Sabians of Harran,” who followed Hermetic teachings, were less fortunate.107

All these communities face the same fundamental problem. They have a Sacred Book that guides their lives and their understanding, both in this world and beyond it. Their first and final task is to understand that Book.

But what does it mean to understand something, or to help someone else understand it? This is what the word hermeneutics, from the Greek hermeneia, refers to: the work of interpretation. Whenever we understand something, we understand a meaning. Here the aim must be to discover the Book’s true meaning.

But how we understand depends on who we are—on our very way of being. A revealed Sacred Book therefore raises more than a question about this or that human action. It raises a question about what it means to be human at all. In philosophical terms, it calls our whole understanding of the human person into question.

A believer’s inner life grows out of the meaning they find in the Book. Their lived situation is therefore one of interpretation: the true meaning comes to light for them, and in that same moment gives truth to their own existence. This is why the phenomenon of the Sacred Book shapes not only a particular view of human nature but an entire form of culture.

Its effects are lasting. Indeed, the Sacred Book and the inner life that both gives rise to its interpretation and is shaped by it could provide a starting point for a comparison of spiritual life, or more broadly of religious understandings of the human person, among the peoples of the Book in East and West. The Bible and the Qur’an share more than certain teachings about prophecy.

The search for a true spiritual meaning has also raised comparable questions for Christian and Muslim interpreters. This becomes especially clear when we look at Qur’anic stories that have earlier counterparts in the Bible, including books usually called “apocryphal.” Those who meditate on these stories often find themselves facing similar problems of interpretation. We are led, then, towards the idea of a comparative study of spiritual interpretation: a theology of the religions of the Book that would explore what they have in common, both in what a revealed Scripture demands of its readers and in what it allows them to discover.

Imagine gathering the spiritual interpreters of biblical revelation and those of Qur’anic revelation in one ideal assembly—for the moment, perhaps, in a “castle of the soul,” a House of Wisdom (Domus Sapientiae). What would it mean to bring them together, and what might they discover? Elsewhere I have made a first attempt at such a comparison, using the figures of Adam and Noah as they appear in Swedenborg’s spiritual reading of the Bible and in Ismaili interpretations of Islamic revelation. Some of the parallels are remarkable.108

Sacred Books tell of people and events whose outward form (zahir) belongs to the past. They present figures, actions, and stories from earlier times.

Yet these people and events must mean something different from what they would mean in an ordinary history book. If they matter to the life and death of the person reading them, they cannot be nothing more than events recorded in an old chronicle. We have already seen how important this was to the Shiite Imams. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir (d. 115 AH/733 CE), strongly told his companions: “If the revelation of the Qur’an had meaning only for the person or group of people because of whom a particular verse was revealed, the entire Qur’an would be dead today.

“But no! The Sacred Book, the Qur’an, is alive and never dies. Its verses will come true for people in the future, just as they came true for people in the past.”109 With these words, the holy Imam was already avoiding the trap of what we would now call historicism: treating a sacred text as though its meaning were exhausted by the historical circumstances in which it first appeared.

Consider the Latin word comprehendere, which originally includes the senses “to contain” and “to involve.” To understand a meaning is, in one way or another, to involve ourselves in it, to make it part of our own way of being. Anyone who has not taken that meaning into themselves—who has not truly understood it—will find it hard to explain it to someone else.

And what if the meaning at stake is the meaning of that person’s own life? The verses of the Qur’an are called signs (ayat), and this is exactly the point: we are asked to understand signs addressed to us. Such understanding must happen now, in the present. The sign’s meaning lives in the person who understands it, because that person is the one to whom it speaks.

At the heart of understanding, then, lies a problem of time: the relationship between the time of the events described and the time of the reader who interprets them. That relationship is itself the time and place where the two meet. If we ignore or refuse to face the problem, we miss the encounter. If we recognise it and try to work through it, we begin to examine honestly the assumptions behind every act of interpretation. This becomes especially urgent when what we are interpreting is a text regarded as a revealed Sacred Book.

Later (§ 5) we will see that Islamic spiritual thinkers distinguished different qualities of time. They recognised a special kind of time involved in understanding events that unfold “within the soul.” And to speak of events “within the soul” is also to imply that they take place in spaces proper to the soul—in a world with its own kind of location.

2. The Spaces and Perspectives of Spiritual Interpretation

Perhaps the better we become at seeing events as points in the one-way flow of historical time—dating them, placing them in a sequence, and explaining them through their place in that sequence—the harder it becomes to see them in another way. We may lose the ability to locate them in a space that is not the measurable, uniform space of the physical world: a space where their meaning depends on their enduring place within an ordered pattern of higher and lower levels. As we will see in Chapter V, Shiite interpretation of the Qur’an unfolds the text’s meanings across what we might call several levels of reality, which can even be represented in diagrams.

Jewish Kabbalists and Christian thinkers who seek the inner meaning of the Bible do something similar. There seems to be a basic difference between this way of seeing and what we ordinarily call historical understanding. The two could perhaps be related if we had a way to show how the patterns in one correspond to those in the other. A spiritual interpreter may possess such a method. It is far less clear that a historian, working strictly as a historian, does.

Consider an example that brings the problem of spiritual interpretation into sharp focus, for the Bible and therefore for the Qur’an as well. In one of his major works, where he sets out his theology and philosophy of divine wisdom most systematically, Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772) describes the principle behind his reading of Scripture. Just as there are three Heavens in the spiritual world—the highest, middle, and lowest Heavens—there are three corresponding meanings within the divine Word: a heavenly meaning, a spiritual meaning, and a natural meaning.

What comes first and is most fundamental lies at the centre and becomes the ultimate purpose, just as an end is already present in its cause and therefore in its effect. The Word has an outer natural, or literal, meaning. This is the covering, the vessel, and the support of an inner spiritual meaning. That spiritual meaning, in turn, contains a meaning deeper still: the heavenly meaning. In Islamic inner teaching, this would correspond to what is called “the inner meaning of the inner meaning” (batin al-batin).

Both inner meanings are present at the same time within the literal meaning. Swedenborg then explores what such coexistence involves. In Heaven and in the world, he says, things can be arranged in two different ways. One is a successive order, where parts follow one another from highest to lowest. The other is a simultaneous order, where the parts are arranged from the innermost to the outermost, as though in concentric circles spreading towards their edge. Imagine the successive order as a column in a temple, narrower at the top and gradually widening towards the base.

What is highest and comes first in that vertical order corresponds to what is most central and inward in the simultaneous order. What comes last, at the base of the successive order,110 corresponds to the outer edge of the simultaneous order.

To picture how one arrangement becomes the other, imagine the highest and earliest parts of the successive order becoming the inmost heart of the simultaneous order. Meanwhile, the lowest and latest parts become its outermost regions. It is as though the column were to slide down into itself, like the sections of a telescope, until it became a flat surface. The column’s top would now occupy the centre.

According to Swedenborg, this correspondence between sequence and coexistence—and the way coexistence arises from sequence—can be found throughout the material and spiritual worlds. The principle is constant: what is highest and first moves towards the innermost centre, where the ultimate purpose is found. In the divine Word, heavenly, spiritual, and natural meanings unfold in succession, but finally coexist in a single structure. The heavenly and spiritual meanings are both present within the natural or literal meaning, which contains and shelters them.111

The great Swedish visionary could hardly have made the problem of Scripture’s many meanings clearer. It is, at heart, a problem of how forms arranged in time relate to forms arranged in space. Only by posing the question in this way can we begin to imagine an other history, distinct from the material history of outward, observable facts. It also helps us avoid confusing spiritual meaning with allegory.

Swedenborg opens up to spiritual understanding the spaces in which “events in Heaven” take place and can be perceived. By showing how events that follow one another can also exist together, he may be revealing a secret of the deepest spiritual life. It is the same secret suggested in Richard Wagner’s final opera, when Gurnemanz answers Parsifal: “I have scarcely taken a step, yet already I feel so far away!” “You see, my son,” Gurnemanz replies, “here time becomes space.”

This correspondence between forms in time and forms in space is a remarkably subtle example of two different structures sharing the same underlying pattern—what we might call isomorphism.112113 It also suggests that there are several kinds of space. The space we perceive with our physical eyes may not even be the most important. After all, what concerns us in interpretation is the divine Word. It is a sound, a calling that brings beings into presence and remains their deepest, hidden nature. Once this nature has taken form in a being, it cannot be seen with ordinary eyesight. It reveals itself to another kind of sight, an inner vision able to perceive other spaces.

Yet these are still spaces, with their own properties, different from those of the physical world. We therefore need to understand how the space of sound corresponds to those worlds beyond the senses, where the vibrations of the Word spread like “arpeggios laden with distant lights,” to borrow Joseph Baruzi’s phrase.

It seems, in the end, that this way of seeing the inner and spiritual meanings of Scripture as present together with its outer and natural meaning is common to the great mystical traditions of divine wisdom that have arisen in religions based on revealed Books. As I have already suggested, there is something shared between Swedenborg’s reading of the Bible and the ways Twelver and Ismaili Shiites, or Sufis from Ibn Arabi’s school, read the Qur’an and the traditions that explain it.

We can identify this common ground only by looking at the structures of their experience. It may take a careful study of how consciousness forms and recognises meaningful patterns to see what is happening and why it matters. Here I can only point to a few signposts.

One particularly promising place to look is the philosophy of light developed in both Christian Europe and the Islamic East, especially Iran, during the same broad period. The spiritual challenges faced in the two traditions already show a similar underlying pattern. Their ideas about light may help us discover its foundation.

As Étienne Gilson observed, the heavenly hierarchies described in writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite and the study of optics developed by Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) seem closely connected: the ordered outpouring of divine illumination and the philosophy of light belong together. The same is certainly true of Suhrawardi’s (d. 587 AH/1191 CE) “Eastern philosophy of divine wisdom.” Its foundations are a philosophy of light and an ordered world of archangels, drawing on both later Neoplatonism and the ancient Persian Zoroastrian tradition of divine wisdom (see Book II below).

Medieval thinkers’ interest in optics, and especially in works on perspective derived from Arabic texts, grew from this joining of the science of light with the philosophy of divine illumination. Robert Grosseteste was a leading figure in bringing the two together. In his account of the origin of the universe, light is the very substance of being. It is the first and most subtle form of bodily existence, the original principle from which worlds take shape. His treatise On Light, or the Beginning of Forms (De luce seu de inchoatione formarum) has an exact parallel in the teachings of Suhrawardi’s school, the Ishraqiyun, thinkers devoted to the wisdom of light or “Eastern wisdom.”

The laws of optics themselves open up the space—or perhaps the higher-dimensional space—needed to understand how spiritual meanings can be hidden within things we perceive with our senses. In his On Light, Bartholomew of Bologna (twelfth century) places the seven ways physical bodies receive light alongside the seven ways angelic and human minds share in divine Light.114115 We might compare these in turn with the seven inner levels of the Qur’an, which the Sufi thinker Simnani links to seven subtle centres or organs of spiritual perception, each marked by its own colour and degree of light (see Book IV, Chapter IV).

We can now understand Roger Bacon’s extraordinary praise of perspective. For him, it is the most fundamental of the natural sciences, the key to intellectual knowledge and the spiritual sciences alike. Why? Because both concern a kind of seeing. The laws and images of outward illumination help us understand what happens when light reaches us inwardly. This is also why thinkers paid such close attention to geometrical figures, particularly the sphere and the pyramid, and to their properties. They could turn these shapes into symbols by relating them to the nature of light.

A kind of map of the spiritual worlds then becomes possible. In Shiite teachings on divine wisdom, for example, Qazi Sa'id Qummi argues that there must be exactly twelve Imams. He bases this on twelve functional relationships that determine the shape of the cosmic Temple or “Throne,” regarded as the original pattern of the Kaaba’s cubic form. The diagrams found throughout Ismaili works and the writings of Ibn Arabi’s school—like those in the Kabbalah or the work of certain followers of Jacob Boehme—may look fantastic at first.

In fact, they possess both strict internal order and real value for understanding. They show and test patterns that, for their authors, are real and are perceived through a particular way of knowing. The safest way to appreciate these diagrams is to follow the approach shared by philosophies of light in Iran and the West: to read the laws of optics and perspective for their inner spiritual meaning, against the background of a shared account of the universe’s origin in light.

Of course, I am not suggesting that spiritual worlds can be reduced to the familiar rules of visual perspective. Quite the opposite. What matters is a turning back, a return to the very source of every perspective. That is why Suhrawardi and those who followed him so often appeal to the science of mirrors or use the mirror as an image.

If mirrors can help us discover principles of structure that point towards the kind of space opened by spiritual interpretation, we might also have much to learn from those who study the experience of music. This would bring us back onto the path opened by the philosophers of light themselves, when they found a spiritual meaning in the laws of perspective.

One influence on my thinking here has been the work of our late friend Victor Zuckerkandl. I have in mind especially the pages where he describes a room of mirrors: a room with mirrors on every side. He suggests that it offers an excellent way of understanding how a particular feature of musical experience shares the same structure as the mirror effects so often invoked by our visionary thinkers.116117

I am thinking especially of a tradition reported by Ibn Arabi in his account of the mystery of the “heavenly Earth.” This is the world of pure imaginative perception, where God has created a universe corresponding to every individual soul. When a mystic looks into that universe, the mystic sees their own soul reflected there.

Ibn Arabi says that this was what Abd Allah ibn Abbas, one of the best-known companions of the Prophet and the First Imam, meant when he declared: “This Kaaba [the sanctuary in Mecca] is only one dwelling among fourteen. In each of the seven Earths there is a being who is our image. In each of the seven Earths, therefore, there is an Ibn Abbas who is my image.”118

This is surely one way these writers expressed their experience of a whole series of worlds, arranged in an order and corresponding to one another. Their inner experience allowed them to be present, in some way, in those different worlds.

Yet this outlook feels so strange to us today, so distant from our ordinary habits of thought and our sense of the universe, that we will have to renew our methods of inquiry if we are even to begin to understand such an experience.

We must find a way to give it the recognition its participants mean by tahqiq: to establish its reality as an experience. Otherwise we are left with explanations that reduce it to history, psychology, or a particular theory of social and intellectual change, whether dialectical or not. If we refuse those reductions, there is no avoiding the urgency of the task.

We may find it easier to make the passage—the exodus—from the space of the senses into spaces beyond the senses if we study the problem directly. The relationship between the space of hearing and the space of sight gives us a way to do so. Seen from another angle, this is the relationship between forms in time and forms in space—or, in Swedenborg’s language, between successive order and simultaneous order.

What struck me in Zuckerkandl’s discussion was his account of the room of mirrors as the place where visual and audible space come closest together. What happens in that room? Two things. First, we find repetition: things multiply themselves.

Second, we find a movement that, even as it advances, returns to its starting point. I will call this a return or reversal, as I did earlier on page 143.

First, in a room of mirrors, every object appears again and again, reflected from one mirror into another.119120 No object is present in only one lonely place. Its appearance in one position immediately implies its appearance in others, multiplied into as many images as the mirrors and their reflections make possible. Something similar happens in the space of music. A sound is repeated from octave to octave. Its presence at one pitch is accompanied by its recurrence at the corresponding pitch in each successive octave. In fact, an entire musical key, with all its relationships, repeats from octave to octave, just as the whole room reappears again and again in its mirrors.

We can sing the same hymn in different keys. The notes will be higher or lower, and therefore different in pitch, yet the tune remains unmistakably the same.

This brings us to Zuckerkandl’s suggestion that musical experience lies at the very origin of the theory of Gestalt: the study of a form or pattern as a whole, rather than as a collection of separate pieces. How can a melody remain the same when the notes that make up its physical sound have changed? We discover that the melody’s essential “material” is not the individual notes but the relationships between them. The tune is preserved because those relationships remain the same.

This principle of preservation is the key, I think, to understanding the basic rule that governs both Swedenborg’s reading of the Bible and the inner Islamic interpretation of the Qur’an and its vast collection of traditions. The same story can truly happen again on different levels, as though it were being played at ever-higher octaves, until we reach the level of events beyond ordinary history. Swedenborg does this when he interprets Genesis, Exodus, and Revelation.

Twelver and Ismaili Shiites do something comparable when they recognise the spiritual meanings of Qur’anic verses and traditions at the level of the eternal company of the holy Imams, and of the ranks of spiritual beings that proceed from them (see Chapter V below). Without this idea of worlds repeating the same essential relationships at different levels, we could not understand the spiritual body or “resurrection body” described in our own time by the Shaykhi school of Shiism.

At each higher octave, the defining relationships of a person, a situation, or an event remain intact, even though they appear in a different form. If we approach interpretation in terms of Gestalt, we may also see why modern empirical scholarship so often meets the entire practice of spiritual interpretation with indifference, rejection, or even hostility. It sees only arbitrary readings where there is, for those who practise this interpretation, an organic necessity of form. Perhaps there is such a thing as being deaf to meaning, just as there is such a thing as being tone-deaf.

Second, the very structure of musical space seems to impose a law of return. Any movement away from a note on the musical scale can lead us forward until we arrive again at that same note, an octave higher. In the room of mirrors, too, each movement outward from a point is also a movement towards that point as it appears in a reflected image.

In our musical system, the interval of a fifth—the dominant—marks the furthest point from the opening, fundamental note. From there the direction changes. The movement forward becomes a return to the starting note at the octave. It is understandable that people have spoken of the “miracle of the octave,” something apparently without parallel elsewhere in the world of phenomena.121

Yet if we look at the relationships involved, we find a similar pattern in the cycle that governs the origin and final destiny of the universe in Islamic inner teaching. Its two key terms are mabda' and ma'ad: the point of origin and the place of return (see page 127 above). The movement between them is not a straight line of development but a return.

Our world’s course takes the form of a cycle: it goes back to its source, to the very level where the “drama in Heaven” gave rise to this passing material universe. The children of Adam have ahead of them the heavenly state they left behind them. Just so, as we move upwards through an octave, the starting note we have left behind is also the note towards which we are climbing.

To set out from any point in the visible earthly world—the molk—is therefore to move towards its origin. The first destination is the world of Hurqalya, the mundus imaginalis, or intermediate world. Here the spiritual takes on body and form, while bodily things become spiritual, appearing as independent Forms and Images.

Our authors repeatedly tell us that these forms have no need of any material substance apart from their own light, just as a mirror image seems to exist through light alone.122 This is also the basis of the multiplied presences described in Ibn Arabi’s tradition quoted above. It corresponds to what the study of sacred images calls different “levels of meaning.” Take the story of the holy Shiite Imams, who began the cycle of spiritual initiation that follows the cycle of prophecy (see Chapter VI and Book VII below).

We can understand their story at the level of earthly life—which, for us modern readers, is usually simply the level of history.

But we can also understand it across one intermediate world after another, all the way to the highest spiritual fullness (see Chapter V). It is no coincidence that Ismaili thought arranges the Imams in groups of seven, just as it arranges prophecy in a pattern of seven, rising through one octave after another.

Someone may object that this reading of music rests, in the end, on the tonal system that developed in the West and on our understanding of how harmony works.

But that is precisely the point. It is especially we in the West who need to begin with the means already available to us and find our way back to an experience that opens up a different kind of space from the one we inhabit every day. That experience might allow us to recognise the visionary worlds of our “Eastern sages” as having a reality of their own, rather than hiding a refusal to consider them behind explanations drawn from historical studies or sociology. It is not enough, for example, to say that the teachings of Ishraq were developed in the seventeenth century.

Nor does it explain them to say, rather absurdly, that they were “a product of their time,” if by time we mean only the calendar of historical events. So what is being revealed to us in this form of human experience? How is it possible? Perhaps we are trying to rediscover a “lost continent.” Finding it may be as difficult for us as it is for someone studying lived experience to grasp the world that opens through the rhythms of musical space.

It is not only the Bible and the Qur’an that confront us with an undeniable fact: for a great many readers, a text has meanings beyond what its outward words (zahir) appear to say. Much of Persian literature poses the same problem, including mystical epics and lyric poetry. How many Western scholars of the East have been surprised, even scandalised, to discover that so many Iranian readers hear a mystical meaning in the poems of Hafez!

Yet the fact remains, and no amount of deafness to spiritual meaning can make it go away.123

So when I speak of an interpretive perspective, I mean different levels of meaning that correspond to the echoes of the divine Word across different levels of reality. By connecting this with the questions raised by musical perspective, I am not speaking merely in metaphors. I know that the approach I have sketched goes against the prevailing tendencies in theology and the study of Scripture today. More simply, it goes against the world as it appears to what we call historical consciousness.

But further texts will show why we must question the assumptions behind that way of seeing. Otherwise we risk the gravest misunderstandings whenever we try to meet people whose experience of the world still remains open to the perspectives of traditional culture, as is true in parts of Iran even today.

What we call historical development generally moves along a horizontal line. It is guided by a supposed “direction of history,” an idea that has taken hold of so many modern minds almost like a secular religious dogma.

But this way of looking at time goes hand in hand with the loss of another dimension: the dimension of height, the vertical or polar direction. Traditional cultures orient themselves by a “heavenly pole,” a “cosmic north.” The terms mabda' and ma'ad mark two movements along this axis, one descending and the other ascending. Suhrawardi draws attention to this when he says: “You are told: Return!

“But the very idea of returning means that you were there before. And woe to you if you imagine that the place of your return is Damascus, Baghdad, or any other earthly homeland!”124125 We should therefore ask whether the loss of this vertical dimension is what leaves modern readers facing a false choice whenever they encounter an ancient sacred text: is it myth, or is it history?

Neither myth nor history. We escape that narrow choice only by accepting that events can be entirely real while taking place in a space other than the physical world, which we usually treat as the only stage on which “historical” events can occur. Our authors developed a remarkably detailed account of the nature of this other space. They called it alam al-mithal, the mundus imaginalis: not an imaginary world, as though it were unreal, but the imaginal world.

I have examined it at greater length elsewhere. Modern readers who pose the choice between myth and history usually assume, without saying so, that what counts as real history must be made up of outward, material facts. They also lump spiritual meaning, symbol, myth, and allegory together without first asking whether they are the same thing. This confusion is everywhere.

What has to happen for a genuine spiritual meaning to be lost and turned into mere allegory? Such a loss is a decline in spiritual forms, closely linked to the disappearance of the vertical, polar dimension we have just described. We need to take our earlier comparison of Christianity and Islam further and ask what conditions each tradition has provided for spiritual interpretation. I noted above that Islam has no institution corresponding to the Christian Church.

We might ask whether the growth of that kind of institution tends to favour literal and historical readings, admitting at most the occasional pious interpretation in which an earlier figure or event stands for a later one, or else a moral allegory. Such readings may be deeply edifying, but they are also harmless to established structures, both in philosophy and in society. In Christianity, the tradition of spiritual interpretation has most often survived and renewed itself among groups outside the official churches. Modern biblical scholarship, however, has frequently dismissed their readings as arbitrary, artificial, or even a violation of the text.

Conditions were different in Islam, as we noted earlier, even though periods of political success could be a trial for Ismaili and Twelver Shiism alike. We would still need to explore why Islamic spiritual thinkers found it possible—or necessary—to resist compromising their personal spiritual demands with collective rules that would turn religion into something governed by society.

Suhrawardi gives this conflict a moving symbolic form in his Tale of the Western Exile (see Book II).

Another symbol lies in the very word for a person following the spiritual path: the salik, a “pilgrim” travelling through spaces beyond the visible world. It recalls the expression peregrinare pro Christo—to wander or make a pilgrimage for Christ—used in the early Celtic Church.

But every question we have raised here ultimately depends on one greater question: how are the world beyond the senses and the world we can sense related? How can powers beyond matter be present within material forms? And what relationship, if any, exists between spiritual ranks and the hierarchies of earthly society? This is the first and the final question, because it helps explain the different paths taken by the traditional East and by the West.

We find a beautiful account of this relationship between the spiritual and the visible world in the writings of the late Shaykh Sarkar Agha, the leader of the Shaykhi school in Iran. His account fits perfectly with the philosophy of light. When he speaks of souls entering this world, he says we should picture the way a person’s image appears in a mirror.

Or think of sunlight striking a reflecting surface from high above. The burning body of the sun does not literally “come down” to Earth. In the same way, souls—spiritual selves together with their original spiritual bodies—do not physically descend into this world “in person.” The mirror through which a soul appears in earthly life can shatter, but the original image belongs to another world and continues to exist in its own right.

An image’s presence “suspended” in a mirror is nothing like the way blackness, for example, spreads through a black object. The material of the mirror is not the material of the image reflected in it. The mirror shows the image. And by showing it, the mirror reveals that the image is present “elsewhere,” in another dimension. This is pure appearance through light.126

Here we find an understanding of being, life, our presence in the world, and its ultimate purpose that differs sharply from what Western readers ordinarily associate with incarnation. This brings us back to an earlier question, and it is a decisive one. What would a world in which the religious doctrine of the Incarnation had never prevailed make of that doctrine’s transformation—or decline—into a secular doctrine of social incarnation, expressed as collective consciousness? Such a doctrine can foster the illusion that merely by leaving behind individual existence we enter something like the divine.

Would the development of the world of Forms follow a parallel path? Shiite inner spirituality has a very different centre of gravity: the ghaybat, the hiddenness of the Hidden Imam. This is an extreme instance of the mystical dimension that surrounds all things and makes them shine with a reality beyond the senses. The fundamental contrast, then, is between historical consciousness and gnostic consciousness: between a way of seeing shaped by outward history and one shaped by inner spiritual knowledge.

3. Historical Consciousness and Gnostic Consciousness

Historical consciousness is a subject that people today readily accept as important.

But if we want to do justice to gnostic consciousness—a way of knowing through inner spiritual insight—we must move against many of today’s theological currents and break with deeply rooted prejudices. Otherwise we will simply treat it as one more “historical phenomenon,” which would defeat the purpose of our inquiry. Our first warning, whenever the opportunity arises, must be against the common confusion between allegory and spiritual meaning.

The methods Christians used to interpret their sacred writings can teach us much about the beginnings of Qur’anic interpretation. Especially valuable are the different approaches associated with the early schools of Antioch and Alexandria. I cannot review the whole field here; I must refer readers to the major studies of early Christian interpretation127 and recall the old formula that came to express the famous doctrine of Scripture’s four meanings: littera (sensus historicus) gesta docet; quid credas, allegoria; moralis, quid agas; quid speras, anagogia.

In English: “The letter, or historical meaning, tells you what happened; allegory tells you what to believe; the moral meaning tells you what to do; and the higher, or anagogical, meaning tells you what to hope for.” This formula has a poor reputation today. Even mentioning it can irritate scholars of language and theologians, who see it as a clever but artificial method for twisting texts and forcing them to say what their interpreters already wanted them to say. We have to admit that the method was often abused. It could dissolve a text’s actual content into a universal system of allegorical readings.

Yet we also have to recognise that the devout readers who used it for centuries would have found it difficult to accept that the most important meaning of Scripture is what we now call its “natural and historical” meaning. Beneath their awkwardness and their sometimes irritating tricks of interpretation, we must try to discover what they were really seeking. Perhaps we are making a different mistake of our own when we fail to ask the basic question: what makes understanding possible? In what kind of space does it unfold? In what kind of time does it happen?

How we answer these questions—we have already tried to answer the first two—determines whether we confuse allegory with symbol or keep them distinct. Among all the People of the Book, we can distinguish two broad tendencies. Some interpreters sought meaning but never went beyond allegory; they are most often found within official religious institutions. Others genuinely sought and practised spiritual interpretation; they are most often found outside the established, majority traditions. There is a reason for this difference. Allegory is harmless. Spiritual meaning can be revolutionary.

Allegorical interpretation often feels artificial because, in the end, it tells us something we could have said without the allegory. It works within fixed boundaries. Those boundaries exclude not only the return of spontaneous, personal prophetic inspiration but also the possibility of a prophetic way of interpreting Scripture. Anything already condemned as “heresy” is unavailable from the outset.

The interpreter’s vision is closed to the pleroma—the fullness of the spiritual world—to the events that take place there, and to all those realities that can reach our awareness only through symbols. An allegory merely restates something already clear to consciousness, something that could always be known and expressed in another way. That is why it can seem both unnecessary and contrived. Allegory can move in several directions, but all those directions stay on the same level of awareness and of our understanding of what exists.

Spiritual interpretation through symbols works differently. It preserves both the words of the text and their hidden meaning—the outward (zahir) and the inward (batin). Only when both are held together can the literal words become transparent to another world. And that other world becomes visible through the words themselves, not by doing away with them.128

When the written words become a symbol, they are not a disposable disguise for something we could easily say more directly. They are the only, and the best, expression available for beings and events that have not yet been put into words: realities dimly sensed, things that have not reached ordinary awareness or may never fully be able to reach it. A symbol can never exhaust the mystery to which it points. Explaining a symbol, therefore, does not abolish it or make it useless, as an explanation might do with an allegory.

We must return to it and uncover its meaning again and again; we must make its meaning real in our own experience. We understand symbols by moving down or up through different levels of being, through deeper levels of consciousness or higher levels beyond ordinary consciousness.

That is why Swedenborg’s interpretation, as we saw in § 2, draws out spiritual meaning while expressly rejecting allegorical interpretation. It does not abolish the literal meaning or what he calls the apparentiae reales, the “real appearances.” Instead it makes them transparent, like windows or images through which a world more substantial than they are can be glimpsed. That world can become visible only through them. The early Gnostics’ reading of Scripture was not mere allegory either.129 And despite all the differences between ancient Gnosis and Islamic forms of inner knowledge, the Shiite interpretation of the Qur’an is no more reducible to allegory than theirs was.

On this point it has yet to receive anything like fair treatment.130 Direct awareness of the original events beyond ordinary history goes hand in hand with this gnostic way of knowing. To force it to submit to the standards of historical consciousness would be to do violence to it. We have already heard the Fifth Imam warn that treating the Sacred Book in that way would bring about its death, because it would destroy the spiritual meaning that is always coming to life anew.

This is why I find it deeply troubling to hear people speak of the “errors” of Gnosis. Such judgments silently take as their standard the rationally stated doctrines that would prevail only in later centuries. Anyone who tries to understand Gnosis as a religious phenomenon, in its many forms, will meet one surprise after another.

We must ask what lies behind the vehemence with which Gnosis was attacked during Christianity’s first centuries—a hostility that returns again and again whenever the gnostic spirit reappears. One measure of the alarm it provokes is the response to Origen. He is a Christian teacher whose name can scarcely be mentioned without also raising the question of Gnosis, despite which—or perhaps because of which—he is so often invoked. It is difficult simply to dismiss those who regard him as a Christian Gnostic. He has been criticised for treating the Gospel more as pure spirituality than as historical revelation.

But the opposite criticism could just as fairly be made of his opponents. The clearest sign of Origen’s outlook, we are told, is the apparently insurmountable difficulty he had with the historical fact of the Incarnation.

Yet perhaps the very idea of a “historical fact” had not yet become established in Christian religious consciousness. Perhaps being historical was not, for those early Christians, the test of truth—or perhaps “historical reality” meant something else to them. Certainly the historical Christ, the Christ of the Incarnation and the Passion, caused Origen difficulty.

But why, in turn, were his opponents so angrily disturbed by the pleroma, the heavenly fullness whose “history” the Gnostics told, and by the figures of the Aeon Christ and Sophia?

Rather than blaming the opposing sides for the beliefs that gave each of them its very reason for being, we would do better to understand what lay behind their positions. Much depends on these unspoken motives, including whether we can grasp the spiritual meaning at issue here.

Throughout Christian history, people with a similar approach to religious experience have shared Origen’s difficulty.131 They have tended to ask questions that conflict with the standards we now apply to historical religion and historical religious events. One might argue that, without the doctrine of the Incarnation as eventually defined by the Church councils—without the idea that divine and human nature are united in the person of Christ—the central object of Christian faith would never have “entered history.”

Yet there were people who were fully Christian and felt no need to make that claim. The need arose only once a particular view of history had been accepted: one that made entry into the record of historical events a condition of something’s truth and reality.

Are we to conclude that Christianity itself necessarily gave rise to the historical outlook we hold today? The fact remains that some Christians rejected this requirement and did not find it self-evident. Take the Cross of Light. It is not an event of ordinary history in the way that the Church councils understood the Incarnation.

But for the Gnostics who wrote the Acts of John, the Cross of Light was no less real or true than the cross on Calvary. In fact, it was more real, because they regarded it as the true Cross. This was a real event, but not one that could be witnessed through the physical senses, regardless of the witness’s inner spiritual condition. It belonged to a reality outside the chain of material events that historians study.132

Here lies the distinction we need to understand: between a theophany, an appearance or manifestation of God, and an incarnation, God taking on human nature. It is also the distinction between a Gnostic way of understanding religion and a historical one.

Real events take place in the Pleroma, the fullness of the heavenly world. Their nature, time, and place are not those of events as conceived by official Church doctrine.

Yet centuries of thinking historically have made us so dependent on the evidence of outward history that, if a religious event loses its claim to material historical reality, we are inclined to think it has lost all reality. From a Gnostic point of view, this is precisely the danger. When people dismiss spiritual knowledge, ridicule the Pleroma, or deny the reality of the beings and events within it, they may be turning Christianity itself into something merely natural and worldly.

Worse still, by restricting earthly events to the limits of historical fact, they rob those events of their deeper substance and make even Redemption a secular idea. So when the Gnostics are accused of having posed the greatest threat to early Christianity, we should remember that they saw matters in exactly the opposite way. For them, it was their opponents who were placing Christianity in mortal danger.

These disagreements were so serious that the heavenly, spiritual meaning cherished by the Gnostics eventually became confused with—or lost beneath—a safer practice of religious allegory. That practice offered a way to bridge the gap between outward, historical Christianity and the Christianity of inner experience without risking a charge of heresy.

But when we encounter Gnosis again in Islam, we also encounter the idea of a real Event that can be experienced without having to become a material event in history. As we have seen, and will see again, Islam began from a different position. Its prophetic calling rests on experiences of divine manifestation; the Qur’an’s understanding of Christ has affinities with that found in the Acts of John; and an appearance can remain a genuine Event, grounded in a reality that precedes the heavenly world as we know it. This did not spare Islamic mystics the troubles faced by their counterparts elsewhere.

But the circumstances were different. We have tried to show what that difference meant for the spiritual struggle of Shiism. It also makes us consider the upheaval that our modern historical outlook, with its philosophy of history, may bring to a religious consciousness that never shared its assumptions—a consciousness that believed in this world only because it also believed in its end, in both senses of the word: that the world is finite, and that it has a purpose.

Earlier, I suggested that the strict limits placed on harmless allegorical interpretation, wherever it was still allowed alongside the literal and historical meaning of scripture, went hand in hand with the suppression of freely inspired, prophetic interpretation. Those who see the suppression of the Montanist movement in the second century as a decisive turning point in Christianity are probably right.133 Montanus and his followers claimed that angels were bringing new revelations. They were rejected as heretics who threatened the teaching handed down by the apostles.

From then on, fresh expressions of the Spirit—whether through prophetic messages, visions, or new prophetic readings of earlier revelations—were no longer permitted. The institution of the Church, with its authority to define doctrine, took the place of free prophetic inspiration. Could we say that such inspiration simply “continued” in another form? It seems more accurate to admit that the Church could not accommodate prophecy that spoke freely, or spontaneous revelations of the Spirit.

Tradition therefore had to become fixed in the words of doctrine. The ending of prophetic inspiration, the removal of Gnosis, and the exclusion or destruction of writings labelled apocryphal that had emerged in Gnostic circles—some of them rediscovered only recently—all point in the same direction. They reveal, with striking consistency, the demands of a historically grounded religious outlook in its conflict with the Gnostic outlook.

Other consequences followed. The history of Church doctrines came to be treated as a one-way process. Once Church authorities condemned a teaching as heresy, it belonged to the past. It had supposedly failed to follow the “course of history,” understood as the development of official doctrine. It had been superseded, and there was no reason to reconsider it as a living interpretation that might still challenge us.

At most, scholars could study it as a doctrine of an earlier age. And they could do so without challenging whether it had been orthodox in its own time: after all, it would make little sense to condemn it by appealing to standards that had not yet been established.

But the history of doctrine no longer had any obligation to recognise or respond to signs that speak to us now and might call everything into question. It could only present such writings to present-day readers with a suitably modest air of “objectivity,” showing them the doctrines “as they appear.” Fair enough.

But to whom do they appear? We may refuse to ask, but then we miss the central problem of interpretation. Meaning is never simply there on its own; something has meaning only for someone to whom it speaks. What meaning can a spiritual history hold today for someone who believes it has long since been left behind?

We do not find the same pattern in traditional Islam. As we already know, a central teaching of Shiism is that the end of the cycle of prophets who bring religious laws opens a new cycle: one devoted to discovering the hidden meanings of divine revelations. This is the cycle of walayat, the spiritual guidance and closeness to God associated with the Imams.

Our authors will show us that, under this name, a hidden or inner prophetic function continues in Islam (nobowwat batina). It is a kind of contemplative prophecy through which inspiration carries on in its own distinct forms (see Chapter V below).

Spiritual seekers also understand the mystic’s calling and experience through the model of prophetic experience, as a renewal of the gift once granted to the prophets. The walayat of the Imams—their appointment as “people of God,” God’s friends and beloved ones (Awliya Allah)—cannot be compared to the authority of a senior priesthood.

Indeed, the Imamate is now in a state of concealment, or ghaybat. Nor are Muslim writers who catalogue heresies historians of doctrine in the technical Western sense; an accusation of unbelief (takfir) has never had more than a limited, local effect.

What is striking is the extent to which different schools and systems of thought remain present and alive for an Islamic thinker, always capable of being brought to life again. A doctrine is judged by its relation to a spiritual centre, or “pole,” rather than by where it stands in an assumed evolution of doctrine. These schools and ideas send out signs, and the thinker responds according to his own ability to receive them. They present themselves to him, not to an imagined figure from a dead and superseded past whom he is merely trying to reconstruct.

This brings us to a question that also concerns many contemporary philosophers. It is especially revealing that reflection on Islam should lead us to it. Is it possible to devise a single “scientific” way of examining religious questions that means the same thing to people who possess a capacity for religious experience and to people who do not—to believers and nonbelievers alike? That may be as unrealistic as designing a musical instrument equally useful to musicians and to people who cannot hear differences in musical pitch.

But the question cuts both ways. Does “scientific” have only one meaning? Could a disciplined method of interpreting spiritual, inner meaning also be rigorous, reliable, and valid?

4. Making Events Historical, or Discovering Their Inner Meaning?

If this really is a choice between two opposing approaches, it is a choice created by the situation we have just examined. Perhaps we can find a way beyond it by questioning the assumptions and categories that produced it in the first place.

Let us briefly recall how the problem developed in the West.

The Reformation of the sixteenth century has been understood in two very different ways. Some see it as hastening the rise of the historical outlook and, with it, the movement towards a secular world no longer shaped by Christianity.

Others see it as holding the remedy for that movement: the possibility of restoring the prophetic inspiration that had been closed off during Christianity’s first centuries. Martin Luther did describe his years as a monk as a time when he “turned everything into allegory.” Later, he wanted instead to tradere Scripturam simplici sensu—to present Scripture in its plain meaning.

Yet we must not forget that his great early discovery grew out of his own mystical training. This was his understanding of significatio passiva: a meaning received and fulfilled within the believer, through faith, in the event of “justification,” by which the believer is made right with God. From this point of view, the literal sense and the sense concerned with a person’s own spiritual life came together.

The old division of Scripture into four meanings, along with its artificial methods, could be overcome only because meaning had been brought inward. Later Protestant orthodoxy would forget the force of this discovery. Its true heirs were those whom Protestant history calls the “Spirituals”: Sebastian Franck, Valentin Weigel, Caspar Schwenckfeld, the followers of Jacob Boehme, and those inspired by the idea of a Rosicrucian Order promoted in the writings of Johann Valentin Andreae. The Thirty Years’ War would crush the hopes attached to that last movement.134

We encounter this same tradition in the “divinatory” or intuitively perceptive approach to interpretation developed by Friedrich D. E. Schleiermacher (1768–1834), the great theologian of German Romanticism. Two things about his work matter especially here.

First, Schleiermacher inspired the philosopher and historian Wilhelm Dilthey to develop an approach to interpretation based on understanding another person’s meaning from within. In doing so, Dilthey offered a positive answer to the question with which we ended the previous section: yes, interpretation of inner meaning can be a disciplined method.

Unfortunately, Dilthey’s approach would become lost in the difficulties of historicism, the belief that everything, including our own understanding, is determined by its place in history. It no longer had a clear direction or a firm point of reference. Today the word hermeneutics, meaning the study and practice of interpretation, is widely used in the human sciences. It is significant that, through Dilthey’s work, this use of the term can be traced back to the problem of interpreting a sacred book.

Second, in our own time, a theological approach has emerged that rejects Schleiermacher’s spirit and fights historicism, yet has ended in a dead end of its own. A Muslim student or researcher is unlikely to be familiar with this particular Western debate. We need to say a little about it, because it matters whenever we compare Christian and Islamic theology or philosophy.

We have just mentioned historicism. Once the historical outlook grows so powerful that philosophers can no longer imagine standing outside history—even their own thoughts being shaped and limited by the age in which they live—they have little choice but to examine human lives as they have been recorded in lasting, accessible works. This was Dilthey’s approach: to look for the inner meaning expressed in those works. Interpretation then becomes a science of understanding, an effort to grasp a meaning that reveals itself only under certain conditions.

Above all, there must already be some connection, in life itself, between the interpreter and what the text is about. There must also be a living connection between the interpreter and the author who speaks about it—a relationship in which the interpreter is already personally involved. Interpretation thus becomes, as it was for the Stoics, a “science of the individual.” Its technical goal is to reach conclusions that can claim objective validity.

But does this not assume that some point of reference can stand beyond history? Certainly, we understand Plato only when we think philosophically alongside him. To do that, though, we must understand what Platonism means. We might say that Platonism belongs to a particular period in the history of philosophy, that the period represents a lost age, or that Plato’s writings are among the “sources” from which we can reconstruct that age. Very well.

But before a work can serve as a source, we have to understand it in a particular way.

We must decide what it means, and even decide what the larger historical subject is for which we are treating it as evidence.135

We can then spend forever moving around the “circle of interpretation,” where understanding the part depends on the whole and understanding the whole depends on its parts. Or we can watch the horizon of meaning recede endlessly as the uniform line of chronological time grows longer, with no direction or destination.

The only apparent escape is for some unacknowledged system of metaphysics to declare where history is going. Such a system may conceal even the true name of its promised final outcome. It may decree the meaning of political, social, or cultural change and construct a “dialectic of History”—a supposedly necessary movement of history—which is little more than a secular retelling of Bossuet’s Discourse on Universal History. All the while, it forgets that its own standpoint is just as much a product of its historical circumstances as any other.
