And no amount of historical criticism can alter this fact: for Shiite believers over thirteen centuries, a particular hadith has truly been spoken by a particular Imam, because its very content is understood as the Imam's own utterance.

So it should not be surprising that we have preferred, and will continue to prefer, the company of teachers who lived within the historical reality of Shiite faith. We have already met Haydar Amuli, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, Qazi Sa'id Qummi, and many others who sustained Shiite spiritual life. Mulla Sadra left us an immense commentary on the traditions collected by Kulayni.195

When we are dealing with the realities of faith, the number of centuries separating two thinkers is not decisive. What matters is their closeness in intention and understanding: a kind of being together across time. We have already seen how this closeness makes possible philosophical reflection that never cuts itself off from spiritual practice. It also helps us understand why traditional Islamic philosophy continued to flourish in Shiite circles down to our own day.

If, then, we study with these Shiite teachers the sections of the great tradition collections devoted to prophecy and the Imams, we find that the teaching about prophecy gives especially clear expression to a central Islamic conviction: human beings need a guide to lead them along the “straight path” (sirat mustaqim) of their return to God. This is the path on which they remain faithful to the timeless covenant made with God before entering earthly life, as we saw in Chapter II. As far as the historical evidence allows us to trace the idea of prophecy and the special spiritual gift of the prophets, we cannot go back beyond the teachings of the Shiite Imams.

The question first takes shape through them, and Islamic thinking about prophecy grows from their teaching. There is a striking agreement between their arguments for the necessity of prophets and those later offered by philosophers such as al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Suhrawardi. They approach this necessity from two directions: from the human side and from the divine side.

For the philosophers who followed Avicenna, the aql—the intellect, or nous—remains only a potential ability in most people. Only in a few does the full human possibility become a living reality.196 These thinkers do not imagine a state of innocence in which people, simply following their natural impulses, could have built a society on their own.197198199 What passes for “natural law” would be what we call the law of the jungle. Avicenna and Biruni therefore hold that a divinely sent messenger, a prophet, is needed to establish law and justice.

Yet these philosophical arguments repeat what we find in the teachings of the Shiite Imams—for example, in the words of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq (d. 148 AH/765 CE), preserved by Kulayni. Left entirely to themselves, people cannot find their way. They must come together in communities; but to do so they need someone who stands above the rest and shows them what is necessary both for safety in this life and for the life that continues beyond it.

The philosophers say that the fourth level of intellect—intellect fully at work—is reached by only a few individuals. Similarly, the Imams speak of five levels of Spirit (ruh), the highest of which, the Holy Spirit (ruh al-quds), is granted especially to the prophets.

For Imam Ja'far, however, the reason for this human inability is explained more directly from God's side. God, being beyond everything created, is inaccessible and invisible. No one has ever seen God or ever will. On this point Shiism differs from certain other Islamic schools: the Karramiyya allowed that God could be seen in this world and the next, and so conceived the vision in terms of space and dimensions; the Ash'arites allowed for vision in the next world, but without a face-to-face encounter or any spatial dimensions. After a long explanation of why no one can see or “touch” God, the Imam concludes:

It follows that there must be people who can command and forbid in the name of the All-Wise, All-Knowing One, and speak on His behalf. These are the people we call prophets (anbiya). They are the chosen ones among His creatures: sages (hukama) who have been taught by Wisdom (hikmat)200 and sent on their mission by Wisdom itself. They share with other human beings the fact of being created and the possession of a physical body. Apart from this, however, they do not share the same ways of being and acting as other people, because the All-Wise, All-Knowing One supports them and inspires them through Wisdom.

Such guidance remains available in every age and every period through the signs and proofs brought by the messengers and prophets. In this way God's earth is never left without a witness who stands as His proof (hujjat)201—someone with a Sign (alam, a symbol) that shows the truth of what he says and the constancy of his justice.

This statement by Imam Ja'far raises three groups of questions.

1. The prophets as mediators. First, the prophets have a special qualification given by God that enables them to act as mediators. Following a long tradition, Mulla Sadra explains that prophetic existence has two sides. One faces divine transcendence and holiness (taqaddus); the other faces material reality and the human condition (tajassum). That is why a prophet can be called “a human being of divine standing” or “a divine lord in human form” (insan rabbani am rabb insani).

Both expressions are striking. They show that, from the beginning, Islamic thinking about prophecy and the Imams faced a problem similar to the one that divided the Nestorians and Jacobites in Eastern Christian debates about Christ.

Yet in Islamic prophecy, the divine qualification belongs only to the eternal prophetic reality—the Muhammadan Reality (haqiqat muhammadiya)—and not to the Prophet's earthly humanity (bashariyat). The Qur'an confirms his humanity in the words: “I am a human being like you, but divine revelation has come to me” (18:111). His divine reality, on the other hand, is suggested by another verse: “It was not you who threw when you threw; it was God who threw” (8:17).

2. How can God be seen? Second, as we have just read, the argument that prophets are necessary rests partly on the claim that God cannot be seen. The Imams' conversations with their close followers return to three related ideas: seeing God is impossible; God can be described only by the attributes God gives Himself; and God can be known only through God.

Yet, in the end, a certain kind of vision does prove possible. What kind of vision can that be?

a) Someone once wrote to the Eleventh Imam, Hasan Askari (d. 260 AH/874 CE), referring to a famous saying attributed to the Prophet—the hadith of the vision: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”202203 The writer asked: “How could anyone worship a God whom he does not see?” The Imam replied: “Truly, God—blessed and exalted be He—made visible to the heart of His Messenger that light of His sublime majesty which the Messenger loved.”

This answer takes us into the territory of mystical experience. It introduces inner vision: seeing with the heart. It is love that makes vision possible—and love is itself the one being guided. What love sees is the very object it loves. The depth of the vision depends on the depth of the love. Mulla Sadra makes the point clearly. Most people see only through their bodily senses; their intellect (aql) never rises beyond a latent possibility. The “holy intellect” (intellectus sanctus, aql qudsi), which is the spiritual heart, is free from the limits of physical time and space.

b) A visitor, a Kharijite, once asked the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir (d. 115 AH/733 CE): “What do you worship? God Most High? Have you seen Him?” The Imam answered:

No. Eyes do not see Him with their bodily power of sight, but hearts see Him through the realities (haqa'iq) of faith. He cannot be known by comparison (qiyas), whether by logical reasoning or analogy, and He cannot be grasped by the senses. His Signs (ayat) reveal how He may be described, and His symbols (alamat) make Him known. There is no violence in His judgments. Such is God, the God of whom we say: there is no god but Huwa—He.204

c) The Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq, also relates an answer given by the First Imam, the Commander of the Faithful, to a learned man who asked: “Commander of the Faithful, do you see your Lord when you worship Him?” The Imam replied: “Take care! I would never worship a God whom I did not see.” The man asked in return: “Then how do you see Him?” “Take care,” said the Imam. “Eyes do not see Him through physical sight. Hearts see Him through the realities of faith.”205206207

The Imams' answers preserve a paradox. On one side stands the refusal given to Moses: “You shall not see Me” (lan tarani, 7:139). On the other stands the prophetic testimony: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”

Indeed, as we shall see in Chapter VII, the Imams' teaching led their followers towards a doctrine that agrees with Ibn Arabi's: a manifestation of God can be seen only in a form suited to the spiritual capacity of the person who sees it (mutajalla lahu). That person sees only his or her own form in the mirror of God; the Guide takes the form of the person being guided.

Vision of the heart, knowledge of the heart (ma'rifat qalbiya): these ideas appear repeatedly in the Imams' teaching. They do not belong exclusively to Sufism and were not invented by al-Ghazali (d. 505 AH/1111 CE). It is important to remember this whenever we ask about the relationship between Shiism and Sufism, or between the teaching about the Imams and mystical experience.208

Let us turn to a remarkable passage from Mulla Sadra to see how fruitful this theme became for Shiite philosophers. It will keep returning throughout our study of prophets and Imams. Sadra asks us to think carefully about what we mean each time we use the word vision.

Among the followers of the later Imams, people often repeated a remark attributed to Hisham ibn al-Hakam, a famous young follower of the Sixth Imam. His argument bears a striking resemblance to certain ideas in Stoic physics: God, he said, must somehow be a body (jism). Otherwise God would be an act (fi'l, a verb)—something unreal that would only acquire concrete existence through the subject performing the action.209210 What looks like a contradiction does not trouble Mulla Sadra greatly.

Unlike many earlier philosophers, he is concerned not primarily with the fixed essences of things but with their act of existing, and here his thinking too has affinities with Stoicism. One and the same essence can exist on different levels. That is true of what we call a “body,” from a body made of physical elements to a spiritual body. It is also true of the human being, whom Sadra understands in three parts. (A threefold understanding of the human being was abandoned in the West at the Council of Constantinople in 869.)

Here is that threefold picture. First comes the physical human being, with an organic body and the senses through which we perceive the physical world.

Second comes the psychic human being, whose “psychic body” has no parts that can be located within the dimensions of this world, because it does not belong to this world. Its way of perceiving depends on imagination and imaginative awareness, whose theory Mulla Sadra developed in particular depth.

Third comes the spiritual human being, with a “spiritual body” that possesses spiritual senses (hawass ruhaniya aqliya): spiritual sight, spiritual hearing, and so on.

That is why certain Qur'anic verses and hadiths must be understood at a spiritual level if we are to grasp them at the level where they actually speak—in what is, for that level, their true literal meaning. If the essence we call “body” can exist in different ways, on levels that differ in dignity and density, we can even imagine, at the furthest limit, something like a “divine body” (jism ilahi).

But we must immediately remember the Qur'anic words: “Nothing is like Him” (42:9).

The home of these spiritual senses is the heart. It is the heart that makes prophetic knowledge possible. For prophetic revelation and mystical experience belong to the same kind of spiritual reality,211 as Mulla Sadra explains:

The source of all mystical unveilings (mukashafat) is the human heart, through its very nature and its understanding212 of light, using the spiritual senses. For the heart has eyes, ears, and all the other senses. Many passages in the classical hadith collections confirm this. These spiritual senses are the source (asl) from which our bodily senses arise.

When the veil between the spiritual senses and outward reality is lifted, the source—the spiritual sense—and what comes from it—the bodily sense—are joined. What bodily senses perceive is then contemplated through the spiritual senses themselves. The Spirit (ruh) contemplates all this through its own power, because at its level all realities (haqa'iq) form a unity, just as they do for the Active Intelligence.213

The heart therefore brings together every form and every level of the teaching about prophets and Imams.

3. Why the Imam must always be present. Third, this same idea of the heart leads us from the necessity of prophets to the necessity of the Imam. This is the last group of questions raised by the Sixth Imam's statement quoted earlier, where he insists that the earth can never be without someone who stands as God's witness or proof (hujjat). The idea is essential to Shiite teaching about the Imams.

From it comes the image of the “pole of the world,” even the “pole of poles,” without whom earthly existence could not continue for another instant. The image is familiar even in non-Shiite Sufism. We have already learned that the Imam, the pole, may be visible and known, or may be hidden, unknown to people, and beyond the reach of their bodily senses. According to the tradition, the latter is our own situation: the age of occultation (ghaybat), the age of the Hidden Imam.

How was this idea established in the first place? We have already seen its foundation. The prophet's task was to reveal the outward wording of the sacred law (sharia). The task of another was to teach its inner spiritual meaning (ta'wil). That other person is the Imam, the “Guardian of the Book” (qayyim al-Qur'an), who keeps its meaning alive.

The Sixth Imam's hadith brings us to this conclusion: God must send prophets, because the great human task is to find the way to live faithfully by the timeless covenant made with God. “Am I not your Lord?” (a-lastu bi-rabbikum?), God asks in the Qur'an (7:171). People cannot find that way without a guide, and that guide is the prophet.

But what happens when the prophet is no longer there? More urgently still, what happens when the prophet who has departed was the final Prophet?

A follower named Mansur ibn Hazim once told Imam Ja'far about his conversations with Muslims who were not Shiites. He would ask them the crucial question: “Now that God's Messenger is no longer here, who will stand before humanity as the witness, the one who can give the decisive answer (hujjat)?” Usually they replied: “The Qur'an.”

But Mansur had studied the Qur'an himself. He knew how fiercely people disagreed about what its words meant. So he had concluded that the Qur'an alone could not serve as the decisive witness without a guardian (qayyim), an interpreter (mufassir), who knew its full inner truth (haqiqat).214 This guardian is the Imam: the Guide.

Mulla Sadra, for his part, argues that this central Shiite teaching follows directly from the fact that God is beyond everything else.215 Philosophy teaches, he says, that whatever has no cause—the uncaused ground, the Abgrund—cannot have its essence defined or be proved by appealing to something else. All other proofs begin from it. We know things that have causes through those causes.

But how can we know the One who causes all causes (musabbib al-asbab) and makes every cause knowable? That is the meaning of the First Imam's saying: “I have never known anything without knowing God before it.” A mystic echoes the same thought: “I know my God only through my God.”

To “know one's God” is to know God's attributes.

But how could we reach such knowledge without either a divine message brought by an angel (wahy) or divine inspiration (ilham)? Those who know about the “origin” and the “return” (mabda' and ma'ad) have received one of these two gifts. The prophets receive the message through an angel. The Imams and the Friends of God receive inspiration, whether in dreams or while awake. This kind of inspired knowledge is what we call sacred knowledge or hierognosis. Everyone who has received neither kind must turn to God's messengers, the prophets.

Yet the question immediately returns: whom are we to seek when there is no longer a prophet?

We now have the basis of the argument. A living witness (hujjat) must always be present, because the Qur'an by itself cannot perform that role. The Qur'an has an outward meaning and an inward meaning (batin)—indeed, tradition speaks of as many as seven inner depths. It is a book of symbols, whose meanings are not immediately visible. Mulla Sadra declares:

The Qur'an is not a book that can be understood through the ordinary knowledge of philosophers. Most educated people already find it difficult to understand the philosophers' books, whether those of the ancients, such as Plato and Aristotle, or those of more recent writers, such as al-Farabi and Avicenna. How, then, could they understand the Qur'an—the divine speech that comes from God and descended into the heart of His Prophet?

Who could guide people through its many hidden meanings, unless that person possessed an inward sight (basirat) illuminated by God, and a spiritual hearing (sama' aqli) able to hear from God and His angels—even without seeing an angel's form or hearing the sound of its speech, as the Prophet himself saw and heard through these two spiritual senses?

As we shall see, the difference between prophets on the one hand and Imams and Friends of God on the other does not lie in whether they possess this sacred knowledge. It lies in the way they receive it and the degree to which they possess it.

Anyone who possesses this double power of spiritual sight and hearing—even if it does not equal that of a prophet-messenger—is therefore capable, after the Prophet, of guarding the Book in the fullness of its meaning. That person is the Imam. We have already noted that this answer to the problem of succession does not appeal to a Church, an official body of religious teachers, or any collective authority. It appeals to a person of God, inspired by God. In this sense, the very need to interpret revelation becomes a scriptural argument for the necessity of the Imams.

On the deepest level of their being, as we have already learned, the Imams inherit a spiritual reality from prophecy, and they have been entrusted with that inheritance from before the beginning of time. Here the argument for Ali ibn Abi Talib's position as Imam rests on something more specific: among all the Prophet's companions, he alone knew the complete meaning of the revelations. Whenever a verse of the Qur'an was revealed, the Prophet dictated it to Ali, made him repeat it, and taught him both its outward explanation (tafsir) and its inner spiritual meaning (ta'wil). Ali himself relates:

And the Prophet prayed to God to enlarge my understanding and strengthen my memory. From the time he made that prayer for me, I have not forgotten a single verse of the Book or a single piece of knowledge that he dictated to me.216

Texts like these help us understand the very heart of Shiism. One can only wish they were more widely known—and, above all, better understood—in the West.

The point becomes even clearer when we discover that the Imam, as “Guardian of the Qur'an,” is identified with the heart. Here we meet again the young Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who stood out among the companions of the Sixth Imam both for his youth and for the fierce devotion he felt towards the Imam. On one occasion, the boy decided on his own to challenge a leading Mu'tazilite teacher, Abu Marwan Amr ibn Ubayd, who held public discussions in Basra. The Mu'tazilites represented a tradition of reasoned theological debate within Islam.

The Imam later asked Hisham to tell him about this bold expedition into argument. Hisham had jumped onto his camel and ridden from Kufa to Basra, where he found the teacher giving his Friday lesson in the mosque, surrounded by disciples. It was a solemn gathering.

But Hisham asked to speak and began posing questions that the teacher at first found absurd. “Do you have eyes?” he asked. “What do you do with them?” He went on in the same way through each of the five senses.

The teacher played along. That allowed Hisham to reach his final question. In the teaching about the body's subtle inner faculties, the heart—as the seat of awareness—is what finally decides whether information from the senses is trustworthy or doubtful. In that sense, the heart is the Imam, the guide, of our bodily perceptions. The Mu'tazilite teacher had to agree that he possessed such a heart. Hisham then replied:

Abu Marwan! So God has not abandoned the organs of your senses without giving them an Imam—one who confirms what is true and enables them to settle their doubts. Would God, then, have left all human beings to their confusion, doubts, and bewilderment, when He has given you an Imam to whom your own senses can bring their doubts and confusion?217

It is especially important that the need for an Imam is established here by comparing the wider world with the smaller world of the human being. At the very moment when we discover why the human community needs an Imam, a path opens towards finding the Imam within the spiritual life of each person. The teaching about the Imams meets the most personal kind of spiritual fulfilment.

What is said about the Imam's role in the community continually sheds light on what takes place in each person's inner life, and the reverse is also true. A believer's chosen bond with one of the Imams can be experienced as the presence of an inner guide.

In Ismaili thought, for example, this insight developed into the symbolism of Mount Sinai and the olive tree. Mount Sinai stands for the mystic. At its summit—or in its heart—grows the olive tree, which represents the Imam: the “soul of the soul” (jan-e jan), the mystic's personal inner guide.218

We can go further. In the light of what we have learned about the spiritual senses, realities belonging to the inner world must be understood literally at their own level. That is how Mulla Sadra reads Hisham's story. As we saw in Chapter V, at each spiritual station (maqam) the spiritual truth is the literal truth proper to that station. Sadra writes:

The heart is a subtle body of light (latifa nuraniya). It must be distinguished from the cone-shaped organ of flesh (qalb sanawbari). The thinking soul (nafs natiqa) is the leader and Imam of all its powers. The heart, as the soul's permanent dwelling and the throne on which it sits, is the leader and Imam of the organs through which those powers work.219

The same relationship holds on the larger scale. It is essential for life that the sign of the Imam should stand in every age. That is why the invisible presence of the “Hidden Imam” is necessary, even during a period of occultation (ghaybat) such as our own. According to Mulla Sadra, this conclusion about divine wisdom holds regardless of the differences between sacred laws (sharia) and religions. For, as Imam Ja'far tells the young Hisham in approval, it is written in the divine Books (kutub ilahiya) and the heavenly Psalms (zubur samawiya): “in the books of Abraham and Moses” (87:19).

As Mulla Sadra reminds us, this is where the question that divided Islam from within comes into focus. What makes someone an Imam? Why must an Imam be present in every age, whether openly known or hidden from most people? The Shiite answer becomes clearer once we return to a distinction we made earlier: the divine communication (wahy) received by prophets sent with a mission, and the inspiration (ilham) granted to the Imams and God's friends.

By distinguishing prophets according to how they receive knowledge, the Shiite understanding of prophetic knowledge also tells us where the Imam belongs in the wider story of prophecy.

Put another way, the future of the community as a spiritual community depends on what it accepts or rejects of this philosophy of prophecy. This is why I have placed that philosophy at the very foundation of philosophical thought in Islam—although my reasons have not always been understood. For the thinkers who sustained Islam's spiritual consciousness, it was through reflection on prophecy that they came to understand Islam's calling in the world.

2. The Different Kinds of Prophets and Walayat

The Arabic word for prophet, nabi,220 comes from forms of a root meaning “to bring someone news.” A nabi is someone who brings news from God (mukhbir 'an Allah).

But what, in its deepest sense, makes someone a prophet? Mulla Sadra says that we cannot answer until we have explained how knowledge is placed—or, in his own striking image, “cast”—by God into the human heart (ilqa al-'ulum).

In seeking an answer, Shiite philosophers developed a theory of knowledge from the teachings about prophecy passed down by their Imams. This is a distinctive feature of the philosophy that grew out of Shiism, or the inner, spiritual understanding of Islam. It sees the Holy Spirit, Gabriel—the angel who brings revelation—as fundamentally the same being as the angel through whom knowledge becomes possible, what philosophers call the Active Intellect.

We must not mistake this for an attempt to reduce revelation to ordinary reason. The Arabic word 'aql has a wider meaning than the English word reason. It can describe forms of understanding ranging from the philosopher's fully awakened intellect to the sacred understanding of a prophet. And Mulla Sadra's central claim is not about abstract reasoning at all. It is about the heart, and the way truth can become present within it.

The human heart (qalb al-insan)—always the central image here—is, by its very nature, capable of receiving the reality of anything that can be known. Such knowledge may come through religious teaching: sacred texts and the established religious sciences ('ulum shar'iya).

Or it may come directly from the giver of knowledge, the Holy Spirit understood as divine Intelligence ('Aql, Ruh). That is why the sciences called 'ulum 'aqliya cannot simply be equated with what we call rational knowledge. They can reach beyond philosophy in its usual sense. Broadly understood, they are the spiritual sciences.

Mulla Sadra divides these forms of spiritual knowledge into two groups: truths known from the outset, such as first principles, and truths that must be acquired.221 Acquired knowledge may come through teaching (ta'allum) and the indirect work of reasoning. This is the path of philosophers and scholars who build arguments.

But knowledge may also arrive suddenly in the heart, as though placed there, without the person's deliberate effort (ijtihad).

That sudden gift may come without any awareness or vision of the being who gives it. This is inspiration (ilham), the way the Imams—heirs of the Prophet—and God's spiritually initiated friends (awliya) receive knowledge. At other times, the appearance of knowledge within the heart is accompanied by seeing or hearing the angel who brings it, either in a dream or while awake.

The teaching thus takes account of several different states of awareness. At its highest level comes divine communication through the angel (wahy), reserved for the great prophets entrusted with revealing a new sacred law (sharia). The entire account of prophecy will depend on these distinctions.

Mulla Sadra explains how knowledge reaches the heart by describing the angel's part in it. Gabriel, or the Active Intellect, is the being the Qur'an refers to as the Pen (al-Qalam, 68:1): the one “through whom God writes on the tablets of hearts.” This angel is a sacred spiritual being, made of light. He stands between God and human beings so that knowledge can become present in their hearts.

As Mulla Sadra puts it, the angel plays this part “just as the pen stands between a writer and the surface—paper or tablet—on which the written marks appear.”

The relation between this luminous being and the things we can know is therefore like the relation between light and the things we can see. The comparison works for both kinds of sight: our outward vision (basar al-zahir) and our inward vision (basirat al-batin).

Our eyes see when sunlight makes things visible. The heart, which is the seat of understanding, knows when the angel—the Pen, the Active Intellect—sheds its light. The heart is like the eye in another respect, too: it can be blind.222

But there could hardly be a view of knowledge further removed from the belief that ultimate reality is beyond our knowing. This is a theory that grew out of the philosophy of Avicenna.

The image that keeps returning is that of two mirrors. In the first is the Preserved Tablet (Lawh mahfuz), bearing everything God has inscribed upon it.

The second is the human heart. Divine knowledge appears in the heart as the image in one mirror may be reflected into another. At first, a veil separates them. Philosophers try to draw it aside through their own efforts.

But sometimes a breath of divine wind lifts the veil from the eye of the heart ('ayn al-qalb). That is what happens to those who receive inspiration.

So the philosopher's knowledge and inspired knowledge are not two completely different kinds of thing. Mulla Sadra insists that the angel of knowledge is also the angel of revelation. Inspiration differs from knowledge reached through effort not in what is known, not in where it is received—the heart—and not in its source—the angel, the Pen, the Active Intellect. The difference is how far the veil has been lifted, something human choice alone cannot bring about.

Whenever knowledge becomes real within our hearts, it does so through the angel (bi-wasitat al-mala'ika). This, Mulla Sadra says, is what the Qur'an means when it says: “It is not given to a human being that God should speak to him except through communication [by an angel, wahy], or from behind a veil. Or He sends a messenger who, by His permission, conveys whatever God wishes” (42:50–51).223

We now have what we need to understand how the central idea of Twelver Shiism takes shape: the Imam as a spiritual guide. His position becomes clear once we distinguish the different kinds of prophets according to the ways they receive knowledge.

A long teaching attributed to the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, and preserved in al-Kulayni's great collection, sets out four kinds of prophets.224

  1. The prophet whose calling concerns only himself. This nabi, unlike a messenger sent to others, is a prophet for himself alone. He is not charged with passing on the signs or divine inspiration (ilham) that he receives. We might call this a form of prophecy that never goes beyond the prophet's own person.
  2. The prophet who encounters the angel in dreams. This nabi receives signs and inspiration, but also sees or hears the angel who brings him knowledge. He does so through spiritual sight or hearing, and only in dreams, not while awake. He, too, has no mission to a particular community. Lot is given as an example: he lived under the guidance of Abraham, who was both his prophet and his Imam, and followed Abraham's sacred law. Muhammad before his first waking vision of the angel bringing revelation is another example. Until then, he was a nabi, but not yet a messenger (rasul).

These first two kinds of prophecy, neither of which involves bringing a new law, are especially important to Shiite thought. We have already learned that what Islam calls walayat—the spiritual initiation associated with God's friends (awliya)—continues, under a different name, a form of prophecy that began with humanity itself. Shiism rests on the conviction that this hidden or inward prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya) will continue until the end of time.

  1. The prophet sent to a community without bringing a new law. This nabi possesses the spiritual gifts of the first two kinds, but has two more: he can see and hear the angel while awake, not merely in dreams, and he is sent to a community, whether large or small. He is a prophet-messenger (nabi mursal). Jonah and, more generally, the prophets of Israel are examples. They brought no new sacred law but followed the law of Moses.
  2. The prophet-messenger who brings a new law. In addition to the spiritual gifts already described, this messenger no longer lives under the law of an earlier prophet. He is sent to reveal a new sacred law to humanity. This is law-giving prophecy (nubuwwat al-tashri'). The Sixth Imam's teaching names five such great prophets. Other lists usually give six, beginning with Adam, or sometimes seven if they include David, whose Psalms are treated in the Qur'an as a separate revealed book. The great periods of law-giving prophecy are then marked by Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, and Muhammad. These are the prophets called ulu'l-'azm: people of unwavering resolve.225226

Each of these great prophets began as a nabi before becoming a messenger. Their mission matured gradually under divine guidance. During their lives, they were also Imams: spiritual guides. As we will see, Ismaili thought differs on this point.

But Twelver Shiism goes on to explain the qualities an Imam must possess in order to succeed a prophet. It does so through the Qur'anic account of Abraham's appointment as Imam, cited here as 2:118.

Shiite theologians regularly appeal to this verse to defend their understanding of the Imam and answer Sunni objections. God says to Abraham: “I am making you an Imam for the peoples.” Abraham asks, “And from among my descendants?” God replies, “My promise does not include the wrongdoers (al-zalimin)—those who act unjustly.”

Abraham was asking that his descendants should share in the office of Imam. God's reply means that an Imam must possess an inner spiritual purity that physical descent alone can never confer. By insisting that the Twelve Imams of the Prophet's family (ahl al-bayt) possessed this special purity ('isma), Shiites reject the misleading claim repeated by certain Orientalist scholars that their idea of the Imam rests simply on family descent. There have been thousands of imamzadehs, children of Imams, but only twelve Imams.

The Imam therefore requires more than ancestry. He must be expressly designated by the preceding Imam (nass) and possess 'isma. We should not translate this last term simply as infallibility, which has acquired a particular and rather narrow meaning in the West. More accurate words are protection from wrongdoing, freedom from sin, and purity—the qualities suggested by the Greek anamartetos.

This explains the name “the Fourteen Pure Ones” (Chahardeh ma'sum): the Prophet, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams.

As we have already seen, this Shiite understanding prevents us from treating the line of Twelve Imams as though it were just another ruling dynasty. The spiritual gift of the guardians of the Grail, after all, does not come from the political legitimacy of one dynasty over another. Sunni and Shiite theologians may both use the word Imam, but they mean fundamentally different things by it.227

Seen in this light, Mulla Sadra's account of knowledge develops what Ja'far al-Sadiq had already taught about prophecy. The Sixth Imam distinguished the prophets by their capacity for spiritual vision and knowledge of sacred realities. That distinction laid the foundation for a philosophy of prophecy.

We can now use it to understand the Imam's own spiritual rank—and why prophecy, in a sense we must define carefully, can continue to the end of time even though the revelation of new sacred laws has ended.

The Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, father of Ja'far al-Sadiq, was asked about a Qur'anic verse (19:55) that calls Ishmael, son of Abraham, a prophet and messenger—the third kind in the scheme above. His answer confirms the earlier teaching:

“A nabi in the simple sense,” he said, “is one who sees visions in dreams and hears the angel's voice, but does not see the angel with his eyes while awake. A messenger (rasul) hears the angel's voice and sees him in dreams, but also sees and hears him while awake. […] The Imam, however, hears the angel's voice in dreams without seeing him.”

Mulla Sadra's very important discussion of this teaching is quoted in the note.228 The final distinction matters enormously. In the way he receives knowledge, the Imam resembles the nabi of the second kind.

We will soon see what follows from this.

The Eighth Imam, Ali al-Rida (d. 203 AH / 818 CE), repeats the teaching in another reported saying. He also identifies the angel through whom knowledge comes: Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, the Pen. Mulla Sadra then takes the explanation further. He begins with the different names the Qur'an gives Gabriel and shows how they support the identification of Gabriel with the philosophers' Active Intellect.229

Gabriel, he explains, “brings divine communication (wahy) to the prophets, inspiration (ilham) to God's friends (awliya)—the Imams who are close to God—and truthful visions in dreams to spiritual seekers.” The degree of spiritual knowledge therefore depends on how the angel appears: seen while one is awake, seen in a dream, or heard without being seen. Since the person who will guide others must first be guided by the angel, we have to be careful not to misunderstand these experiences.

We must use the capacities of spiritual perception to understand, at the level where they are true, Qur'anic passages that speak of Gabriel “descending” (nuzul) into the messenger's heart, or taking human form before him. Mary (Maryam), for example, is said to have seen the angel “take the form of a faultless human being” (19:17)—a form of perfect beauty.

A philosophy of prophecy therefore needs a theory of knowing through images, and of the imaginal world: a world encountered through spiritual imagination, but not dismissed as unreal. Mulla Sadra developed just such a theory with remarkable skill.

He begins by challenging many Islamic philosophers (hukama' islamiyin) and others who claim to speak for philosophy. They regard forms seen in visions, and sounds heard inwardly, as nothing more than impressions on the faculty of imagination (hiss mushtarak). On their view, this faculty is a bodily power located towards the front of the brain, and it disappears when the body dies.

Mulla Sadra argues throughout his work for something very different: imagination is a spiritual power. It does not die with the physical body. It is, in a sense, the soul's subtle body.230 The opposing view, he says,

comes from a profound lack of knowledge of the world of Malakut—the angelic world of heavenly souls—and from a weakness of faith in the angels, in revelation as it takes form, and in the Book. For these are beings that exist concretely in their own right. They do not need something else in which to exist, as passing qualities do.

Indeed, their existence is much more real than that of outward things. Yet theirs is another world, one that cannot be perceived by our impure senses.

After Mulla Sadra, his whole school continued to stress imagination as a way of knowing, distinct both from the physical senses and from pure intellect. This view of angels and knowledge fits remarkably well—and may even help inspire—a philosophy that says all sensory perception already involves active imagination. What we perceive is not the form of external matter in itself, but the form present within the soul.231

Active imagination can turn through the senses towards the outward appearance (zahir) of the visible world.

But appearances in the world of ordinary experience ('alam al-shahadat) can be misleading: what something seems to be may differ from its hidden reality. Things are different when imagination turns towards the world beyond the senses.

When light from the higher world of Malakut reaches the innermost heart (sirr al-qalb), the image that takes shape reveals divine realities as they are. Here the visible form agrees with the inward truth. Its beauty does not deceive. This is true imagination (imaginatio vera).

Mulla Sadra knows that remarkable secrets lie here. The forms appearing in someone's dreams, for example, can reveal the person's hidden reality—the “inner person” (batin).

We have now identified the human capacity through which the angel's action and the different kinds of prophecy meet. Through it, divine communication (wahy) occurs when the angel appears to a messenger while he is awake. Inspiration (ilham) occurs when a nabi who is not a messenger sees or hears the angel in dreams. This makes it easier to understand why Shiite thinkers compare the knowledge given to an ordinary nabi with the knowledge given to an Imam.

Their situations are, in fact, the same in one decisive respect. Both belong among the muhaddathun: “those to whom the angels speak.” A saying frequently attributed to the Prophet declares: “In my community there are people who converse with the angels, people to whom the angels tell things (muhaddathun).” This teaching has enormous consequences for the history of spirituality in Islam, and its full meaning cannot be separated from what the Shiite Imams taught.232

Commenting on another teaching of the Fifth Imam,233 Mulla Sadra explains that those to whom angels speak do not necessarily see an angel face to face, or even in a dream. This angelic conversation (tahdith) takes place within the most deeply hidden region of awareness (fi batin al-sirr). It is spiritual speech (kalam 'aqli), a spiritual account or communication (hadith ruhani). Borrowing the language of Semnani, we could call it a conversation between a spiritual seeker and “the Gabriel of their own being.”

At this point, the philosophy of prophecy reaches its highest expression in the presence of an inner guide. This guide is the source of teaching that is secret or inward in the fullest sense (ta'lim batini): teaching received through spiritual hearing.234

We can now see why these Shiite teachings challenge an understanding of Islam that treats religion merely as an inherited law and confines its meaning to the outward words of an earlier revelation.

Among the spiritual states described by the philosophy of prophecy, set aside the special case of seeing Gabriel and hearing him speak while awake, when his words bring a new sacred law. All the remaining states are shared, in various ways, by messengers (rusul), prophets who are not messengers (anbiya), and the muhaddathun, those to whom angels speak—that is, the Imams and God's friends (awliya).

As the Imams say, the earth is never without people who carry divine secrets, even if most human beings do not know who they are.235 Mulla Sadra explains that hidden, inward prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya) therefore continues until the final Imam appears openly.

What has ended is only the form of prophecy that brings a new sacred law (nubuwwat al-tashri') and, with it, the use of the title nabi. Even the mission of the messenger (risala) and divine communication (wahy) have ceased only in a particular sense, since warnings (indharat) and encouraging signs (mubashshirat) continue.

Muhammad was indeed the Seal of the Prophets. There will be no new nabi.

Yet this other, hidden form of prophecy continues without end. Understood at its source, it is called walayat. These ideas were already present in the teachings of the Shiite Imams at the beginning of Islam.

Yet when placed beside official Islam as it developed historically, they have a truly revolutionary force.

Let us gather these ideas together and draw out what they mean.

First, what makes Muhammad's knowledge distinctive, as the Seal of the Prophets? We need not enter into every detail of the Islamic and Shiite understanding of prophetic inspiration—though a comparison with the different Christian explanations of how scripture is inspired would be valuable. Instead, let us follow Mulla Sadra's comments on the teaching of the Fifth Imam cited earlier.236 He writes:

The revealed Books—the Books “sent down from heaven” (munazzala)—have reached their completion in one Book, the Qur'an. It is the Word of God (Kalam Allah), through which Truth descends into the heart of His servant. As God Himself says, Gabriel brought down into your heart the Book that confirms the sacred Books before it (2:91).

This means that Gabriel truly brought down into the Prophet's heart the spiritual realities (haqa'iq) of the Qur'an, not merely the outward form of words—words written on tablets and readable by anyone who understands Hebrew or Syriac. No! What he brought down was the inner, spiritual reality (haqiqa), not just the outer form.

What, then, distinguishes the revelations given to the earlier prophets who “brought a Book” from the revelation bestowed upon the Seal of the Prophets? Mulla Sadra explains by bringing together several Qur'anic verses. The spiritual content—the inner reality (haqiqa)—of the Qur'an descended into Muhammad's heart before its outward form of words and letters, before the Word (Kalam) was spoken, and before the heavenly speaker, the angel, appeared to him.

It is this spiritual essence of the Book that the Qur'an calls “a light by which We guide” (42:52). The light of the Word (nur al-Kalam) is this inner reality. And the light that filled the Prophet's heart shines in turn upon those joined to him not merely through outward family descent (munasaba suriya) but also through a spiritual bond (ma'nawiya): the Twelve Imams. Their relationship to Muhammad has both dimensions, spiritual and familial.

The other heavenly Books, by contrast, were brought down to earlier prophets in an outward form, in keeping with the outward aspect of those prophets' missions ('ala zawahiri-him). They were written on tablets or pages that anyone able to read could understand. Both the prophets and their communities were guided by those Books. The Qur'an says, for example, that God “sent down the Torah and the Gospel as guidance for humanity” (3:2).

For Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, something different took place. The eternal lights of the Qur'an became present in his heart, and this made him personally the bearer of guidance (hidaya). After him, the Twelve Imams inherited that role. Mulla Sadra puts the difference like this. Each earlier prophet brought his people a Book that served as a light: “The One who sent down the Book Moses brought as light and guidance” (6:91).

But Muhammad's own heart had become light, and with that light came a Book: “A light has come to us from God”—understood here as Muhammad—“and a clear Book”—the Qur'an (5:18).

That is the essential difference. Its source lies in the mystery of the primordial Reality of Muhammad, which we discussed in Chapter Five. In the earlier pattern, a prophet is sent and brings with him the light of a Book. In Muhammad's case, the prophet is himself light, and a Book accompanies him.

For the Muslim understanding of sacred scripture, the Book therefore takes on a unique, final significance through its connection to the Seal of the Prophets. We have just seen what makes Muhammad pre-eminent among the prophets.

In Shiite teachings about divine wisdom, the faith of his community (iman, something deeper than merely outward submission, islam) is, at heart, knowledge of that light. It is not simply agreement with the written words, because the words themselves presuppose the light they express.

This is how the verse is understood: “He has inscribed faith upon their hearts and strengthened them with a Spirit from Himself” (58:22). What faith recognizes in the coming of the final Prophet is the manifestation of the divine Name that gathers all the Names into itself. Muhammad is the earthly manifestation of the glorified Word—the eternal prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya).

Now the question we raised earlier returns of its own accord. The final Prophet has come, but he is no longer here. He revealed a Book whose written words form the outward covering of the light present in his heart. After him, who will keep people from stopping at that outward form? Who will lead them towards the inner reality that gives it light?

There must be a guide whose task is not to reveal another sacred law (sharia), but to uncover the hidden meaning of the law already given. The earth can never be without such a guide, whether everyone knows who he is or he remains hidden. That, as we have seen, is the heart of the Shiite understanding.

The age of prophecy has been followed by the age of walayat, the initiation into inward spiritual knowledge. There are no more nabis, but there are still God's friends (awliya), people who know the hidden truths of faith.

Walayat begins with God's particular love for the Twelve Imams, whom that love sets apart as His friends. Their very persons are manifestations (theophanies) of divine love. Among their followers, walayat is also the devoted love directed towards the Imams as the forms in which God's love appears. By taking part in this loving devotion, their followers, too, can become friends of God (see Chapter Seven below).

The age of walayat is therefore an age of initiation into the ultimate purpose of love and into the secret that inner knowledge discovers beneath the words of prophetic revelation. Such knowledge recognizes those who, at each stage of the spiritual journey (maqam), become the “place where divine revelation appears” (see Chapter Five above). That is why the writers we are studying say that without walayat no faith is acceptable to God.

Walayat opens the hidden meaning of prophecy (batin al-nubuwwa), and God's friends are the guides who lead others into that meaning. More precisely, we have seen that a nabi who is not a messenger possesses a kind of knowledge of sacred realities also shared by the Imams, God's friends, and the muhaddathun, “those to whom the angels speak.” It is therefore accurate to say that one form of prophecy continues under the name walayat.

This is not, and never again will be, the law-giving prophecy of the great messengers. It is inward or esoteric prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya), concerned with realities hidden within the outward forms of religion.

Because that inner prophecy spans the whole history of humanity, we might say that Shiism glimpsed the beginnings of a wider understanding of religions and their histories—one whose centre cannot be an event left behind in the past. This is why Shiite thought looks towards a future disclosure, a horizon associated with the Paraclete, the promised spiritual helper.

We will not be surprised to find the Twelfth Imam identified with the Paraclete by Haydar Amuli and other thinkers.237

We have already noted something Shiite writers often say. In the prophetic ages before Muhammad, the term wali—a friend of God, plural awliya—was not used. Such people were called nabis.

Yet what Islam now means by walayat is precisely what earlier ages called prophecy in the sense of nubuwwa without risala: prophecy without a mission to bring a new sacred law. The idea has not changed; only the name has. Muhammad proclaimed himself the Seal of the Prophets (Khatim al-anbiya), and so the word nabi can no longer be used of those who come after him.

Yet the final Prophet's community must still contain the people of whom he said, “There are people who are not prophets, and yet the prophets envy them.” These are the Imams, the friends of God, and those who are friends of those friends. When Muhammad said, “There will be no prophet after me,” he meant that law-giving prophecy had come to an end. There would be no new law, no new revelation of a sharia.

But we have also learned that, with the Prophet no longer present, the Qur'an on its own cannot serve as the living witness and answerer. Its words hold hidden meanings that cannot simply be learned from outside. They are handed on by those who possess inspired knowledge (ilham). This is why inward prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya) must continue until the end of time.

It is the prophecy of the Witnesses. Their unbroken succession will lead to the Resurrection (Qiyama) that ends our present aeon—our age of the world. Then the one who has until now been the unseen guide of all these Witnesses will at last appear openly: the Twelfth Imam.238

When our writers repeatedly say that prophecy (nobowwat) is temporary while walayat is eternal, they mean two different things. What comes to an end is the kind of prophecy that brings a divine law (nobowwat al-tashri). What continues forever is walayat: the spiritual bond with God that belongs to God's friends and guides. In this sense, it is an eternal form of prophecy, and its religion is the eternal religion of spiritual humanity.239

We know that walayat is also a central idea throughout Sufism.

But now that we have brought its specifically Shiite meaning back into view, an important question arises. Can we go on discussing walayat in Sufism without mentioning its Shiite origins? Worse still, can we ignore the fundamental place it holds in Shiite theology?240 Its meaning could hardly be further from the religion of outward legal requirements that characterizes orthodox Sunni teaching. In the past, even the suspicion that someone was secretly Shiite could have terrible consequences.

Consider the trial of Suhrawardi, who died in Aleppo in 587 AH (1191 CE). The crucial question put to him was: “Have you claimed in your books that God can create a prophet whenever He wishes?” The accusation really concerned the opening of his great work, The Philosophy of Illumination (Hikmat al-Ishraq), where he maintains that there must always be a Qotb, a spiritual “pole” without whom the Earth could not exist.

We now understand what that claim involves. Suhrawardi tried to defend himself by asking whether God was inherently incapable of creating another prophet. But that question alone was enough to bring a declaration of unbelief (takfir) and his condemnation (see Book II below).

So far, we have examined the relationship between the Prophet and the Imam in terms of knowledge. After the prophet who brought the divine law, there still had to be guides with the special gift of leading people into the inner meaning of prophetic revelation. The usual definition is that walayat is the inner dimension of prophecy (batin al-nobowwat).

But if the Prophet represents the outward side and the Imam the inward side of one reality, their connection must go deeper than their roles in earthly history. It must be rooted in the very nature of spiritual reality. The idea of prophetic inheritance—the Prophet's spiritual heirs—expresses, here on Earth, the structure of an eternal prophetic reality: the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya). We have already considered this reality at different levels of the spiritual universe. Now we must look at it in relation to the Prophet's mission in this world.

3. Prophetic Inheritance and the Imamate

Here I shall follow mainly Haydar Amoli, a fourteenth-century thinker we have often met already. He is especially skilled at drawing out the meaning of the sayings handed down from his Imams, while staying faithful to them (see Book IV, Chapter 1 below). When we speak of a prophetic religion or a prophetic philosophy, we naturally assume that prophecy exists. Earlier (p. 235), we explained what the word itself means. It has nothing to do, in the first instance, with “predicting the future.”

But if prophecy is what guides humanity on Earth, and if that guidance has always been necessary, when did prophecy begin? We should not expect an answer based on a dateable event in ordinary history.

But neither should we expect merely a myth. As we have seen, these thinkers recognize events belonging to a realm beyond recorded history, which we have called metahistory. For them, prophecy really begins there: in Heaven, before human beings existed on Earth (see Chapter V above). Versions of this idea appear in both Twelver Shiite and Ismaili spiritual thought. The first prophet was the being known by various names as the Heavenly Human, or Anthropos.

The different kinds of prophet described by the Shiite Imams correspond to distinctions that Haydar Amoli also draws.241 Shiite authors distinguish two things when they speak of prophecy (nobowwat).

First, there is prophecy that teaches (nobowwat al-ta'rif). We might call it “gnostic” prophecy, because what it teaches is direct spiritual knowledge (ma'rifat) of God's Essence, Names, and Attributes. It includes the first three kinds of prophet in the scheme discussed earlier (p. 238): the 124,000 prophets mentioned in tradition, whose missions together cover the whole history of religions.

Second, there is prophecy that establishes a law (nobowwat al-tashri). In addition to teaching spiritual truth, it brings a sharia, a divine law. This is the fourth kind of prophet in that earlier scheme.

Prophecy also has two dimensions: one absolute and universal (motlaq, 'amm), the other limited, relative, and particular (mogayyad, khass). The particular dimension appears in each individual prophet. Each is a visible manifestation (mazhar) of the eternal reality of prophecy. But only the Seal of the Prophets manifests prophecy in its absolute, universal form.

To understand this, we have to look back to prophecy's very beginning, to the primordial Muhammadan Reality discussed in Chapter V. We must consider the Prophet's reality as something that existed before time. This is the meaning of the paradoxical saying: “I was already a prophet when Adam was still between water and clay”—that is, before Adam had even taken shape. These words refer to a primordial, ideal prophecy (nobowwat haqiqiya), which begins before time and continues from age to age (nobowwat azaliya baqiya).

In Ismaili spiritual teaching, the herald of this primordial prophecy is the First Intelligence, or Archangel ('Aql awwal), belonging to the heavenly fullness of beings, the Pleroma.242 Twelver Shiite spiritual teaching gives this being many titles: the Supreme Successor, the Pole of Poles, the Sublime Spirit (Ruh a'zam), the Supreme Pen, the Greatest Human (Insan kabir), and the True Adam (Adam haqiqi). These names tell us that the Heavenly Human of ancient spiritual traditions has become the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya): the Muhammadan Word, the eternal model of the Prophet, the reality of Muhammad beyond time.

The earthly Prophet is not this eternal reality made flesh. Rather, he reveals it, as a mirror reveals an image. This is how Muhammad, as the Seal of the Prophets, manifests prophecy in its absolute and universal form. It is also the meaning of sayings endlessly repeated by Muslim spiritual thinkers: “The first thing God created was the Intelligence”; or “the Pen”; or “the Spirit.” All these forms come together in the saying: “The first thing God created was my Light”—the Muhammadan Light (Nur mohammadi).

And because this Heavenly Human, this True Adam, is the being God created in His own image ('ala surati-hi), the one who reflects that divine image can say: “Whoever has seen me has seen God.” This saying, with its clear echo of the Gospel, is also frequently attributed to the Imam.243 That is because the eternal reality of prophecy is, in fact, a unity made up of two inseparable sides.

We find this idea well before Ibn Arabi in the great works of Ismaili Shiite spiritual thought. There it appears as a pair: the First Intelligence and the Soul, or the first two Intelligences of the heavenly realm. The eternal prophetic reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya) has two faces, two dimensions. Its outward face is prophecy (nobowwat); its inner face is walayat, or the Imamate. This is why walayat is called “the inner dimension of prophecy” (see Chapter V above, on the Twelve Imams as the successive places where the prophetic mission is fulfilled). The same eternal reality is thus the source of both primordial prophecy and primordial walayat (asliya).

For that reason it is called the Spring of Life ('ayn al-Hayat). We must search for it through the darkness of nature and beyond the limits of religion understood only in its literal sense. What we seek is the spiritual Light that, as we have seen, was present in the Prophet's heart before his revelation took the form of words. That Light passes from his heart to the hearts of his spiritual heirs, the Twelve Imams.

As one text puts it: “The Spring of Life is the inner reality of the divine Name the Living (batin al-ism al-Hayy). Whoever truly understands it drinks from the Spring of Life; and whoever drinks that water will never die, because that person lives with divine life. Every living being in the world lives through the life of this Perfect Human (kamil, teleios), because his life is the very life of God.”

Like prophecy, walayat must therefore have both a universal, absolute aspect and a particular one. Its particular form had already appeared in all the Friends of God (Awliya) of earlier prophetic periods, when they were simply called prophets (Nabis). Its universal form, the inner reality of the Heavenly Human, appeared on Earth in the person closest to Muhammad by both spiritual and family ties: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the First Imam, the Commander of the Faithful.

And because the Twelve Imams share one spiritual essence (haqiqat), the Muhammadan Imamate as a whole is the Seal of walayat: the completion of the inner knowledge found within every prophetic religion. Just as Muhammad was the Seal of the Prophets, the Muhammadan Imamate seals walayat in two ways: through the First Imam, as the Seal of universal walayat, and through the Twelfth Imam, as the Seal of specifically Muhammadan walayat, or spiritual knowledge. This is why the First Imam could echo the Prophet's words and say: “I was already a wali”—a friend of God, an Imam who knows the inner truth of eternal prophecy—“when Adam was still between water and clay.”244

These broad outlines help us understand a group of traditional sayings that insist on the unbreakable unity of Prophet and Imam, prophecy and spiritual initiation, outward meaning (zahir) and inner meaning (batin). In one saying, the Prophet declares: “Ali and I are one and the same Light.” In another: “Ali and I were one Light before God, fourteen thousand years before He created Adam.” These are not years measured by our calendars, of course, but the time of the heavenly world245—the “absolutely subtle” time described by Qazi Sa'id Qommi.

Another saying explains the eternal Imam's relationship to the temporary mission of prophets who bring a law: “Ali was sent secretly alongside every prophet; with me, he was sent openly.” In other words, every prophetic religion has had an inner spiritual teaching, but its existence was kept hidden. The final Prophet's mission was different: he openly announced that this inner teaching existed, while leaving its instruction to the Imam. In a sermon of remarkable importance, the Khutbat al-Bayan, quoted earlier, the Imam declares: “I am the one who holds the secret of God's Messenger.”246 The Muhammadan Imamate is therefore the inner dimension of every earlier religion.

But this spiritual knowledge will only be fully revealed, without concealment or veil, at the return of the Mahdi, the Twelfth and final Imam. As the Seal of Muhammadan walayat, he also completes universal walayat.

These texts show us how the Shiite understanding of the Imams grows naturally out of its understanding of prophecy. They also reveal how closely the major themes of Shiite thought fit together. The idea of the Heavenly Human—the eternal reality of prophecy—helps us understand why the Imamate, through its knowledge of inner meanings, inherits prophecy. It also explains why the Imam's kind of knowledge is understood as a spiritual inheritance, unlike knowledge gathered from outside. This distinction is crucial.

Shiite spirituality reaches its height in personally discovering the truth of the saying: “Whoever knows himself”—his own soul—“knows his Lord,” which here means his Imam. Its goal is to discover one's own spiritual Guide, the one we must come to know if we are not to die having lived in unawareness. This is not knowledge we acquire from outside. It is something given to the soul as an inheritance.

To grasp the full meaning of knowledge inherited by the soul, we first need to understand how Shiite writers describe the passing of the Prophet's spiritual inheritance to the Imam. Above all, this means the passing of the Light that made the Prophet and the Imam a single, two-sided reality before either appeared on Earth. From the creation of Adam onwards, that Light—their shared Spirit (Ruh mohammadi)—was passed down through successive generations, kept free from every impurity, especially shirk, the ignorance that breaks apart the understanding of God's oneness. It reached Abd al-Muttalib, the common ancestor of Muhammad and Ali. In these two descendants, the original unity of Prophet and Imam finally appeared as two distinct people.

This helps explain why Shiite thinkers have had to repeat a point so often misunderstood, sometimes completely. No one was ever worthy of being an Imam or the Prophet's successor merely because he was related to the Prophet by blood (nisbat jismaniya, hissiya, suriya). Spiritual kinship (nisbat ma'nawiya) is also essential. And that kinship has its origin in the primordial Muhammadan Reality, which existed before the world. We have stressed this already.

What we have just read suggests that the Imams did not become Imams because they belonged to the Prophet's family. Rather, they had to belong to the Holy Family (ahl al-bayt) because they were already Imams. Their earthly family relationship simply makes visible a unity that existed among them in the heavenly world. It is never merely a matter of blood. From the beginning, it is a spiritual relationship.

This double kinship, both earthly and spiritual,247 together with each Imam's personal designation (nass) and freedom from error and sin (ismat), identifies the Twelve Imams as the Prophet's heirs (Awsiya). But they do not inherit his outward office of bringing a divine law. What they inherit is the inner reality of his mission.

We must always remember the definition: walayat is the inner dimension of prophecy. The inheritance consists of their knowledge and, just as importantly, the way in which they know. Their right to this inheritance goes back beyond their family relationship on Earth, to their existence in the heavenly realm before the world began. What passes to the Imams is not tanzil, the act of “bringing down” revelation, but ta'wil, the act of leading the words of revelation back to their source, so that their deeper meaning can be understood.

The Prophet's relationship with the First Imam—and, through him, with the other eleven—is expressed in an especially important saying. After the Battle of Khaybar, the Prophet is reported to have addressed Ali in these words:

If I were not afraid that some of my community might say about you what Christians say about Christ (Masih), I would tell people something about you today that would make them gather the dust from your footsteps wherever you went, hoping to find a remedy in it because of your extraordinary purity.

But let it be enough for you that you are part of me, just as I am part of you. Whoever inherits from you will therefore inherit from me. For you stand in relation to me as Aaron stood in relation to Moses, with this one difference: after me there will be no other prophet.248

This saying confirms what we have been discussing. The eternal, essential reality (haqiqat) of the Seal of the Messengers and that of the Seal of God's Friends (Awliya), the bearers of spiritual knowledge, are one and the same. We see its outward prophetic dimension in the Prophet, and its inner dimension of walayat in the Twelve Imams. With that heavenly kinship established, let us look at how it is understood to appear in the visible world ('alam al-zahir).

Another saying, attributed to the Prophet, describes the Imam in these terms:

His secret is that he lives my life and dies my death. He is like a branch that my God planted with His own hand. God said to it, “Be,” and it was.

This image means that the Imam’s ancestry reaches upwards to the divine will; it is not simply the result of human birth. Earthly descent follows from that higher origin (2:111 and elsewhere). The saying continues:

So may God watch over Ali after I am gone, and over the heirs (Awsiya) who descend from me—the other eleven Imams. They will be the Guides (hodat), the Faithful, those accepted by God. God will give them my understanding and my knowledge. This means that they share my spiritual rank and are worthy to succeed me and to hold the Imamate.

What qualifies the Imams as the Prophet's heirs, then, is that they possess the same level of understanding and knowledge as he does. This is also why, as we have seen, each is called Qayyim al-Qur'an, the one who safeguards the Qur'an and keeps its meaning alive. For the mission of bringing divine law has ended. We said a moment ago that the Imams do not inherit that part of the Prophet's work. They inherit his walayat.

But this means that there must be something in the Prophet beyond his mission as the bearer of the law—something that Islam understood only in terms of outward rules cannot explain, but that Shiite spiritual teaching affirms. A very simple diagram makes this clear.

During his life on Earth, a Prophet who is also a Messenger (Nabi-Rasul) does not begin by holding the rank of Messenger. Abraham and Muhammad himself are the favourite examples. Such a person is first a wali, a Friend of God, or an 'arif, someone with direct spiritual knowledge. The two terms often appear together; we have called this kind of person a “gnostic.” He then becomes a Nabi, a prophet, and finally a Nabi-Rasul, a prophet who is also a Messenger. In Muhammad's case, this final stage is marked by the Angel's visible appearance. Being a Messenger (rasul) therefore requires both walayat and prophecy (nobowwat).

But someone can be a wali or a Nabi without ever becoming a Messenger who brings a divine law.

Shiite thinkers have reflected deeply on the relationship between these three spiritual states: walayat, the condition of being God's friend and receiving divine love; ordinary prophecy (nobowwat); and the Messenger's mission to establish a law (risalat). Moving from walayat to the mission of a lawgiving prophet means moving from the deepest inward level towards the outer world. Writers such as Haydar Amoli therefore picture the three states as circles within circles.

Walayat, the state of divine friendship, spiritual initiation, and inner knowledge, is the inner reality of prophecy. Prophecy, in turn, is the inner reality of the Messenger's lawgiving mission. And because closeness to God increases as spiritual life becomes more inward and less dependent on outward things, walayat has the highest rank of all. Haydar Amoli compares the outward mission of bringing a law (risalat) to the shell of a nut, inner prophecy (nobowwat batiniya) to its kernel, and walayat to the oil contained inside that kernel (see the diagram below).

A whole series of other comparisons expresses the same relationship. Moving from outside to inside, the three levels correspond to sharia, the outward observance of religious law; tariqat, the spiritual path; and haqiqat, the inner reality that is personally experienced. They also correspond to outward meaning, inner meaning, and the inner meaning within that inner meaning (batin al-batin). And they correspond to three levels of certainty: knowledge based on information ('ilm al-yaqin), certainty gained from seeing something for oneself ('ayn al-yaqin), and certainty gained through direct inner experience (haqq al-yaqin).

Before the Prophet could become a Messenger who brought a divine law (rasul), he therefore had to pass through the state of wali or 'arif. His walayat, the spiritual knowledge of one close to God, comes before his mission as a Messenger because it lies deeper within him. This is a principle our writers repeat constantly: walayat is higher than the state of a prophet who is also a Messenger, because it comes first and is the source of that mission.

Twelver Shiism, however, makes this comparison within the person of the Prophet himself. All three states are present in Muhammad, and he passes on to the Imams the walayat that forms his own deepest spiritual life. It is in the Prophet himself that walayat is higher than nobowwat.

Here, Haydar Amoli explains, lies an essential difference between Twelver Shiism and Ismaili Shiism—or at least the reformed Ismailism of Alamut, which proclaimed the Great Resurrection on 8 August 1164. Ismaili spiritual teaching takes the superiority of walayat over lawgiving prophecy to mean that the Imam himself is higher than the Prophet. Something of this tendency may have existed in Shiism from its beginnings; perhaps the Ismailis of Alamut were simply faithful to that older impulse.

But the result was a radical transformation of Islam into a religion of the Spirit alone. With the abolition of the sharia, divine law, it was almost an early arrival of the end of time: an anticipation of the liberation that the last Imam, the Mahdi, is to bring when he establishes the reign of the pure spiritual meaning of prophetic revelations.249

Our concern here, however, is the middle path represented by Twelver Shiite spiritual thought. Although it continues to give the Prophet precedence over the Imam, there is always at least an underlying tendency to see the two as equals. The reason is that walayat stands above the lawgiving mission within the Prophet himself, and it is precisely this walayat that the Imam inherits. Prophet and Imam share one eternal essence in the heavenly world. The Prophet makes its outward side visible; the Imam, as the Seal of universal walayat, reveals its inner meaning.

We may recall the saying: “Ali was sent secretly alongside every prophet; with me, he was sent openly.” The Imam thus possesses, as his defining quality, the spiritual state that is higher than the Prophet's lawgiving mission within the Prophet himself. There is, of course, an ongoing tension in Shiism between spiritual knowledge and religious law. A prophetic religion remains truly prophetic only by continually reaching beyond the revealed words, while never cutting itself off from them.

We saw earlier that the Qur'an's spiritual reality (haqiqat) descended into the Prophet's heart before it took the form of words and letters—that is, before the Angel visibly appeared to “dictate” the text. Reflecting on this has led our thinkers into the deepest questions about how a prophet knows and experiences revelation. They find evidence that the Prophet remains inwardly a wali, whose spiritual state is higher than his mission as a lawgiving Messenger, in a famous saying cherished in both Shiism and Sufism:

There are moments when I am with God in such a way that neither a prophet who is a Messenger nor an Angel of the highest rank could contain what I experience.

Here the Prophet is no longer speaking as the Messenger who must receive the text that the Angel “brings down” (tanzil) and communicates to him (wahy). He is speaking as a wali, someone who knows God through direct, overwhelming experience. Haydar Amoli explains that the Prophet's inner being (batin al-nabi)—the part of him that belongs to his walayat—receives the divine outpouring (al-fayz min Allah) directly, without any intermediary. From there, it reaches his outward being, the level of prophecy.

At that second stage the Angel appears visibly while the Prophet is awake. At the first stage, before Gabriel—the Angel of Revelation who guides the Prophet—communicates anything outwardly, the Prophet encounters, at the deepest limit of his inner awareness, the “Gabriel of his own being.” That is what the claim means when it says that a wali draws from the very source from which the Angel receives the revelation he brings to the Messenger. The writers' account of prophetic experience thus reveals something essential for our theme: the guide who is also guided. To understand what the Angel means in prophetic knowledge, we must understand knowing through the heart and through the heart's “spiritual senses.”

Yet the Prophet is not himself meant to show the world that deepest state of his spiritual life, the state of walayat. It lies above his mission as a lawgiving Messenger and makes that mission possible. His prophetic message (risalat) has its source there. The one whose task it is to make walayat visible in the earthly world is the Imam.

At the deepest level, the Imam is formed from the same Light, the Light that is the Spirit and essence of eternal prophecy, the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya). It is true that Islamic spiritual teaching, through this idea of the eternal Prophet, partly echoes the Verus Propheta, the “True Prophet,” of Jewish-Christian traditions: a true prophetic presence passing from one prophet to the next until it comes to rest in Muhammad, who follows Jesus.

But there is something else we must add. For Shiite prophetic philosophy, this eternal prophecy can never be separated from the way its meaning is understood and interpreted.

Prophetic revelation has “descended” from the heavenly heights with which the Prophet's deepest awareness (sirr) is in contact, taking the outward form of written and spoken words. This is tanzil. To discover the spiritual meaning of a text that has come down in this way, we must lead it back to its origin. That is what ta'wil, spiritual interpretation, means both in the word's origin and in the idea itself. For this reason, each prophet in the prophetic line is accompanied by an Imam in a parallel line of spiritual guides, beginning with Seth, the son and Imam of Adam.

Ta'wil is the Imam's task, because walayat—the inner reality of prophecy—is what the Imam inherits. This eternal walayat, which existed before our earthly world and will outlast it, is the foundation of the Imam's work of spiritual initiation as Qayyim al-Qur'an, the guardian who keeps the Qur'an alive. He must preserve the Book from being reduced to its literal words alone, as it would be in an Islam concerned only with outward observance. He does this by keeping it connected to the Spirit that first inspired it in the Prophet's heart—the Spirit that is its true meaning.

All this lies at the heart of the Shiite idea of the Imam as the Prophet's heir. The inheritance is not founded merely on descent by blood. Or rather, as we have seen, the earthly kinship linking the Twelve Imams to the Prophet is a visible sign of a relationship that already existed before this world. Their union in the heavenly realm is the model and source of every spiritual bond.

4. The Knowledge Inherited from the Prophets
