The relation between knowing ourselves, knowing the Imam, and knowing God becomes clearer through what we might call Kermani's account of the Highest (al-ali, what is above) and the lowest (al-dani, what is below). The Highest cannot descend as it is, in such a way that the lowest could directly perceive and understand it. The absolute difference between them would remain, still making knowledge and love impossible. Nor can the Highest descend by changing its own essence, giving up its true nature so that it becomes like the lowest.

But there is another possibility. Kermani writes:

If this descent takes place not by altering or emptying the Highest of its nature, but through a manifestation of God (tajalli), an appearance (zuhur), an attribute (sifat), a Light (nur), then we have found what we are looking for. For if this manifestation did not correspond to the faculties through which Shiite believers perceive (masha'ir), we would still face the same problem.

But if it does correspond to them, the manifestation has something in common with the believers. It belongs to their own being, and they can reach it.

What is present in the manifestation is also present within them. Otherwise, it would make no sense to require them to reach it.

So the Highest makes itself known to the lowest through an attribute that the lowest can perceive, know, and understand. This is the highest level the lowest can reach, the furthest point of its thought. It is its own soul—its self (nafs)—and its heart. As the tradition says: “Whoever knows himself, his own soul, knows his Lord.” The Qur'an points towards the same truth: “And within yourselves are signs. Do you not see?” (51:21). And again: “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within their souls”—that is, within themselves (41:53).

In this way, God makes himself known to Shiite believers through their own selves, their own souls. When they come to know themselves, they have fulfilled what is asked of them: they have reached the one who stands ahead of their being, their Imam [...]. They are manifestations of their Imam, just as the Imams are the manifestation and meaning of God. It is of them that the Ziyarat al-Jami'a says (see Chapter V above): “Peace be upon those whom, if you know them, you know God, and if you do not know them, you do not know God.”288

Kermani's words, together with our discussion so far, lead to a clear conclusion. The Imam is the form in which God becomes manifest (mazhar). Through that form, God can be known and loved. To reach it is to reach knowledge of God, because it is the only form in which God can be known.

For the human being, it is therefore the highest possible level of existence, understanding, and love. Every manifestation of God creates a relationship between the one who reveals himself (mutajalli) and the one to whom he appears (mutajalla lahu). What appears must take a form suited to the person receiving it. Ibn Arabi had already insisted on this point.

But here the relationship is understood specifically through the teaching about the Imam. It is this teaching that makes the relationship possible without compromising God's oneness.

A manifestation of God (tajalli) is possible because the form in which God appears has something in common with the person who receives it. And because that manifestation is the highest reality that a person living in this lower world can reach, to arrive at its “place”—the believer's own mystical Mount Sinai—is to reach the summit, or the deepest centre, of one's being: the self, the soul (nafs). The form in which God appears there, the Face revealed at the summit of the soul, is the Imam. This is why knowing oneself, knowing one's soul and all that belongs to its world, means knowing one's Imam. And for each person, that is what knowing the Lord means.

The Imam is the form taken by the revealed God (Deus revelatus) when self-knowledge becomes knowledge of God. The Imam is the form through which I know and love God. When a believer comes to know the Imam, this knowledge reveals itself as the very form of the believer's love—and therefore as the secret of the believer's existence, because that existence is itself an act of love. That is why love of the Imam, the religion of walayat, is also an initiation into self-knowledge.

In the Shiite understanding, it embraces the whole of an eternal prophetic religion and the followers of every prophet. The Self it reveals is not an empty, impersonal Absolute. It is the Soul and Beloved of the soul (jan-e jan): a “you” at the centre of my “I,” the one who “walks ahead of me.” This is the Imam, in the original meaning of the word itself.

Shiite devotion and spiritual life thus reach their fullest expression in walayat, love directed towards the Imam as the form through which the hidden God reveals himself. It is through this form that the hidden God becomes someone who can be loved—God's lovability (mahbubiya). In that sense, every love of God, simply because it is love directed towards a God who can be loved, is walayat towards the Imam. Sufis outside Shiism struggled to find such a way forward, longing to escape what Ruzbihan calls the “madness of the unreachable.”

What matters here is that Shiism itself has already asked the question and answered it through the teaching about the Imam. This is the meaning of the many titles given to the Imam in Shiite prayers. The titles echo those the Imams use for themselves in their sayings: Guide, Pole, A'raf, Witness of God, and others. Each points back to the same central insight. To know oneself is to know the Imam; and knowing the Imam is knowing God, because no other knowledge of God is available to human beings.

We can explore only the titles I have just mentioned. To bring this account of Shiite spiritual life to a close, I want to show how they were understood by thinkers for whom philosophical reflection could never be separated from personal spiritual practice and experience. Above all, I shall turn again to Mulla Sadra Shirazi, whose work we have encountered so often already.

Along with Saleh Mazandarani, Mohsen Fayz, Qazi Sa'id Qummi, and others, Mulla Sadra belongs to a group of Shiite thinkers who produced immense works of commentary on the sayings of the Imams. Their writings help explain why their philosophy is sometimes called “prophetic and Imamic wisdom” (hikmat nabawiya wa walawiya, the second adjective coming from wali). At other times they call it “Yemeni divine wisdom” (hikmat yamaniya), a reference to the symbolic meaning of Yemen and the Yemeni corner of the Kaaba. The expression also recalls a saying that plays on the similar sounds of iman, meaning faith, and Yaman, meaning Yemen: “Faith comes from Yemen, and wisdom—divine wisdom—is Yemeni.”289290

“Yemeni divine wisdom” and “Eastern divine wisdom”—the Illuminationist teaching (Ishraq) of Suhrawardi, an especially Iranian and Islamic form of Neoplatonism—draw their strength from the same sources. Both look to the traditions of walayat and to the Imam as a Figure of Light, the Face of God who reveals himself only by remaining veiled. From this comes the understanding of the Imam as the Witness of God. At the highest point of the believer's soul, the Imam is the believer's living awareness of God—the witness within who bears witness to a God otherwise beyond all reach.

In Mulla Sadra's work, to which we shall return particularly in these final pages, this becomes a philosophy of the witness and the act of witnessing. The person who contemplates and the reality contemplated become one. Existence itself is understood through presence: the soul's growing presence in more and more worlds. As it becomes present to those worlds, it is freed from confinement to this mortal world.

The understanding of the Imam as part of spiritual experience undoubtedly shaped Mulla Sadra's philosophy of existence. Rather than giving first place to the fixed natures of things, as older philosophy often did, he gives priority to existing itself (see Book V below).

But the journey towards self-knowledge requires the possibility of a transformation that reaches into the very substance of a being. Mulla Sadra calls this “substantial movement” (harakat jawhariya), and it is fundamental to his philosophy. It is also the key to the Mabda' and the Ma'ad—the beginning and the return—which open the possibility of sensing transformations that took place before we can remember, and future renewals of our existence. The two “arcs,” one of descent and one of return, enclose a vision of existence far wider than what the West has usually meant by evolution.

2. The Imam as Guide and Spiritual Centre

Everything we have discussed so far has brought this central idea of prophetic philosophy into view. Here, we need only bring its essential points together. The first is the question we have put so directly: what happens after the Prophet is gone, when there will be no further prophet? The true meaning of his revelation cannot be found in the outward words alone.

Nor can anyone arrive at it simply by constructing an argument or drawing a series of conclusions. It can be revealed and passed on only by someone who knows. The Shiite traditions answer this question by joining the Imam and the Qur'an into a single, inseparable reality: the Qur'an is the silent Imam, and the Imam is the speaking Qur'an.

As the speaking Qur'an, the Imam is the guide who is always present: the one who leads people into the true meaning of Qur'anic revelation and keeps the Book alive as God's living word. We have already discussed sayings of the Fifth Imam that anticipate and overcome the danger of reducing revelation to the history of the time in which it appeared. The Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, makes the same point when he tests one of his disciples. “Abu Muhammad,” he asks, “the Prophet was the Warner, and Ali was the Guide.

“But is there a Guide (hadi) today?” His disciple replies, “Yes, may my life be given for yours! In your family, one guide has always followed another, down to you.” The Imam answers, “May God have mercy on you, Abu Muhammad! If a verse revealed on the occasion of a particular person's life were to die when that person died, the entire Book would be dead by now.

“But no! The Qur'an is alive. It will continue to find its fulfilment among people in the future, just as it did among those who lived in the past.”291292

The meaning could hardly be clearer. If we could understand the sacred Book only by relating it to “its own time,” to the social and historical circumstances in which its verses first appeared, the Qur'an would have been dead for centuries. Without the continuing walayat—the spiritual bond and authority of God's Friends—in this world, the Book of God would have no future. The life of the Imam and the life of the sacred Book depend on each other.

The Imam and his companions must therefore remain present in the world. This was the subject of the First Imam's conversation with Komayl ibn Ziyad, quoted above (III, 3). We had already encountered the idea of a spiritual centre, or pole, without which the human world itself could not endure.293 Mulla Sadra echoes the First Imam when he writes: “The Earth can never be without an Imam, a guide for every age. Otherwise the Qur'an would have to die when those who sustain it die.

“But the Qur'an is alive and will never die before the Day of Resurrection. At every moment, until the final Hour, someone living guides people towards it.”294295296

This is precisely what we find throughout the sayings collected in the chapter of Kolayni's great work devoted to the Imam as Guide and as God's witness and guarantor (Hojjat): the one who speaks for God before humanity. We should remember some of these sayings, in which the Imams show their unwavering awareness of who they are. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, declares: “God is my witness!

“From the moment Adam's soul was taken—that is, from Adam's death—God has never allowed an earthly world to exist without an Imam to guide people towards Him. That Imam is God's witness before His servants, and the world is never left without an Imam who stands before humanity as that witness and guide.” The Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi, says: “Truly, the earthly world is never without a witness and guide. And God is my witness: at this moment, I am that person.”297

Abu Hamza, a disciple of the Sixth Imam, recalls: “I asked Imam Ja'far, ‘Can the Earth remain without an Imam?’ He answered, ‘If the Earth were left without an Imam, it would sink away.’”298 The Fifth Imam also says: “If the Imam were taken away from the Earth for even an hour, the Earth would heave in waves, tossing its inhabitants as the sea tosses the creatures living within it.”299

These declarations suggest a mysterious bond—almost a sacred bond—between the Imam's presence and the continuing existence of the human world. Several consequences follow.

First, the need for an Imam is plainly not just another political or social question. It concerns the unseen order and structure of reality itself. The Imam is the spiritual Pole, the Pole of poles (qotb al-aqtab), the centre on which the world depends.

Mulla Sadra explains this in a particularly dense passage. The need for an Imam expresses an inner law of existence: every higher level of being is the goal towards which the level below it moves. The lower level exists through the higher one, and can reach fulfilment only in it. The lower level therefore presupposes the higher; the reverse is not true. This is more than a law of development. It is a movement upwards towards a higher kind of being that already exists.

Humanity follows the same pattern. It can reach fulfilment only at the highest level of human perfection. This is what the Imamate means. “The degree of the Imamate,” Mulla Sadra explains, “means the Perfect Human Being (al-insan al-kamil, anthropos teleios), who is the king of the earthly world.”300

But this kingship belongs to the Perfect Human Being as the very goal of existence. It does not arise from political circumstances, or depend on them. To treat the Imam simply as a rival to the Umayyads or Abbasids would place him on the wrong level altogether. We are dealing with something that social history alone cannot describe: a form of kingship that does not, by its nature, require political success in this world. Still less does it depend on the claim that majorities are always right because they are the ones who “make” history.

Another history is unfolding without their knowing it. It is the history of a hidden spiritual kingship over the visible world—something like the role played by the guardians of the Grail.

Other consequences follow immediately. As we have seen, the idea that the Imam might remain unknown was already present in the Prophet's declarations limiting the Imams of his own line to twelve. With a fixed number of Imams, the Imamate must eventually enter a state of concealment (ghaybat). The Shiite believer's present relationship with the Imam, as the spiritual centre of their own being, is therefore not a relationship with an institution in this world. It is a relationship with a world beyond what the physical senses can perceive. The Twelfth Imam appeared briefly in the earthly world, but his continuing presence is now invisible.

This means that his mode of existence transcends the ordinary biological conditions of earthly life. Such a presence can be experienced only in visions or through encounters in which his identity remains hidden.

Yet this invisible presence lies at the centre of Shiite devotion. Ordinary believers and scholars alike live in a sense of familiarity with the Imam (see Book Seven below). He need not be visible to the physical eye, any more than he needs to be known or recognised by the masses or by worldly rulers.

Being an Imam is intrinsic to what he is: the Perfect Human Being. Human ignorance or blindness cannot take that away from him. Here we reach the fundamental difference between the Shiite understanding of the Imam as guide and spiritual centre and the Sunni understanding of the Imam. The two concepts cannot be reduced to one another.

We have already stressed this difference when discussing Mulla Sadra's treatment of a long account of the Imam by the Sunni theologian and philosopher Fakhr al-Din Razi.301 In the Shiite understanding, the Imam is the centre on which the coherence and unity of existence depend. His presence is necessary at the deepest level of reality. His task is to lead people into spiritual knowledge, and it opens towards the events of the last days, when the Twelfth Imam is to appear as the Mahdi. His role and its necessity belong to what he is. They do not change according to whether people recognise him.

In the Sunni account discussed here, by contrast, the Imam is the centre of social order, and there is no need to appeal to the hidden structure of reality to explain his role. He is necessary because of the requirements of life in this world. The concept is not sacred in the sense of giving the universe a sacred structure; it belongs to public and political life.

Neither the Imam's person nor his office requires the kind of spiritual necessity or end-time role found in the Shiite account. Consequently, this view does not require him to know the ta'wil, the inner meanings of the Qur'an; to possess knowledge inspired directly by God (ilm laduni); or to be protected from every impurity and failure (isma). Choosing him is therefore a matter of agreement among people: he is elected.

The Shiite reply is that people can elect a political leader or president, or appoint someone to religious office, but it makes no sense to speak of electing a prophet or an Imam. Their special calling is not created by human choice. More than that, most people cannot even perceive the quality that makes them what they are.

As the saying puts it: “My Friends (awliya'i) are hidden beneath My tents; no one knows them but Me.” And consider the saying we have just seen at the heart of Shiite spirituality: “Whoever dies without knowing the Imam of their time dies the death of those who know nothing.” To apply that saying to the Sunni idea of the Imam described here would not merely empty it of meaning. It would make it monstrous.

This brings us to an objection Sunnis have often raised against Shiites, and to the Shiite answer. The objection runs as follows: “You say the Imam is necessary because God has made him necessary. In that case his rule should never be interrupted; there should be no concealment (ghaybat).

“But you also call him a gift of divine grace. Either he is necessary, in which case he is not a gift of grace, or he is a gift of grace, in which case he is not necessary.”

The Shiite response is: “The Imam's existence remains a gift of divine grace, whether he exercises political power or not. As the Commander of the Faithful [the First Imam] said: ‘The earthly world is never left without someone who speaks for God, whether openly and with public recognition, or secretly and unknown to others.

“Otherwise the signs of God and His manifestation would disappear from the Earth.’ The Imam's freedom to exercise outward rule would be another gift of grace. The prophetic mission that brought religious law has reached its end and been sealed; but the Imamate, which is the inner meaning of prophecy, endures until the Day of Resurrection. This remains true whether people recognise the Imam or reject him.

“A messenger of God is still a messenger even if no one believes his message, as happened, for example, with Noah. In the same way, the Imam remains an Imam even if no human being recognises him. A doctor does not cease to be a doctor simply because no patient comes seeking treatment or healing. The same is true of the doctors of the soul, who treat spiritual sickness and the afflictions of the heart: the prophets and God's Friends.”302

The answer is unmistakable: the Imam remains the Imam under all circumstances, even when he must carry out his mission in secret. Public opinion, official recognition, or the absence of recognition tells us nothing about whether his presence is necessary. The Imamate and the prophetic mission form a single reality in their deepest nature (haqiqat wahida bi'l-dhat).

The line of Imams therefore continues, whether openly or in concealment, in order to preserve the Prophet's spiritual inheritance—not to maintain any particular political order. In fact, apart from the First Imam, none of the Twelve exercised earthly political authority. Yet each was fully an Imam. This is central to Shiism and shapes its understanding of Islam.

We have been told that the Prophet and the Imam do not exist merely because human beings need them to manage their religious and worldly affairs. Of course, the proper conduct of those affairs presupposes their existence.

But the Earth continues to exist through the Imam for a deeper, spiritual reason: his level of being is that of the Perfect Human Being. Because the Perfect Human Being is the purpose and ultimate goal (ghayat, telos) of the earthly world, the human world could not even continue to exist without him.303

This is precisely the meaning of the mysterious existence of the Twelfth Imam, “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his followers.” He is the spiritual Pole of existence, and that is what he remains. His Imamate does not depend on anyone recognising him. As we have said, the line of Imams is not just another dynasty among other dynasties. An Imam is not a claimant to the Imamate. He is the Imam. “We are like the Israelites among Pharaoh's people,” declared the Fourth Imam.304 The line of Imams has withdrawn into concealment, like the last guardian of the Grail.

Yet through this line there continues, without interruption until the Last Day, the silsilat al-irfan: the living succession of spiritual knowledge that the First Imam taught his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyad.305 The spiritual centre of this succession is the Twelfth Imam, the Imam now in concealment. Those who belong to it recognise and are recognised by the people who call themselves the people of the A'raf. This gives the Imam's role in Shiite spirituality an even deeper meaning: he guides us towards knowledge of ourselves.

3. The Imam as the A'raf

The A'raf is the mysterious barrier mentioned in the Qur'an between Paradise and Hell. The seventh sura takes its name from it.306 In verses 44–45, we read: “On the A'raf stand people who recognise each person by their appearance” (7:44). A disciple relates an answer given by the Sixth Imam, who repeats a saying of the First Imam, when someone asks about the people of the A'raf:

“It is we [the Imams] who stand upon the A'raf. We recognise our companions by their faces. And we ourselves are the A'raf, because God can be known only through knowing us. We are the A'raf because, on the Day of Resurrection, God knows us as the Way (sirat). No one enters Paradise except those who know us and whom we know. No one enters the Fire except those who deny us and whom we deny.

“Had God Most High wished, He could have made Himself known to humanity directly. Instead, He made us His thresholds, His way, His path, the Face towards which people must turn. Whoever turns away from our walayat—refusing us the devotion of love—or prefers others to us, turns away from the Way.”307

The Imam's answer moves through three stages, until the Imam and the A'raf are identified with one another. Mulla Sadra begins by showing how commentators concerned only with the outward meaning of scripture have largely missed the point. Even interpreters outside Shiism who seek hidden meanings have failed to grasp what is essential about the A'raf. He therefore follows the Imam's words one phrase at a time, looking for an interpretation rooted in the Imams' own teaching.308 The name A'raf comes from the Arabic root 'rf, associated with knowing and recognising. Once we understand that connection, we can follow the three steps in the Imam's answer.

1. At the first level, the Imam says: “It is we [the Twelve Imams] who stand upon the A'raf.” This means that they stand at the summit of knowledge (ma'rifat), its highest point. The height is spiritual, not a location somewhere in physical space.

2. At the second level, something remarkable happens. The Imam no longer says simply that the Imams stand upon the A'raf; he says that they are the A'raf itself. In other words, all human knowledge of God passes through knowing them. They are not merely people who know, whose knowledge stands at the summit of all knowledge. They are also what makes this knowledge possible. They are the very reality reached by the highest knowledge—its object as well as its source.

Here a person's name, or the quality that defines that person, is used to name the thing itself: in this case, knowledge, of which the Imams are the source. At the first level of the answer, A'raf refers to knowledge or direct spiritual understanding (ma'rifat). “We stand at the summit of the A'raf” means: we stand at the highest point of that understanding.

At the second level, A'raf names the cause of this knowledge, the reality that makes it possible. “We are the A'raf” means: through us, human beings are able to know God. We are what human knowledge of God reaches, because we are the form in which God becomes manifest—a theophany.

To put it another way, knowledge of God (ma'rifat Allah) is possible only for the person who knows the Imams. We have already seen that the Imam is the form in which God reveals Himself. The Imam is the “Face” through which God is known, the form God necessarily takes in any human knowledge or experience of Him. Without that Face, God remains entirely hidden, the Absconditum. As the A'raf, the Imam is this supreme Face: the one through whom human knowledge of God becomes possible.

We recognise here the meaning of the Imam for Shiite spiritual life that we examined earlier. The Imams themselves teach the connection between two sayings. An Imam can say, “Whoever knows us knows their Lord.” And the spiritual teachers repeatedly say, “Whoever knows themselves—their own soul—knows their Lord.” The two sayings belong together because, in knowing one's deepest self, or soul (anima), one comes to know one's Imam. And whoever knows their Imam knows their Lord.

Thus the ideas of the Imam and the deepest Self meet: to know one's Imam is to know oneself; to know oneself is to know one's Imam—the Soul of one's soul—and therefore to know one's Lord.309

What Shiite spirituality offers through the persons of the Twelve Imams, through their “forms of light,” is access to this self-knowledge without which there can be no knowledge of God. It is an awareness of the personal relationship through which God is present as this particular God, appearing in this particular way, to the person who worships Him.

This explains the importance of dreams in which the Imams appear. A believer who receives such a vision discovers their most intimate secret: the Imam as the Soul of their soul, the hidden meaning of their own knowledge of God. Earlier we spoke about the human meaning of knowing God.310 Now the Imam also reveals the divine meaning of this human knowledge.

3. At the third level, the Imam goes further still: “We are the A'raf because, on the Day of Resurrection, God knows us as the Way.” Here A'raf refers to what is known in its own essential nature, not to something known incidentally or from the outside.

What does this essential knowledge mean? At the second level, the Imam was the knowledge through which a person knows God. At the third, he is the divine knowledge through which God knows a person.

The Imam says that God knows someone who knows the Imams as a person of Paradise.

The second level tells us that a believer's knowledge of the Imams is their knowledge of God. The third tells us that God's knowledge of the believer is the believer's knowledge of the Imams. By knowing the Imams, a person knows themselves as someone belonging to Paradise, and this is also God's knowledge of them. Conversely, the person who rejects the Imams has a sense of self that is itself their hell.

“No one enters the Fire except those who deny us and whom we deny.” That denial is also the way God knows the person who rejects the Imams. It is the one who denies who drives God out of their own paradise; that is what hell means here. At the point where knowing the Imam and knowing oneself become one, the outward image of the A'raf as a barrier reveals its full meaning: the Imam truly is the boundary separating Paradise from Hell.

This teaching offers the philosopher endless possibilities for reflection. The Imam is the knowledge a human being has of God, and for that very reason he is also the knowledge God has of a human being. The two statements place the Imam at the level of the first manifestation of God, at the very dawn of God's becoming knowable.

We have already witnessed the rising of this dawn in other texts (above, pp. 296–297). There, a particular divine will emerged on the horizon of a universal, primordial Will. That dawn made possible the appearance of a form (tajalli) in which God could become the object of love—His mahbubiya, or being loved.

In that earlier account, the emphasis on divine will went with a view of existence found in a Shaykhi master such as Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani. He refuses to include God's ineffable, indescribable Being within a single, unqualified unity of being (wahdat al-wujud). Here, with Mulla Sadra Shirazi, we encounter a thinker who accepts that unity. His account of reality begins instead with knowledge.

There is, first, an all-encompassing divine knowledge: perfect knowledge identical with the simple, undivided essence of God. It contains no multiplicity, because the divine Essence (dhat) is the source from which the existence of everything flows. When God knows Himself, He knows all things through the very act of knowing that is identical with His Essence. There is also God's knowledge of individual things. This can mean that the essences of things are present to Him as they exist concretely, or that their Ideas are made real in being “before” they exist in the concrete world.

Together these levels form an order of causes and effects. Mulla Sadra explains that its downward and upward movements mirror one another exactly. In the downward movement, angels act as causes that gradually bring creatures' potential existence into reality. In the upward movement, prophets, Imams and all God's Friends serve as causes and guides who awaken the potential angelic nature within human beings. They lift people beyond the merely animal level and bring their angelic possibilities into full reality, so that they become people of Paradise (ahl al-jinnat).

The same pattern applies to divine knowledge. In the order of creation, God knows the beings of this changing world through His knowledge of their angels—the intellectual and heavenly angels described in the philosophical system of Avicenna. That is why angels are called the “witnesses” (shuhada) of creation before God. In the order of the last things, God knows the faithfulness of believers through His knowledge of the prophets and God's Friends. They, in turn, are God's witnesses for humanity on the Day of Resurrection.

Through this idea of the witnesses, the Imam's words lead the philosopher to see the parallel between the role of angels in the origin and ordering of the world—the order of the mabda', or Beginning—and the role of the Imams in the return of souls to their source—the order of the ma'ad, or Return.

The second concerns salvation and what awaits us at the end of earthly life.311 Both the teaching about angels and the teaching about the Imams have their deepest foundation in divine knowledge. Both reach their highest expression in the idea of the Witness.

In that idea, a philosophy of presence and a spiritual experience of presence come together. Everything in prophetic philosophy points towards it. The Imam is the meeting point where the Witness, the one who beholds (shahid)—the Imam standing upon the A'raf—is also the one beheld (mashhud), the Witness who is himself present to contemplation: the A'raf itself. He bears witness to the God he contemplates, speaking for God before humanity.

Yet he is also the one human beings behold when God reveals Himself to them. He is the eye through which God looks towards humanity and cares for it, because he is also the eye through which humanity looks towards God and turns towards Him.

We shall see this theme develop in Ruzbihan's mysticism (Book Three below).

The Imams are both the eyes through which God looks upon this world and the eyes through which human beings contemplate the divine attributes, since God's Essence itself is beyond their reach. The Imam is thus at once the one who contemplates and the one contemplated (shahid–mashhud), beheld by God and by humanity. He keeps us from both extremes: denying any meaningful manifestation of God's attributes (ta'til), and making God resemble created beings (tashbih). My knowledge of the Imam is therefore also God's knowledge of me. This is why the Imam is the barrier that separates the people of Paradise from the people of Hell.

As Mulla Sadra puts it: “God's knowledge of the spiritual condition of these two groups passes through His knowledge of the Witnesses in their twofold role: bearing witness to the Paradise of some and the Hell of others. This is the deeper understanding (tahqiq) of the prophets and Imams as God's Witnesses before humanity, and of the Qur'anic verse: ‘What will happen when We bring forth a witness from every community, and bring you forth as a witness against these people?’ (4:45).”

Now the full meaning of the Imam's three successive statements becomes clear. “We are the A'raf” means: in our very essence, we are those whom God knows (ma'rufun bi'l-dhat), those whom He contemplates (mashhudun li'llah), His direct witnesses in contemplation. We do not need intermediaries, because we ourselves serve as intermediaries for others. We are the highest stages of the Way (sirat) through which human beings must pass to reach the greatest possible closeness to God.312313

The A'raf thus emerges as the summit, the protective boundary, of the philosophy of prophecy and the Imams. That philosophy offers the gift of the highest wisdom. The Imam Ja'far explains this to a disciple while commenting on a Qur'anic verse (2:272): “Whoever has been given wisdom has received an immense good” (compare Proverbs 3:13 and following). “This wisdom (hikmat),” he says, “is spiritual awareness, the direct knowledge (ma'rifat) of the Imam.”314

Several ideas prepare us to understand what this wisdom means. The most important is that of the Hojjat, to which Sadra Shirazi returns repeatedly in his commentary on the Imams' sayings. There are two kinds of Hojjat: two kinds of witness, guide and guarantor. The first is the outer guide: the prophet who brings God's message to humanity, and, after the Prophet, the Imams for those who need a guide they can see.

But Twelver Shiism, living under the guidance of the Hidden Imam, naturally leads us towards the second: the invisible inner guide, the Imam within (Hojjat batina, Imam dakhili).

This inner guide is a radiant, holy light. It comes from the divine Throne and rises at the eastern horizon of the soul, at its highest point. It illuminates the “senses of the heart,” through which the prophetic message can be heard in its hidden meaning: the walayat of the Imams. It is a secret, inward prophecy (nobowwat batiniya) concerned with unseen worlds and the hidden life of the soul.315

The idea of an inner guide does not make the teachings about prophecy or the Imams unnecessary. Quite the opposite: it brings them to fulfilment. This is where the teaching of the Imams is meant to lead. The inner guide reached through this process protects the mystic from the intoxication of a spiritual pride that would make them imagine themselves godlike.

Before entering the Way, the mystic is still the person addressed by the Fifth Imam's warning: “You know even less about the roads of Heaven than you do about the roads of Earth.” The Shiite believer's “search for the Imam” is therefore not a search for someone familiar with the physical spaces of the astronomical sky. It concerns another world entirely, one that “corresponds to inward, invisible forms, which cannot be perceived by our physical senses, but only by our spiritual senses.”315316

So when the Imam speaks of wisdom, with its successive levels expressed as faith in God, His angels, His revealed books, His messengers and the Resurrection, Sadra reminds us that wisdom is twofold, just as the Hojjat or guide is twofold. There is revealed wisdom (hikmat makshufa) and veiled wisdom (hikmat mastura). Revealed wisdom is embodied in the visible persons of the sages: they are wisdom made present as living human beings.

Whoever sees one of them with the “eyes of the heart,” which reveal the sage's true nature, sees wisdom in personal form. For ordinary people, this is God's gift of wisdom, the “immense good” spoken of in the sacred text: the visible person of the Imam, who is wisdom itself (nafs al-hikmat).

Veiled wisdom, by contrast, is the wisdom within the hearts of God's Friends (awliya), the prophets and the Imams—the hukama ilahiyun, sages of God, or “theosophers” in the full original sense of lovers of divine wisdom. The Imams' teaching about the A'raf helps us understand why each Imam is a sage from one point of view, and wisdom itself from another.317

A deep joy runs through Mulla Sadra's reflections at this point.318 He reaches the place where Shiite spirituality meets his own philosophy of being and knowledge, shaped by the tradition of illumination. Both come together in the spiritual awareness of the Shiite philosopher devoted to that tradition.

The union of the sage and wisdom, he tells us, is like what happens in the act of understanding: the person who understands ('aqil) and the intelligence actually at work ('aql) become one.319 This expresses the distinctive character of this form of Shiite spirituality, which we have already encountered: philosophical thought and spiritual fulfilment cannot be separated from one another. Each depends on the other (see also Book Two, on Suhrawardi, and Book Five).

The twofold Hojjat and the twofold wisdom are really two ways of describing the same thing. In the Imam, there is a wisdom made visible and a wisdom that remains hidden (makhfiya). The visible wisdom is the Imam's person, present before our eyes. The hidden wisdom is an inward light of spirit and understanding (nur batini 'aqli). This light is the Imam's spiritual life. Through it, the person he guides is able to see the world beyond death, together with the heavenly beings and forms within it. That illumination is the gift of wisdom.

When someone truly understands, the act of intelligence is not something added to them from outside. Their understanding is part of what they are at that moment. In the same way, the sage—the Imam—is wisdom itself. To know this sage through direct spiritual knowledge (ma'rifat) is to know the wisdom that he embodies.

But in that very act of knowing, the Imam's wisdom becomes the wisdom of the believer who follows him, just as intelligence becomes the living activity of the person who understands.

The believer then discovers that two sayings express the same truth from opposite sides: “Whoever knows their Imam knows their Lord,” and “Whoever knows themselves knows their Lord”—which here also means knowing their Imam. To be fully aware of one's Imam, one's personal and invisible inner guide, is to become someone in whom the wisdom embodied by the Imam has come to life. Such a person possesses the “inner Witness,” who is precisely the Imam himself as the Imam within (Imam dakhili), the “divine Face” that remains when everything else passes away.

We said earlier that the Imam is the form in which God appears. In the same way, the faithful believer becomes the form in which the Imam appears. This is the heart of spirituality centred on the Imams: the outer Imam leads us to the inner Imam, and knowing the Imam leads us to knowledge of ourselves.

We can now reflect on what each of the Shiite Imams, and all twelve together in their spiritual fullness, mean for Shiite life. The teaching of the A'raf reaches its highest point in a philosophy of the Witness (shahid) and of the presence experienced through witnessing (shuhud).

The Imam becomes, in a sense, the active awareness of the believer. This is how the silsilat al-irfan, the succession of spiritual knowledge, continues in the world. It is unknown to most people: the hidden line of those who play their part in the sacred history of the age of walayat, and who are truly “alive” in the fullest sense of that word.320

This “community of the living” extends towards a shared spiritual faith that reaches across the whole history of prophecy. Its foundation is the same understanding of the inner meaning of religion. Earlier (§ 1), the idea of universal walayat, of which the Imam is the Seal, already brought us to this point. All the prophets of earlier ages, together with their believers, belong to the same eternal prophetic religion. Together they form a single spiritual body (corpus mysticum), the “Temple of Light” of the Imamate, as Ismaili writers call it.

Mulla Sadra writes: “This has been true in every age, and it will remain true in the future. All the sages of God ('ulama rabbaniyun, the theosophoi), all the prophets and all their Imams, together belong to one religion (din wahid) and one school (madhhab wahid). Or, better still, they form something like one complete spiritual person (shakhs wahid kulli 'aqli). In the same way, the believers who follow them, wherever and whenever they live, are like a single Soul. The school of every Imam is also the school of every other Imam, and at the same time the school of all the prophets and God's Friends.”321

These words of Mulla Sadra could stand as the declaration of faith of Shiite inner spirituality: faith in an eternal Ecclesia spiritualis, a community joined together in spirit.

4. The Imam as God's Witness and the Witness of Contemplation

The texts we have examined and discussed have, I believe, told us what matters most. Yet Mulla Sadra's final pages on Kolayni's Kafi—the pages he still had time to write before his death—add a number of illuminating refinements.

Sadly, they break off in full flight, with the same poignant abruptness as Bach's unfinished Art of Fugue. They end just as we are about to discover the Shiite thinker's deepest meditation on one of the high points of the Imams' own teaching about the Imam, a text he was explaining line by line. Here I can offer only a brief outline and paraphrase of these extraordinarily dense final pages.

The whole commentary on the Twelve Imams as the “Witnesses of God” (shohadâ' Allah)322323324 is guided by a single insight: the degree to which something exists—its very act of being (wojûd)—depends on, and is proportional to, its degree of presence (hodûr, hozûr). And presence is essential to what it means to be a witness (shâhid). Here Mulla Sadra's entire metaphysics of being rests upon the understanding of the Imam and is bound to its central theme.

Sadra begins with an extended discussion of two words, shâhid and shahîd (distinguished in our transliteration by the position of the circumflex). Shâhid, the one who witnesses, is the active form of shohûd—being present to something, witnessing it directly, seeing it with one's own eyes—and is related to moshâhadat, vision or contemplation. In mystical language, this means the visionary perception of worlds that the mystic beholds but that remain invisible to others.

All of this presupposes that one being can be present to another. The shâhid, the witness who contemplates something, is the one to whom, and within whom, the form or image of that thing is present. The shahîd, by contrast, is the Witnessing One—the “martyr” in the word's original sense of someone who bears witness. It is the faculty or power (qowwat) through which the witness's vision (shohûd) and presence (hodûr) become possible.

What, then, makes it possible for one being to be present to another—the very condition of witnessing? Many things, by their fundamental nature, cannot receive the presence of another thing or themselves become present to it. This is true of all material things situated in the perceptible space of our darkened world. None can be inwardly present to another, or present for another; and no other thing can be present in or for it.

We cannot say, for example, that the Earth, as a physical mass, exists as a “presence” for the starry heavens, or the reverse;325 nor that the element air is present to the element water, or the reverse. That is why this world is the dwelling place of unconsciousness and death.

Everything is immersed in darkness and unconsciousness to the degree that it belongs to this world and is remote from the world of Light, Knowledge, and Life—the world beyond, the dwelling place of the Living. Conversely, consciousness and presence grow in proportion to the light received from the Malakut, the spiritual world.326

When Mulla Sadra says that the degree of existence is proportional to the degree of presence, his insight comes close to one expressed in language familiar today.

But we must be careful. For Sadra and the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, this is a way of being in the present world fundamentally different from an existence irretrievably cast into it, abandoned to its “being-toward-death.” What the relation between existence and presence means for Sadra is this: the more intense one's presence becomes, the more one is present to other worlds—and the more one escapes the conditions of unconsciousness, death, and absence.

The more fully a human life becomes Presence, the more that person witnesses other worlds. Such a life becomes less a being-toward-death and more a being-toward-what-lies-beyond-death. A metaphysics of Presence thus unfolds into a metaphysics of vision, of the presence through which one witnesses (shohûd). This has already been announced in the teaching about the Imam and is realized as that teaching becomes an inner experience (above, § 3).327

Presence must therefore have degrees of intensity. These are marked by stages of becoming immaterial (tajarrod) and correspond to different levels of perception and awareness: sensory perception, imaginative perception, and intellectual understanding. At every level, the principle of unity described earlier applies.

What we perceive through the senses, imagine, or understand is not the external material thing itself, but its form—sensory, imaginal, or intellectual—as it is present within us. An understood form is such a form only in relation to someone who understands it. The act of understanding is not something added to the person who understands: it is that person in the very act of understanding. The same holds for sensory and imaginal forms.

Thus, the form understood (ma'qûla) itself becomes, precisely as understood, an understanding form, an active form. The same is true of sensory and imaginal forms.328 Seen in this light, knowing proves to be the very source of spiritual life. This is the spiritual meaning of “oriental presence” (hozûr ishrâqî): presence is called oriental because it rises at the East of the soul, when the soul itself becomes the East, the dawning place, of its own knowing.329

Here too lies the whole metaphysics of Witness and Witnessing. My spiritual awareness (ma'rifat) of the Imam brings about the Imam's presence within me. The Imam then becomes the “inner Imam,” the Witnessing One, the active consciousness present within me (shahîd). This is why we can say that every prophet, and every Imam after him, serves as the very faculty of knowing in each of his followers.

For the follower, precisely as a follower, can have neither knowledge ('ilm) nor testimony (shahâdat)—can neither be “present to” nor have something “present within”—except through the knowledge and testimony of the Imam.330 He becomes, as we said earlier, “the eye through which he sees.”

Let us draw the threads together. The Imam is God's Witness (shâhid).

But what does he witness? In discussing the A'râf, we encountered this declaration by an Imam: “We are what God knows; we are the essential object of divine knowledge.” The Imam as shâhid, the one who contemplates, is at the same time the mashhûd, the one contemplated: the object of God's contemplation and therefore the form and content of divine knowledge—the form in which that knowledge becomes known to us as human beings.

And if the Imam is the Witness of God for his follower, the form through which that follower knows God, then the Imam must at the same time be the one whom the follower contemplates, his mashhûd. He is Witness and Witnessed, Contemplator and Contemplated (shâhid-mashhûd): the Witness whom one contemplates, the Witness of contemplation.

In contemplating this Witness, the follower contemplates the very one whom God contemplates—the object of divine knowledge and contemplation—which the follower can contemplate nowhere except in this Witness. The act of contemplation makes the Witness present within the follower. This mystery of shared presence, of two beings present to one another, is what we mean by the Imam as the inner Witness (Hojjat bâtina). What the follower beholds and attests is what this Witness himself beholds and attests.

Indeed, the follower can see and contemplate it only by contemplating the Witness, because the Witness is necessarily the form in which the follower can know the God to whom the Witness bears testimony. Such knowledge means that the Witness is present within the follower; at the same time, it means that the follower is present to the Witness. And to be present to this Witness is already to be present to the One to whom he bears witness.

As we have said, the follower's knowledge of this Witness is therefore, in that very act, God's knowledge of the follower: God knows the follower in the one who bears witness to that follower before Him. The Imam is the Witness whom God beholds, through whom God is beheld, and through whom God beholds. It is through this inner Imam, the “Imam of one's own being,” that God knows the follower. “We are the essential object of divine knowledge,” said the Imam.

What God knows in this Witness is therefore every person to whom that Witness is present and who is present to him. We have already seen Mulla Sadra draw a fundamental parallel. Just as God knows the beings brought forth in the creation of the cosmos through their Angels, so He knows those making their Return to Him through the Imams and the Awliyâ, the friends of God.

Since the Imam is the essential object of divine knowledge, to know the Imam is, in that very act, to know God's knowledge of His follower. Once again we return to the saying we have repeated so often, because its meaning can never be exhausted: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”

To know oneself—to know the Soul of one's soul—is to know one's Imam. And the Imam is precisely the object of divine knowledge: what God knows of the human being and within the human being. The follower's presence to God and God's answering presence to the follower—this is the Imam, the mutual presence established without either ta'tîl (denying God's attributes) or tashbîh (making God resemble His creatures).

The ishrâqî or “oriental” metaphysics of illumination thus reaches its summit in a metaphysics of the Imamate. At its heart stands a Shiite spiritual life centered on the Imam: God present to the Imam who is present to the human being; God present to the human being who is present to the Imam; the Imam present to the human being who is present to himself.

Through a similar deepening of spiritual understanding, we shall see Semnani use his interpretation of sacred texts to discover the “prophets of your being” (below, Book IV, Chapter IV). For the Sufi master Ruzbihan of Shiraz, every beautiful face—because its beauty testifies that its Creator is present to that beauty—becomes the shâhid-mashhûd, the Contemplator-Contemplated, the Witness of contemplation (below, Book III).

But we may ask whether this disclosure of the divine “Face” in a human face would have been possible, even in Sufism outside Shiism, without the mediation of Shiite teaching about the Imam: without the revelation of God's “Face” in the heavenly Anthropos, the luminous Forms of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.

This mediation is indeed proclaimed in the Quranic verse: “We have made you a mediating community” (2:137). Imam Ja'far explains this verse at length to a disciple.331332 The community occupying this middle or mediating position is not the Arabs, as some interpretations concerned only with the outward meaning would have it.

No: it is the Imams. They mediate between two acts of testimony: they are witnesses for humanity, while the Prophet is a witness for them. As their initiator, the Prophet acts as their active faculty of knowledge and vision, just as each Imam does for his follower.333334

We now come to the last description of the Imams that Mulla Sadra had time to examine before leaving this world. Just as the sage is also wisdom, and the one who contemplates is also the one contemplated, so the Keeper of the treasure of divine knowledge is the Treasure itself.

A disciple relates: “I heard Imam Ja'far declare: We are the guardians of the res divina (amr ilâhî, the divine affair), the Keepers of the treasure of divine knowledge, the Watchers over the secret of divine Revelation.” When the Imam says “we are the guardians,” he uses the word hâfiz.

Philosophers, meanwhile, give this name to the “faculty that preserves” (qowwat hâfiza) the forms of knowledge—the faculty that serves as their storehouse or treasure. They say that imagination is the treasury preserving the forms of sensory perception, while the Active Intelligence is the treasury of things understood by the intellect.

From here Mulla Sadra's meditation takes flight, but we cannot follow it to its destination: that destination would have appeared in the unfinished portion of his commentary. Even so, we can clearly discern the summit toward which his understanding of the Imam was leading.

On the one hand, the Treasures of divine knowledge can only be intellectual Essences, beings of light, free from any mixture with material substance and fully actual in their knowledge and understanding. They cannot, therefore, be forms impressed upon bodies, or even souls, since a soul still possesses only the potential for perfect intellectual understanding.

Mulla Sadra writes: “It is therefore established that there exist spiritual beings, intellectual Essences, in whom all existing things are fully actual in a spiritual and intellectual way. Through them souls are brought to perfection and become beings who understand in actuality, having formerly been receptive beings capable of understanding only in potential. These spiritual beings stand between God and humanity as intermediaries through whom spiritual blessings and influences are continually bestowed and descend.

“They are the Perfect Divine Words (Kalimât tammât), which have neither a beginning nor any possibility of passing away. They are known by many different names, depending on the many different ways of looking at them: the Words of God (Kalimât Allah), the World of the Divine Command ('âlam al-Amr), the Keys to the Divine Mystery (Mafâtîh al-ghayb). They are the Witnesses of God and of His existence. ‘There is nothing whose treasuries are not with Us’ (2:21).”335

To call these “Perfect Words”—these Intelligences or beings of pure light—the Keepers of the treasure is also to say that they are the Treasures of divine knowledge. That is the identity expressed in the Imam's words.

From two different points of view, they are at once Keepers and Treasures. Their difference and their identity are the same, Mulla Sadra observes, as in the cases we have already considered: the person who understands and the act of understanding; the sage and wisdom. “This is true of every attribute of an essence that exists only through the existence of the essence to which it belongs.”

On the other hand—and this is where the highest point of his teaching about the Imam was coming into view—the hadith he is explaining gives the Imams themselves the title “Treasures and Keepers of the treasure of divine knowledge.” Everything just said about the cherubic Intelligences as “Perfect Words” must therefore apply, in one way or another, to the Imams as well.

Mulla Sadra is preparing to take a decisive step: “Now, to show that the persons of the Imams are the Treasures of God's knowledge—that is, that by being what God knows, in and through their act of knowing Him, they are both the Treasures and their Keepers—requires two higher sources, or rather, two sublime oceans from the ocean of knowledge disclosed in mystical divination ...”336 And here the flight is broken off. The sentence was never finished.

Yet we can glimpse the metaphysical summit toward which Mulla Sadra's understanding of the Imam was moving. Other Shiite philosophers of divine wisdom lived long enough to approach it and to say what can be said of it by following, step by step, the Imams' own allusions. Everything in the foregoing pages has sought to draw on their teaching.

Indeed, the Imams' own words about the A'râf already help us understand how what is said of the “Perfect Words” applies to the Imams too.

Our sketch of some essential features of Shiism can thus end, for the time being, where it began. All that has been said in these pages, compared with the great works of Shiite spiritual philosophy, is no more than a drop in the ocean. I have referred several times to a small private study circle in Tehran.

To bring this part of the book to a close, I want to recall one more evening there, a memorable evening in the autumn of 1964. Our discussion was devoted to the recurring theme of Shiite theology, the theme that has guided us throughout the preceding chapters: Tawhîd, the affirmation of God's oneness, and the Imam. How can Tawhîd be realized in its full truth—escaping the twin dangers of ta'tîl and tashbîh—except through the existence of the Imam?

At the end of the evening, we listened as the venerable Shaykh M. H. T., whose knowledge of Mulla Sadra's philosophy was exceptionally deep, brought his meditation aloud to something like a conclusion: “All the Names and Attributes we give to God—or rather, that God gives to Himself in revealing Himself to us—are made possible only by the figure of the eternal Imam, who gathers them all into himself.

“At the height of our spiritual states, these Names and Attributes may be absorbed into the inner human being. That person is no longer himself: the Imam becomes that person.

“But God in Himself remains unknowable and beyond our reach. The Imam is the living, eternal reality, a hidden immaterial splendor, our immaterial bond with the immaterial. He is that Face of God of which the Quranic verses (55:26–27) declare: Everything on earth is passing away, but the Face of your Lord endures, surrounded by splendor.”

To conclude, our shaykh recalled the famous final episode of the birds' pilgrimage in the great mystical epic by Farid al-Din Attar, Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds, twelfth century), one of the masterpieces of Persian mystical poetry. Thousands of birds set out as pilgrims. For years upon years they travel, crossing mountain heights and plunging into abysses.

Almost all are lost in the dramatic trials along the way. Only a few—thirty birds in all—reach the sublime goal and find themselves before the mysterious bird called Sîmorgh, symbol of the distant divinity. Its name goes back to the Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrian Persia, and it reappears in the heroic and mystical epics of medieval Persia (below, Book II).

In Persian, Attar's mystical genius brings a delicate play on words into its name: Sîmorgh can be read as sî morgh, “thirty birds.” And so, at the end of their long and painful quest, Sîmorgh becomes the mirror that reveals to the thirty survivors the mystery of their own being. When they look toward Sîmorgh, it is Sîmorgh they see.

When they contemplate themselves, what they see is again sî morgh, thirty birds. And when they look both ways at once, Sîmorgh and sî morgh are one and the same reality. There are, in a sense, two Sîmorghs, and yet Sîmorgh is one. Identity within difference; difference within identity.337 Meister Eckhart, for his part, said: “The gaze by which I know Him is the very gaze by which He knows me.”

When we reached the end of Attar's famous verses, I asked the shaykh, “That is the Imam, is it not?” “Certainly, that is it. And if there were no Imam, if this were not the Imam, nothing would remain but to sink into mystical intoxication, expressed in the famous cry of the Sufi al-Hallaj: Anâ'l-Haqq! ‘I am God!’ ...”

We have already seen how the experience of walâyat, the bond of spiritual love and guidance, makes Shiism, in its essence, a religion of love. Perhaps we can now sense again how the Imam keeps the mystic from losing his balance in an ecstasy whose paradoxical cry retains, despite every later recantation, a Luciferian echo.

What the mystic can say is what the believer says in the Gnostic Acts of Peter: Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui—“I saw Him as I was able to grasp Him.” He showed Himself to me in the form my own being had the capacity to receive.338 Nothing more and nothing less.

Yet this very correspondence, the immense grace of it, is precisely what the Shiite vision of the Imam means.

We can now understand why Shiite spirituality does not experience the gulf that has troubled so many speculative Christian mystics: the gulf between the idea of the eternal Christ and the historical reality of Christ, with the divinity's “self-emptying” (exinanitio)—extending even to the cry that “God is dead.” That same evening our shaykh said: “Glory be to God!

“In our Shiite Islam, the Imams have reflected the eternal Imam. They are his mirrors, his mazâhir, the forms in which he is revealed. Their task is not to awaken us to consciousness of this world. Their walâyat is not an institution belonging to this world. They are our spiritual bond with the spiritual universes. They open the way for us to ascend, so that the veils may fall—the very veils they themselves have deliberately kept in place, lest the weak misunderstand what is meant by their divine qualification.”

We shall need to remember all these teachings in the final book of this work, devoted to the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Some of our Shiite authors have recognized in him the Saoshyant, the saving hero of Zoroastrian Iran; others have recognized the Paraclete foretold in the Gospel of John.

Henry Corbin

Within Iranian Islam

Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects

★

Twelver Shiism

Within the Islamic community, the Iranian world has, from the beginning, formed a distinct whole. Its character and vocation can only be understood if we regard Iran's spiritual universe as a unity extending across the centuries before and after Islam. Islamic Iran has been, more than anywhere else, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears and its practical consequences—not primarily in the social world, but in the concrete whole that a human being nourishes with his own substance beyond the limits of this life: his spiritual world.

The great work Henry Corbin presents here, in four volumes comprising seven books, is the result of more than twenty years of research carried out in Iran itself. His method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school. He seeks to encounter religious experience by allowing its object to reveal itself as it reveals itself to those who experience it.

The phenomenologist must therefore become the spiritual guest of those to whom that reality appears, and share with them the responsibility of receiving it. Historical considerations will consequently remain within the world of the religious object itself, rather than imposing an alien category from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise.

The first volume (Book I) sets out several essential aspects of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which was firmly established in Iran from early times and became the official religion in the sixteenth century. The inquiry begins with what the author has proposed to call “the phenomenon of the Revealed Book,” as it appears to those whom the Quran calls Ahl al-Kitâb, the “People of the Book,” embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

The second volume (Book II), published at the same time, examines Suhrawardi and the Platonists of Persia.

In preparation: Volume III: The Faithful of Love (Book III); Shiism and Sufism (Book IV); The School of Isfahan (Book V). Volume IV: The Shaykhi School (Book VI); The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry (Book VII); general index.

Since we devoted two years of lectures to the teachings about the Imams in Kolaynî's collection and to Mollâ Sadrâ's unfinished commentary on it, and since we hope to publish at least a partial translation elsewhere, we refer readers here to the summaries in the Annuaire 1962–1963 of the Religious Sciences Section of the École des Hautes Études, pp. 69 ff., and Annuaire 1963–1964, pp. 73 ff. ↩

  25. Mohammad ibn 'Alî ibn Abî Jomhûr Ahsâ'î was one of the great Imami thinkers of the ninth–tenth Islamic centuries (d. after 901/1496). For his statement about the essence of Shiism, see his major work Kitâb al-Mojlî, Tehran, 1324, p. 480. The same teaching can be found in Haydar Âmolî a century earlier, and our authors invariably appeal to statements by the Imams themselves in its support. We must stress from the outset that, in a Shiite context, we consistently use the term walâyat, not wilâyat, the word commonly used in Sufism. In Western writing these terms are often confused and inadequately translated as “sainthood.” Walâyat describes the Imams as God's Friends, Beloved Ones, or those brought close to God (walî Allâh; plural Awliyâ' Allâh). One can immediately see why the mystery of this divine election and sanctification lies at the very heart of the prophetic mission (nobowwat): every prophet (nabî) is a walî, but not every walî is entrusted with prophecy. The fundamental meaning of walâyat is “friendship” (Persian dûstî), and the word is frequently paired with mahabba (love, devoted affection). It also names the love and devotion Shiites bear toward their twelve Imams. For the believer, walâyat toward the Imam is a participation in the Imam's eternal walâyat. In the metaphysical framework of the teaching about the Imams, walâyat has a cosmic meaning and function, revealing itself on different levels of the universe. Wilâyat, in the usual Sufi sense, refers essentially to the mystic's subjective spiritual states. To trace the move from walâyat to wilâyat, and to ask whether one can speak of wilâyat while remaining silent about walâyat, is to raise the whole question of the relationship between Shiism and non-Shiite Sufism. That question would require a book of its own (see vol. III, Book IV below). In any event, the question of prophecy raised here and throughout this book must be understood in terms of nobowwat and walâyat: walâyat is “the esoteric (bâtin), inward reality of prophecy.” ↩

  27. One famous hadîth cited by our authors tells of the Prophet's vision in a dream: he saw a group of men from his community storming his minbar (the pulpit), leaping up it like monkeys and forcing everyone else to retreat. After this dream, the Prophet was never seen to smile again. These men are the “accursed tree” mentioned in Qur'an 17:62. For our authors, there is no doubt that the accursed tree refers to the Umayyads. In his great commentary on Kolaynî (Sharh al-Osûl min al-Kâfî, lithographic folio edition, Tehran, n.d., p. 462), Mollâ Sadrâ sets this theme within a long discussion of the concealment of the Imamate until the end of the present aeon. The twelve Imams do not form a worldly “dynasty.” Their succession has an essentially eschatological dimension: the Twelfth Imam is both already here and not yet here. In the Shiite understanding, supreme “authority” belongs to the invisible—to the world's invisible Imam. ↩

Ivanow, pp. 39–40 of the Persian text. Melchizedek's place in Ismaili Shiite gnosis deserves an extensive study. Qotboddîn Ashkevârî, a student of Mîr Dâmâd, identifies the third of the Zoroastrian Saoshyants, or Saviours, with the Twelfth Imam. It is therefore striking that Melchizedek is explicitly given the name of the first of the three Saoshyants. In the Haft Bâb, p. 41, line 1, the editor's question mark should be removed. The Persian spelling is perfectly correct and should be read Oslâdar: Avestan Ukhshyat-eretha → Pahlavi Hôshêtar → Persian Oshîdar. Raymond Panikkar's article “Eine Betrachtung über Melchisedek,” Kairos: Zeitschrift für Religionswissenschaft und Theologie, I (1959), pp. 5–17, repays reading. Panikkar writes from the standpoint of Catholic theology but senses that Melchizedek's priesthood embodies a universality capable of grounding a general theology of religions. Unfortunately, he seems unaware that Ismaili teachings on prophecy and divine wisdom had developed this idea centuries earlier. Nor does he seem to know that, within fifth-century Christianity itself, Melchizedek was, for the Melchizedekian Gnostics, the supreme figure in which the Logos appeared as divine—the Logos “apart from the flesh” (asarkos). This idea of divine manifestation provides a clue to the connection between the Melchizedek of Melchizedekian gnosis and that of Ismaili gnosis. ↩

  52. Over the centuries, Shiites had filled the Baqî' cemetery with splendid monuments of devotion—domes and shrines. During his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1956, the Iranian sovereign, accompanied by his whole entourage, paid a long visit to Baqî', stopping at the sites of tombs revered by Shiites. The Ziyârat brings together the attributes ascribed to the Imams in earlier hadîth. In Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's profound, densely argued commentary (Tabriz edition, 1276/1860; see below, vol. IV, Book V), it becomes a complete exposition of the divine wisdom and spirituality associated with the Imams. On this work, see our report in the Annuaire 1968–1969 of the Religious Sciences Section, pp. 151–154. The attributes by which the Imams appear to Shiite religious consciousness are, in themselves, the foundation for spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an. ↩

The article mentioned in this book's preface outlines the programme we have tried to pursue over the years in our teaching at the École des Hautes Études. Meanwhile our colleague Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî, professor at the University of Mashhad, is preparing an Anthologie des philosophes iraniens from the seventeenth century to the present, which is to include some fifty Shiite thinkers. ↩

  55. This letter of Imam Ja'far is quoted at length in Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr (above, p. 27, n. 4), pp. 12–14. The people criticized by the Imam are followers of Abû'l-Khattâb and, in the commentator's secondary application, the reformed Ismailis of Alamût. Certain hadîth make the strange assertion that “Prayer is a person,” “Fasting is a person,” and so on. Some followers have used these statements to claim that knowing this person releases them from actually observing religious practices. What lies behind the question, however, is a metaphysics of being that determines the relation between the name of an action (nomen actionis) and the name of its agent (nomen agentis). It concerns personal archetypes, not abstract essences. See our studies “Rituel sabéen et exégèse Ismaélienne du rituel” (Eranos-Jahrbuch XIX, pp. 229 ff.) and “Le Temps cyclique dans le mazdéisme et dans l'ismaélisme” (Eranos-Jahrbuch XX, pp. 208 ff.), which examine important passages from Nasîr Tûsî's Tasawworât. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, in his major commentary on the Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a (p. 378), resolves the issue admirably through the idea of walâyat: the faithful are created through a ray of the light that constitutes the being of their Imams. ↩

  59. This text appears in Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's great commentary on Ibn Bâbûyeh's (d. 381/991) Kitâb al-Tawhîd, Chapter II, thirty-fifth hadîth, third matlab, fol. 136b (Persian manuscript). A follower had come to speak with the Tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî, whom the Abbasid authorities were holding prisoner in the military camp of Samarra. The long record of their conversation amounts to a complete statement of Imami Shiite faith. Qâzî Sa'îd repeatedly returns to the Imamate as a purely spiritual kingship. This matters because impoverished philosophies of history too often try to “explain” a turn toward the spiritual realm and hopes of the end times as compensation for political frustration. Quite apart from entirely missing the point, such explanations overlook the fact that Qâzî Sa'îd was writing at the height of the Safavid period, when Shiism could hardly be said to suffer political frustration. Just as the Imams in the hadîth always discuss religious matters with their disciples, our thinkers have always known that the Imamate's meaning transcends all worldly politics: its essential dimension concerns the ultimate destiny of humanity. ↩

The threefold shahâdat, or declaration of faith, that makes an ordinary moslim (Muslim) into a mu'min (a faithful Shiite believer) therefore comprises affirmation of divine oneness (tawhîd), affirmation of the prophetic mission (nobowwat), and affirmation of the Imams' walâyat. See, among others, Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr, Moqaddamât I, Maqâlat II, pp. 23 ff. ↩

  61. There is a necessary connection between Shiite negative, or apophatic, theology (tanzîh) and its teaching about the Imams. This teaching assigns the Imams an “epiphanic function” (mazharîya): they make manifest not the divine Essence (dhât) itself, but God's action or “energy” (fe'l). See our paper “Imâmologie et philosophie” (Strasbourg conference, 1968; above, p. 65, n. 46). Negative theology is set out with complete rigour in a long sermon (khotba) delivered at Merv by the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ, and included in Ibn Bâbûyeh's Kitâb al-Tawhîd, Chapter II, second hadîth. Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's commentary on this text is fundamental. ↩

  62. In his Jâmi' al-asrâr (published in La Philosophie shî'ite, cited above, p. 56, n. 29), pp. 424–425, Haydar Âmolî recalls a moving exchange between the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sâdiq, and Abû Hanîfa, who had once been his pupil. Abû Hanîfa asks the Imam to come to Kufa and forbid people to insult the memory of the Prophet's Companions. “The Imam: They would not accept what I told them. — Abû Hanîfa: How could they refuse to accept it from you, when you are a descendant of God's Messenger? — The Imam: You yourself are the first to disregard me. You entered my house without my permission. You sat down without my asking you to. You speak without consulting me. I hear you argue by syllogisms? — Abû Hanîfa: Yes. — The Imam: Beware, O No'mân! The first to make a syllogism was Iblîs [Satan], when he was ordered to bow before Adam. ‘You created me from fire,’ he said, ‘whereas you created him [Adam] from clay.’” (The Imam then asks Abû Hanîfa a series of questions about religious law, fiqh, and Qur'anic commentary, tafsîr. Every time Abû Hanîfa answers, the Imam asks, “Why, then … ?” until Abû Hanîfa's position becomes impossible to defend.) Haydar Âmolî continues with magnificent vehemence: “This is how that man [Abû Hanîfa] spoke to the Pole of poles during his lifetime. Yet this is the very man whom the gnostic ['ârif, Dâwûd Qaysarî] counts among the most eminent Friends of God [Awliyâ]! I call God to witness: it is an enormous imposture. Truly, the hostility toward Shiites and toward certain other Sufis arises from absurdities of this kind. If I were not afraid of making this too long, I would explain some of their principles [osûl] and their derivative rulings [forû'], which would allow us to judge their position. But it is better to be silent.” ↩

Qâzî Sa'îd writes: “What comes to mind in trying to explain this mysterious account is that the best explanation is that the covenant [mîthâq] was received in several successive dwellings or levels, as the thing descended from the higher heavens to the lower heavens” (fol. 183). Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr draws the same teaching from a long hadîth of the Sixth Imam, which says, among other things: “Then He created the angels, revealed Himself to them, and received from them the covenant [mîthâq]: toward Himself with respect to divine lordship [robûbîyat], toward Mohammad with respect to prophecy [nobowwat], and toward 'Alî with respect to walâyat” (p. 29). There was therefore a covenant before the one required of Adam, ancestor of earthly humanity (Qur'an 7:171). We shall also have occasion to note that the angels ordered to bow before Adam (Qur'an 2:28) were only the lower angels (malâ'ika), not the four angels supporting the Throne ('arsh), nor those called al-'âlûna (“the Sublime Ones”). These latter are the Veils, the Lights of the Haqîqat mohamma-dîya (the eternal Muhammadan Reality) of which the Throne is composed; it was precisely before these Lights shining within Adam that the lower angels bowed. Nor did the command concern the Karûbîyûn (Cherubim), called the “angels of the Veils.” See Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, commentary on Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a (above, n. 48), p. 117. Like Ismaili teachings about Adam, Imami teachings recognize Adam on several levels: Adam al-akbar, the greater or cosmic Adam; Adam al-asghar, the lesser or little Adam; and so forth. ↩

  79. We must mention here one of Mollâ Sadrâ's most powerful passages, commenting on Qur'an 7:171 in his great commentary on Kolaynî, Sharh al-Osûl min al-Kâfî, Tehran, n.d., p. 321. Sadrâ speaks of the different levels on which souls become manifest: the world of Intelligences, the Malakût (spiritual kingdom), the mundus imaginalis or barzakh (intermediate imaginal world), and finally the physical world. He invokes Plato's teaching on the pre-existence of souls and finds it entirely consonant with Qur'an 7:171. Yet he believes that “pre-existence” alone is not enough: one must recognize that “there” souls have another mode of being and another way of appearing. The zohûr referred to in the verse, the “loins” that contained Adam's descendants, were precisely the Intelligences, the 'Aqûl, regarded as their “fathers” in their pre-existence on the level of the world of Intellect. We shall return to this interpretation in a book devoted specifically to Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. For now, let us simply note that Mollâ Sadrâ was not the first to find an agreement between Platonism and Shiism concerning the pre-existence of souls. Seven centuries earlier, Ibn Bâbûyeh had already taught pre-existence, in language with striking Platonic echoes, in his Kitâb al-I'tiqâdât (Book of Beliefs), a fundamental work of Shiite thought. ↩
